Title: Dodo Alive! - Resurrecting the Dodo with Robotics and AI
Description:
CONTENT:
Imagine that you are at the natural history museum. You wander around and take a look at different parts of the museum. Suddenly, a robot in the form of a long extinct species – the Dodo – moves towards you, starts talking to you and tells you about itself. This course covers constructing an autonomous, intelligent walking Dodo-like robot, which requires a combination of a wide spectrum of fields, including design, control, navigation, locomotion, perception and AI. During this laboratory course, the students will develop the necessary skills to design and construct various components of “Mecha-Dodo”, as part of a long-term, iterative project.
After some introductory classes, a practical phase will follow in which the students work closely together in interdisciplinary groups. The students will be divided into groups: 
1. Modelling and Control in Matlab/Simulink; 
2. BLDC motor control & electronics 
3. Mechanical CAD design, which encompasses the mechanical design of links and frames as well as 3D printing of the respective parts.
4. Learning based locomotion
All components will be integrated in a unified prototype. The long-term goal is to bring the famous Dodo back to life within a collective effort.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing this module, students will have gained broad knowledge in developing various mechatronic hardware and/or software components for real dynamically walking robotic platforms. They will also acquire problem solving and team-working skills. The students will have obtained practical and methodological skills to gain diverse competencies far beyond basic theory.

Title: Biochemie reaktiver Sauerstoffspezies und freier Radikale
Description:
CONTENT:
The main focus of the course is on biochemistry of free radicals and reactive oxygen species, their role in biochemistry and medicine and their control by antioxidants. In this regard antioxidant capacity of natural compounds is evaluated in vitro by several model systems, generating relevant oxidants thought to be important in vivo. These systems range from simple to more complex ones. Results are critically discussed and conclusions are drawn.

OBJECTIVES:
Be able to conduct measurement of antioxidant capacity of natural compounds

Title: A Practical Course in Numerical Methods for Engineers
Description:
CONTENT:
The module focuses on the practical implementation of numerical methods in
engineering sciences on selected exercises.

Based on the structure of the lecture Numerical Methods for Engineers,
exercises for following topics are treated:
(1) fundamentals of numerical methods and Python,
(2) interpolation and approximation,
(3) numerical differentiation and integration,
(4) numerical solution of ordinary differential equations,
(5) approximation of eigenvalues
(6) introduction to the finite element method,
(7) basic linear algebra,
(8) solution of linear equations: direct and iterative, and
(9) solution of nonlinear equations.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful participation in the course, students implemented the most important numerical algorithms with Matlab. With the knowledge gained from this they are able to select suitable algorithms and apply them autonomously to new problems.

Title: Abenteuer Kreativität. Methoden zur Ideenfindung und Problemlösung
Description:
CONTENT:
Wer seine Perspektive ändert, die Wahrnehmung erweitert und außergewöhnliche Zusammenhänge erlaubt, steht schon an der Startlinie zur Innovation. Wie das funktioniert, erfahren die Teilnehmenden in diesem Kurs, denn auf geniale Ideen zu kommen, ist erlernbar.

Unterschiedliche professionelle Techniken für einfallsreiche Problemlösungen werden theoretisch besprochen und als Einzel- und Gruppenaufgaben praktisch ausprobiert. Wir beschäftigen uns u. a. mit dem kreativen Prozess, dem individuell optimalen Setting sowie schöpferischen Denkblockaden. Wir wollen Kreativitätsmythen beseitigen und auch selber Kreativ werden! Kreativitätsspiele und Reflektionen helfen, Schritt für Schritt bewusst und mutig neue Wege zu gehen.
Dadurch wächst das Vertrauen in das eigene kreative Potential, das im Rahmen des Workshops zum Einsatz kommt.

Der Kurs vermittelt ein großes Repertoire an sofort anwendbaren Methoden, um Herausforderungen in Studium, Beruf und Alltag effektiv und zielorientiert zu meistern. Auch wer in Zukunft künstlerisch arbeiten will (oder das bereits tut), wird hierfür Impulse und Strategien bekommen!

OBJECTIVES:
Methoden und Techniken zur kreativen Arbeit für einzelne Personen, im Zweierteam und in der Gruppe anzuwenden und Ideen systematisch zu bewerten. Darüber hinaus lernen die TeilnehmerInnen ihr eigenes kreatives Potential kennen und reflektieren über ihr individuell optimales Setting für kreative Impulse.

Title: Academic Prompt Engineering and Management
Description:
CONTENT:
This module builds on the lecture and provides students from all parts of Technical University Munich with a solidification of knowledge concerning the use of generative AI. The course combines hands-on training in effective prompting techniques with an exploration of the legal, ethical, and societal responsibility issues surrounding the use of LLMs for text generation.
Through a two-day interactive seminar, students will deepen their knowledge by using practical skills in prompt engineering while developing a nuanced understanding of the broader implications of this rapidly evolving technology. Topics covered include:
• Application of techniques for prompt engineering in text generation using LLMs, including methods for measuring prompt effectiveness, advanced techniques, and addressing issues like hallucinations and ensuring accuracy.
• Implementation of responsible development and deployment of LLMs, focusing on selecting appropriate models, identifying and mitigating biases, ensuring transparency, and evaluating decision-making capacity.
• In-depth exploration of human-computer interaction with LLMs, including decision-making processes, the future of work in the context of LLM-powered text generation, and their applications in academic research.
• Considerations for designing and evaluating large language models, focusing on performance, fairness, transparency, and robustness.
• Application of requirements of intellectual property, copyright, fairness, diversity and other legal and ethical issues related to LLM-generated text.
• The transformative potential and rapid progress of LLMs, highlighting their ability to reshape interactions with technology and information across various domains.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module, students will be able to:

• Describe and apply techniques for prompt engineering in text generation using large language models (LLMs), including methods for measuring prompt effectiveness, advanced techniques, and strategies for addressing issues like hallucinations and ensuring accuracy.
• Explain the importance of responsible development and deployment of LLMs, and demonstrate the ability to select appropriate models, identify and mitigate biases, ensure transparency, and evaluate the decision-making capacity of LLMs.
• Analyze human-computer interaction with LLMs, including decision-making processes, and discuss the future of work in the context of LLM-powered text generation and their applications in academic research.
• Evaluate the design and performance of large language models, focusing on key considerations such as fairness, transparency, and robustness.
• Identify and discuss intellectual property, copyright, and other legal and ethical issues related to LLM-generated text.
• Assess the transformative potential and rapid progress of LLMs, and explain their ability to reshape interactions with technology and information across various domains.

Title: Academic Skills
Description:
CONTENT:
All actors must rehearse before they perform live: they do hundreds of exercises, rehearse the same lines again and again, think and replay their scenes in their minds. Academic skills are the rehearsal equivalent within academia: these skills must be learned, practiced, re-learned, practiced again, and repeated. In this course, you will read, understand, re-read, and hopefully understand some more, to such a degree that you will be able to clearly write what you have understood and include its source.
Together, we will learn and practice how to effectively read, understand, and synthesize key findings from STS academic literature, and write academic texts that reflect what we have learned and understood. We will also focus one course on literature reviews and one course on citations, research, reference styles, and bibliographic software databases. We will also discuss plagiarism and how to avoid it.
The course is designed to guide you through the most basic of academic skills – reading academic texts, understanding academic texts, and writing academic texts – so that you are well prepared for your academic assignments from the STS department, including the MA thesis for your final degree. 
At the end of the course, you will write an academic essay (ca. 2000-3000 words) based on an STS topic of your choice to show your newly gained or improved academic reading and writing skills. 
Whether you trained at the academic equivalent of Broadway or your local school’s after-school theater, there is something to be gained by exercising your skills together in this class. I look forward to seeing you.

OBJECTIVES:
In this course, students will learn how to effectively read, understand, and synthesize key findings from STS academic literature, and how to translate these academic understandings into written form, including a literature review or a scientific report.

Title: Active Distribution Grids
Description:
CONTENT:
Distribution grids are more important than ever due to the changing energy policies, as higher renewable shares at consumer level and advent of smart power electronic devices allowing bidirectional power flow. To understand the so-called Active Distribution Grid, one must first understand how they are traditionally planned, sized and operated. The lecture will then move to the concept of a Microgrid and how it extends the conventional paradigms. The individual component modelling and control philosophies for a microgrid will be studied. Tutorials will be provided for methods explained in these lectures. MATLAB projects will be part of some of these exercises to teach applicability of the concepts.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending the course, the student is able to:
- Describe planning and operational issues of a distribution grid.
- Be able to set up simple dynamical models of a microgrid using MATLAB.
- Perform load flow analysis,
- Design controllers for power electronic based microgrid operation,

Title: Active Learning
Description:
CONTENT:
How do young children learn so much about the world, so quickly? A rich body of research has demonstrated that that active engagement with the world is a crucial component of learning: As soon as they can sit or walk,
infants spontaneously grab and manipulate objects and approach or avoid people. As language develops, young children ask about the meaning of words, request the labels of objects, and inquire about the many new and puzzling phenomena they encounter. Active learning has been a topic of interest for philosophers, psychologists, cognitive and computer scientists.

What is active learning? Are children efficient active learners? Is there a developmental trajectory for active learning? Is active learning better than more passive forms of instruction? This seminar examines these questions across domains such as visual attention,  hysical reasoning, causal learning, and problem solving; readings will also address issues in explanation, exploration, and other related topics. The seminar involves a mix of lectures, group readings and discussions, as well as an active learning workshop designed to offer students a hands-on experience on how questions related to active learning are investigated experimentally, from identifying the research questions and hypotheses to interpreting and presenting the results obtained.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the module, students will be familiar with the theoretical background and the computational bases of information search and active learning theories and models, tackled from a develpomental perspective, and will have developed an understanding of how the results from active learning research can impact education.

Title: Adaptive and Array Signal Processing
Description:
CONTENT:
*  Motivation: Application areas of adaptive filters; Adaptive Equalization; Single channel (single-sensor) temporal processing; Multichannel (multi-sensor) spatial/spatio-temporal processing.
    * Mathematical Background: Gradients; Linear equations; Matrix decompositions (EVD and SVD); Subspaces of a matrix; Correlation and covariance matrices; Quadratic Optimization with Linear Constraints.
    * Linear Optimum Filtering (Wiener Filtering): Spatial Filtering: Minimum Variance Distortionless Response (MVDR) Beamforming and Generalized Sidelobe Canceller (GSC); Iterative solution of normal equations: Gradient descent and Least Mean Square (LMS) algorithm.
    * High Resolution Direction of Arrival (DoA) Estimation: Subspace Estimation; Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC); Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariance Techniques (ESPRIT);

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the module students are able to understand adaptive filtering both in the temporal domain and in the spatial domain. They can design simple signal processing systems for adaptive equalization and spatial filtering for communication applications.

Title: Additive Fertigung im Bauwesen - Materialien und Prozesse
Description:
CONTENT:
In der Vorlesung werden zunächst werkstoffübergreifend grundlegende Kenntnisse zu den verschiedenen additiven Fertigungsverfahren im Bauwesen vermittelt. Anschließend wird ein besonderer Fokus auf den 3D-Betondruck und die digitale Fertigung mit Lehm gelegt. Es werden die übergeordneten Themenbereiche 3D- Betondruck-Verfahren (Selective Cement Activation, Selective Paste Intrusion, Large Particle 3D Concrete Printing, Beton-Extrusion, Shotcrete 3D Printing, Injection 3D Concrete Printing), Werkstoffentwicklung (betontechnologische Zusammensetzung, Einsatz von Zusatzmitteln), Prüfung von additiv gefertigten Objekten (Rheologie, Mechanik), Qualitätskontrolle und Anwendung in der Praxis behandelt.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme an der Vorlesung sind die Studierenden in der Lage, eine einsatzorientierte Wahl additiver Fertigungsmethoden im Bauwesen zu treffen und die baustofftechnologischen, prozesstechnischen und robotischen Aspekte zu charakterisieren und zu beurteilen.
Die Studierenden können wichtige Material-Prozess-Interaktionen erkennen und anhand erlernter Zusammenhänge bewerten. Grundlegende Berechnungsmethoden zum Material- und Strukturverhalten werden erlernt und auf verschiedene Anwendungsfälle angewendet. Zudem liegen Kenntnisse über die Zusammensetzung von Materialien für die additive Fertigung vor, die mittels des erlernten Wissens weiterentwickelt und anschließend hergestellt werden können. Die Studierenden kennen zudem relevante Untersuchungsmethoden zur Bewertung eines additiven Fertigungsprozesses, können diese anwenden und die gewonnen Daten evaluieren.

Title: Additive Fertigung im Bauwesen 1
Description:
CONTENT:
This course introduces the principles, technologies, and design implications of Additive Manufacturing in Construction (AMC). 
It explores material systems and additive manufacturing processes specific to the construction context, with a focus on how these influence design thinking and fabrication strategies.  

You will gain foundational knowledge of various additive manufacturing techniques, including both established and emerging processes. 
The course addresses rheological and mechanical aspects of printable materials, strategies for reinforcement integration, and sustainability considerations, including the use of natural materials like clay and earth. 

In parallel, the course discusses how additive manufacturing transforms architectural design workflows. 
It introduces process-aware design principles, explores toolpath generation (planar and non-planar), and covers practical aspects of robotic implementation, including kinematics and path planning. 
Practical implementation scenarios—both on-site (e.g. mobile robotic systems, gantry setups) and off-site (e.g. prefabrication in controlled environments)—are discussed to evaluate the logistical, structural, and architectural implications of AMC deployment.
Case studies and application scenarios illustrate the relationship between design decisions and fabrication constraints in AMC.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending the course, you will be able to: 

- Classify, explain and select key AMC processes and material systems. 
- Understand, assess and characterise the aspects of building material technology, process technology and robotics. 
- Describe relevant test methods for evaluating additive manufacturing processes, apply them and evaluate the data obtained. 
- Understand the rheological and mechanical principles behind AMC. 
- Recognise and evaluate important material-process interactions. 
- Perform basic calculations for material and structural behaviour and apply them to various use cases 
- Assess the implications of different AMC setups for design and construction. 
- Understand slicing and toolpath strategies for both planar and non-planar workflows. 
- Understand the interaction between design goals, fabrication constraints, and robotic control in AMC.

Title: Additive Fertigung in der Gießereitechnik
Description:
CONTENT:
Folgende Inhalte werden im Modul behandelt:
•	Additive Fertigungstechnologien
•	Komplexität von Produkten
•	Formkonstruktion im Gießereiwesen
•	Modellabformung von FDM Bauteilen

•	Binderjetting-Verfahren

•	Montage von Gussformen
•	Gießen

Die Inhalte werden anhand folgende Vorgehensweisen vermittelt
•	Erstellung eines Demonstrators entlang der Gießprozesskette im Sandguss mittels oben genannter additiver Fertigungstechnologien unter Berücksichtigung rechnergestützten Methoden (CAD, Simulation)
•	Abgerundet wird das Praktikum mit einer Führung durch das Fraunhofer IGCV Gießereitechnikum, um den Studierenden einen Einblick in die praxisbezogene bzw. industrielle Gießereiforschung zu geben
•	Die Inhalte werden in Form von Gruppenarbeiten erarbeitet (Die Teilnehmerzahl ist auf 10 Personen begrenzt)

Nach der Teilnahme am der Modul sind die Studierenden in der Lage, ein Verfahren für die Erstellung von metallischen Bauteilen mit Additiven Verfahren anhand verschiedener Zielstellungen auszuwählen. Durch den erhaltenen Überblick über die mehrstufigen Technologien sind sie in der Lage die Vor- und Nachteile für die Qualitätsmerkmale von Bauteilen zu bewerten. Nach dem Praktikum können sie Datensätze für 3D-Druck erstellen und fertigungsgerecht manipulieren. Auf die Gießereitechnik bezogen verstehen sie die Funktion und Wirkung von Anschnitt und Gießsystem. Sie können dabei neben der Anwendung von Ent-wurfsregeln ebenso die Wirksamkeit der Konstruktion mit der Simulation überprüfen. Speziell für hoch-komplexe Formgebung können die Studierenden den Binder-Jetting-Prozess auf die Fragestellung über-tragen und dafür notwenigen Formkonstruktionen kreieren.

Title: Additive Fertigung mit Kunststoffen Vorlesung
Description:
CONTENT:
This lecture provides deepened knowledge of the basic principles of additive manufacturing with plastics. The processes 
-	Laser-Sintering
-	Material Extrusion 
-	Stereolithography
-	Binder Jetting  
will be analyzed towards their respective materials, the curing mechanisms and the resulting part properties. Each additive process will be discussed in detail, starting with the initial processing of the materials (Powder, Filament and photopolymers) and followed by the basic principles of the individual additive manufacturing technique, which includes the present physical mechanisms. Further, the dependence between process properties and part properties is discussed. The addressed materials of this lecture are not restricted to basic polymers, but also include composite materials. Specific examples from different industrial fields are used to deepen the basic understanding of the additive processes and to derive fundamental design criteria for additively manufactured parts.

OBJECTIVES:
Through participation in this course of study, students are able to comprehend the different processes of additive manufacturing with plastics. This includes differentiation of the fundamental mechanisms of the additive building process of each manufacturing technique. Based on the application the students are able to derive a suitable manufacturing technique with the respective material.

Title: Advanced Algorithms
Description:
CONTENT:
The module begins with a brief review of algorithm design and analysis techniques and computational complexity. The module then mainly focuses on techniques for dealing with intractability and decentralized computation systems, such  as approximation algorithms, parameterized algorithms, randomized algorithms, exact super-polynomial algorithms, online-algorithms and linear programming. Students also learn about associated complexity classes that allow them to show that no (significantly) faster algorithms can exist.

In addition, the module covers selected topics of advanced efficient algorithms and data structures that require a
 deeper level of understanding of algorithmic concepts.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the module, the students are able to analyze and
to assess the runtime and the memory requirements of
algorithms. Furthermore, they have a good understanding of
numerous fundamental algorithms and data structures. This
understanding enables them to design algorithms and data
structures for new algorithmic problems.

Title: Advanced Analysis of Variance Procedures
Description:
CONTENT:
This seminar deepens knowledge of advanced analysis of variance (ANOVA) procedures and their applications in empirical research. Topics include multifactorial ANOVA designs (fixed, random, and mixed effects), repeated measures ANOVA, MANOVA and MANCOVA, hierarchical and nested designs, as well as generalized linear models (GLM) and their relation to ANOVA. Special emphasis is placed on the assumptions underlying each method, strategies for dealing with violations (e.g., sphericity, homogeneity of variance), and robust alternatives. Further topics cover contrast analysis, planned comparisons, post-hoc procedures, effect size estimation, and statistical power analysis.

In addition to classical approaches, the seminar introduces students to AI-supported data analysis methods. This includes the use of machine learning algorithms for pattern detection, natural language processing for automated reporting, and AI-assisted statistical software to streamline model specification, computation, and interpretation.

Students will work with real and simulated datasets to practice both traditional and AI-augmented approaches. Statistical software (e.g., R, SPSS, or equivalent) and AI-based tools will be used for hands-on exercises and project work. The seminar combines theoretical input, guided practice, and independent application to provide a solid foundation for conducting advanced quantitative analyses.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of the seminar, students will be able to:

Explain and differentiate between advanced ANOVA procedures and their underlying assumptions.

Select appropriate analysis strategies for complex research designs in the social and behavioral sciences.

Apply advanced ANOVA techniques (e.g., repeated measures, MANOVA, mixed models) using statistical software.

Critically evaluate statistical results, assess model fit, and interpret findings in the context of empirical research.

Identify limitations of ANOVA approaches and discuss robust alternatives when assumptions are violated.

Utilize AI-assisted data analysis tools to enhance statistical modeling, automate reporting, and explore large datasets.

Independently design, compute, and present analyses of empirical datasets using both classical and AI-based methods.

The seminar equips students with methodological competences required for advanced research projects (e.g., master’s theses, empirical studies) and strengthens their ability to critically reflect on quantitative findings in an era of increasing AI integration.
Skills: ['Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)', 'Statistical Software', 'Multifactorial Designs', 'Generalized Linear Models (GLM)']

Title: Advanced Concepts of Programming Languages
Description:
CONTENT:
This is not a beginners programming course – Instead, this lecture focusses on the semantics of various programming language concepts, and their implementation from the point of view of a compiler engineer. Topics may include, among others:
- Relaxed Memory Models
- Wait-/Lock-free Programming
- Locks, Monitors & Condition Variables
- Transactional Memory
- Gotos, Co-Routines and Continuations
- Single/Multi-Dispatching
- (Multiple-) Inheritance
- Delegation and Prototype Based Programming
- Aspect Oriented Programming
- Meta programming

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of this module, students are familiar with an assortment of programming language constructs from popular programming languages. They understand the semantics of these constructs as well as the implementation consequences, that they inflict on the implementation as well as the runtime behavior of compiler and runtime system. They are able to analyze and compare different language based approaches, to discuss their relative merits and potential workarounds in case certain language features are missing. By means of this knowledge, they are able to extend existing compilers to handle the aforementioned constructs as well as able to re-encode concepts from one language by means of another language.

Title: Advanced Control - Lecture -
Description:
CONTENT:
1. State space models of linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamical systems
     - Mathematical modeling of lumped dynamical systems from physical laws 
     - Control tasks and controller structures
     - Equilibria and stability
     - Linearization
     - Stability criteria for linear systems

2. Design of linear state feedback controllers in a two-degrees-of-freedom structure
     - Eigenvalue placement
     - Controllability and controller canonical form
     - Flatness-based control
     - LQR optimal control

3. Design of linear state observers
     - Observability and observer canonical form
     - Duality between controller and observer design
     - Separation principle
     - Decoupling control and effect of zeros

4. Methods for disturbance rejection

5. Extended controller structures

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module the students are able to
- represent real-world dynamical systems in state space form, determine their equilibria and to obtain linear state space models by linearization.
- compute the solutions of linear state differential equations and analyze the dynamical system for stability, observability and controllability.
- understand the purpose and advantage of a two-degrees-of-freedom controller structure.
- design feedforward controllers that guarantee zero output error in nominal steady state.
- design state-feedback controllers using the pole placement method and as a Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR).
- design a Luenberger state-observer to reconstruct non-measurable states of the system.
- further modify the closed loop system by adding measures to cope with different disturbances. 
- have a basic knowledge about flatness-based feedforward control for linear systems.

Title: Advanced Earth System Modelling
Description:
CONTENT:
The contents of this seminar will provide examples of how scientists use Earth System Models (ESMs) to gain understanding about the Earth’s climate, and about major limitations of these models.

Topics comprise:

Content:
• Earth system components & their interactions; land-atmosphere feedbacks, component coupling
• General circulation: What would the Earth’s climate look like if the Earth rotated in the opposite direction?
• Global carbon cycle and vegetation in the climate system: Do forests cool the planet? What would happen without evapotranspiration on land?
• Zero-emission commitment in ESMs: What happens after humans stop greenhouse gas emissions?
• Numerical approaches, different discretization approaches, model grid structures
• Tipping Points and alternative stable states: What happens if we switch off the Sun? How does model complexity affect stability? Are ESMs too stable?
• Model intercomparison projects; the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project and its experimental design
• Uncertainties in ESMs, especially regarding structural and parameter uncertainty; climate model biases
• Machine learning approaches in ESMs, data-driven modelling and hybrid models
• ESMs as the basis of policy recommendations: Downscaling, Bias adjustment and impact modelling.

OBJECTIVES:
Students will be able to explain how Earth system models (ESMs) are applied, what kinds of experiments they can be used for, and how these lead to insight, what the most crucial limitations of ESMs are, and how they inform policy recommendations.

The seminar format will also entail that students learn to read and summarize scientific studies, and present them on a level and in a format that is tailored to the target audience (fellow students).

Description:
CONTENT:
This module gives an introduction to basic theoretical knowledge in scientific conceptualization of culture, the determinants of culture, cultural differences and difficulties as well as their overcoming. During the module, various scientific definitions of culture and different scientific approaches of cultural dimensions are outlined. By means of selected cultural characteristics and practical examples it is explained how to deal with different matters occurring when people with different cultural background interact. Additionally, different management styles in view of different cultures are declared. During the module, explanatory approaches to difficulties, which result from different cultural backgrounds in an international business environment are elaborated. Further approaches how to overcome these difficulties are outlined by means of practical examples in a global working environment and in international teams. 
In addition, basic theoretical knowledge in communication and different models of communication are provided. Furthermore, it is defined how to deal with different communication styles of different cultures and how to communicate adequately in an international context. For this purpose, selected cultural characteristics and practical examples are used. Within the framework of the course, students are asked to reflect, analyze and evaluate already experienced situations in view of the discussed theoretical models. Additionally, ethically relevant problem areas in international/intercultural businesses are outlined.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending this module students are able to apply basic scientific approaches to culture and cultural differences. On basis of appropriate knowledge about cultural theories and the determinants of culture, students are able to understand why countries are different concerning culture and development. The students are able to analyze cultural differences and difficulties in an intercultural business context, as well as to interpret and overcome them.
Additionally, students are aware of different communication styles in different cultures and know to apply this knowledge in intercultural communication situations. Furthermore, students will bear integrity, ethics and responsibility in mind when making management decisions in a multicultural business environment. Students are also able to reflect their experience abroad with scientific intercultural knowledge and develop an open-mindedness and sensitivity with respect to cultural differences.

Title: Advanced Power Electronics Systems - Design and Implementation of a DC-DC Converter
Description:
CONTENT:
This is a project-based course where the students will develop, build and test a power converter.

The main contents are:
1. Electrical and thermal design of a DC-DC converter.
2. Electrical design of an electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) filter.
3. Selection of power semiconductors and their gate drivers.
4. Calculation of power semiconductor losses and cooling requirements
5. Design of a high-frequency transformer.
6. Design of an inductor.
7. Selection of capacitors and EMC filter passive components.
8. Design of auxiliary circuits.
9. Design of a printed circuit board (PCB) for the implementation of the designed DC-DC converter.
10. Introduction to design review practices.
11. Construction of a laboratory prototype.
12. Testing of the prototype.
13. Analysis of the achieved results.

The course will be taught as follows:
The projects shall be done in teams of two or three students, who will receive a set of specifications and guidelines to perform their respective projects.
The tasks will be presented using slides and/or handouts. The students then execute the design tasks using their computers or hardware provided by the academic supervisors and CAD software available from TUM. Typical design tasks include the definition of power circuits, the choice of power components, the design of auxiliary circuits (gate drivers, current/voltage/temperature sensors), the design of magnetic components, the design of the cooling system, estimation of the lifetime of some components, the design of a printed circuit board (PCB), and the design of the mechanical assembly.
A feedback session will follow each design task, and a redesign can be done if necessary. The final construction of the power converter will require ordering electronic components and printed circuit boards. The realization and testing of the designs follow.
Support for students will be available during the weekly contact hours. The work results will be presented and discussed amongst all participants, allowing for experiences to be shared. Finally, a final report on the work carried out must be delivered.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the module, students can:
- understand the steps and tools required to construct real electronic hardware to perform the specified tasks,
- understand the procedures for designing and implementing power converter systems,
- perform the project management tasks required to develop a power converter,
- evaluate the interactions between active, passive, and parasitic components in a power converter,
- construct and test a power converter system,

In addition, students will acquire practical lab skills such as measuring currents, voltages, and power with oscilloscopes and sensors, designing and winding magnetic components, soldering electrical components, systematic troubleshooting of hardware setups, and awareness of safety considerations whenever testing electrical equipment.

Title: Advanced Practical Course - Message Correlation and Inter-Instance/Process Communication in Process Aware Information Systems
Description:
CONTENT:
Process Aware Information Systems (PAIS) are a means of automation, based on graphical process modelling and execution. The idea is to allow non-programmers and domain-experts to realize flexible/easily adaptable automation and automation evolution. Different Views on processes, for example the single product view vs. the production line view, require a synchronization mechanism. For example from the POV of a production line parts are moved forward. For each part a individual process instance exists that tracks its state and changes.
So a change at the production line also affects one or many individual parts, leading to the necessity of synchronization between the a production line view and the part view.
Furthermore, process engines have to support the asynchronous interaction with external systems. For example a process instance might wait for a specific message/document in order to continue to the next step. In order to reduce complexity and increase transparency, external systems are not intended to address individual process instances, but just send messages to a single catch-all endpoint, which then forwards to individual instances. In order to do so, during process modelling for each task awaiting information, rules detailing the nature and possible content of the message/document have to be consigned.
All of theses interaction or inter-process communication scenarios are handled by specialized components called message correlators.
In this courses we will explore message correlation patterns and implement custom message correlators in order to support inter-instance and inter-process synchronization as well as choreographies between different process aware information systems.

OBJECTIVES:
Understanding how message correlators can support process engines for choreography scenarios, and inter/intra-process synchronization.
Students will furthermore understand correlation patterns, dealing with data retention.
Skills: ['Process Aware Information Systems (PAIS)', 'Business process modeling', 'Automation', 'Workflow automation', 'Process mining', 'Business Process Simulation (BPS)', 'Python']

Title: Advanced Practical Course - There and Back Again - Foundations and Applications of Process (Re-)Discovery with Petri Nets and Process Trees
Description:
CONTENT:
Process mining subsumes algorithms for the (semi-)automatic creation and analysis of process models given event data recorded from business process execution. It is typically divided into three pillars: Process discovery, conformance checking and process enhancement. This course focuses on the first: Process discovery. Process discovery algorithms take an event log or event stream that consists of recorded events from the business process and mines a process model that represents the control-flow behavior of the business process according to the recorded events. As process models describing the actually executed process behavior are often missing, process discovery algorithms fill that gap such that algorithms belonging to conformance checking and process enhancement can still be applied. To develop and test process discovery algorithms, a known process model either artificially created for that purpose or taken from an application domain can be used to generate event logs or event streams on which the process discovery algorithm is tasked to rediscover the process model underlying the event generation. We focus on Petri nets and process trees as the formalism to define process models both for event generation and for representing the output of process discovery algorithms.

OBJECTIVES:
Understanding how process discovery algorithms are designed and developed. Additionally, understanding of process models from a programmer's perspective for event (stream) generation, and as the target of process discovery algorithms.

Title: Advanced Practical Course Building an Advanced BPM Research App
Description:
CONTENT:
Business Process Simulation (BPS) is a key technique in both academia and industry for analyzing, predicting, and improving process performance. It enables organizations to experiment with process changes in a virtual environment before applying them in reality.
This practical course focuses on a novel approach to BPS — one that integrates human-in-the-loop (HITL) concepts to enhance simulation accuracy, trustworthiness, and usability.

The project will be carried out in teams following the agile Scrum method, with development guided by the principles of maintainable and modular software design. The Information Systems group will act as both the customer and mentor, aiming to provide students with real-world experience in collaborative software development for process analysis.

We will start the course with two introductory sessions. The project phase will follow, during which we will meet regularly with each team to review progress, plan the next steps, and refine deliverables. Students will also meet with the product owners as needed to clarify requirements and distribute work. There will be plenary sessions for both intermediate and final presentations.

Please join the first meeting, where we will present the general topic and course organization.

OBJECTIVES:
- The students are able to work with a modeling language used in industry
- The students are able to extend an existing scientific approach and evaluate the results following a clear methodology
- The students demonstrate that they can deal with a given project goal within a given time frame
- The students are able to work in a team, apply agile methods, and use appropriate tools to support the team work
- The students have the competence to document their approach and the results in an oral and written form

Title: Advanced Practical Course Deep Learning for Audio, Speech, and Language
Description:
CONTENT:
Hearing describes the intelligent processing of audio signals and is one of the key human senses to navigate the world. In particular, speech has always served as the main means of information exchange for humans. Its great power comes from the combination of discrete language information and continuous paralinguistic information, resulting in a rich but complex communication signal. In turn, this mixture poses particular challenges to machine learning algorithms and their capabilities concerning speech analysis and generation, which need to be addressed accordingly.
Correspondingly, this course revolves around the intertwined topics of audio (e.g., audio event detection, audio tagging), speech (e.g., speech emotion recognition, speech recognition), and language (e.g., large language models). The tasks participants will be confronted with shall be explored with state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms. 
Participants in this course will be presented with the most crucial aspects of audio, speech, and language in the context of deep learning research. This includes a theoretical basis of the task data, as well as valuable tools for practical application.
After an introduction of available topics, participants will form groups of three to four students and, together with their supervisor, define projects that aim to push forward the scientific knowledge on their assigned topic. These projects will be carried out throughout the semester; results shall be produced in a reproducible manner and presented at the end of the semester.

OBJECTIVES:
After the successful participation in the module, students are able to independently suggest and address reasonable hypotheses around the research topics of audio, speech, or language. They will further be able to implement, deploy and validate deep learning models in the specific field, analyse their results and, finally, present them to their fellow students.
Skills: ['Deep Learning', 'Audio signal processing', 'Speech processing', 'Natural Language Processing (NLP)', 'TensorFlow', 'PyTorch', 'Python', 'Machine Learning', 'Signal processing']

Title: Advanced Rheology
Description:
CONTENT:
In the exercise "Advanced Rheology" the students learn the experimentally application of rheological principles for the analysis and modelling of the deformation behaviour of viscoelastic liquids and solids. The exercise mainly comprises the following subareas:
- Definition of common rheological parameters 
- Exercises to build rheological models for the description of the deformation behaviour of viscoelastic materials 
- Practical courses to determine a relationship between rheology and microstructural effects 
- Fundamentals of rheometrical measurement methods 
- Selection of suitable rheometrical measurement methods for different materials 
- Execution of rheological examinations including analysis and evaluation of the results

OBJECTIVES:
After successful participation in the “Advanced Rheology” exercise, students are able to apply basic rheological parameters in order to describe the deformation behaviour of viscoelastic fluids and solids. They additionally learn to assign the phenomenological deformation behaviour to the appropriate rheological models. They are thus able to model the deformation behaviour of viscoelastic substances during technical processes, such as flow and mould filling processes. Through the practical exercises, students can finally identify initial connections between the rheological behaviour of the viscoelastic fluids and their microstructural composition. In rheometric experiments, the students can practically apply the measurement methods learned in the lecture to determine the rheological deformation behaviour of viscoelastic fluids. They learn the proper handling of the rheometer itself, the evaluation of the experiments as well as the ingenious assessment of the measured data.

Title: Advanced Robot Control and Learning
Description:
CONTENT:
This course delves into advanced methodologies in robot control, integrating theoretical foundations with modern approaches applicable to real-world robotic systems. The course begins with essential preliminaries in robotics and nonlinear control, establishing a strong base in kinematics, dynamics, and system stability. It then progresses through a spectrum of control techniques including model-based, adaptive, and robust control methods. A significant portion of the course is dedicated to modern challenges in controlling redundant robots, force and impedance control strategies, and advanced passivity-based control methods, especially in the context of teleoperation. Students will develop both theoretical insights and practical skills, reinforced through simulations and case studies of contemporary robotic systems.

1. Introduction 

2. Preliminaries in Robotics: 
Dynamics 
Differential Kinematics

3. Preliminaries in nonlinear control 
State Space Representation 
Stability Analysis

4.Motion Control : 
Joint Space and Task Space Control
Model-Based Control Approaches
Adaptive and Robust Control
Redundant Robot Control

5.Interaction Control 
Force Impedance Control
Energy based approach/ Tank Energy

6. Networked robots
Bilateral teleoperation
Passivity based control  

7. Robot Learning

OBJECTIVES:
After successful participation in the module, the students are able to:
- to understand the theory behind different approaches in motion and interaction control of robot manipulators
- Solve modern control problems with advanced methods
- Understand and exploit the concept of redundancy in robotics
- Understand and use learning methods in robotics

Students will learn how to model and control robotic platforms, integrate learned models into control frameworks, and address real-world challenges such as uncertainty, disturbances, and model inaccuracies.

Title: Advances in cryo-electron tomography – “Mr. Tompkins explores the cryo-world’s wonders”
Description:
CONTENT:
We will offer a lecture series and a guide on how to do cryo-electron tomography as of today. We explain and show how cryo-ET has advanced, what is now state-of-the-art and what can be expected in the future. Mr. Tompkins, the protagonist of a series of popular science books by the Russian physicist George Gamow, will accompany us on our fantastic voyage to the inner space of cells by cryo-ET. 
Tomography on frozen-hydrated cells is a formidable tool to visualize cells with the transmission electron microscope (TEM) in three dimensions (3D) and at molecular resolution. Cryo-electron tomography has a lot in common with cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and single-particle analysis (SPA). However, there are decisive differences and one is quite apparent: tomography allows imaging of molecules in cells quasi in vivo, while in SPA molecules are investigated separate and apart from their cellular hosts and their interacting partners, thus in vitro. Tomography therefore can be used to image the cellular proteome and to study the biogenesis of molecules and proteins as well as their degradation in their native environment. Moreover, protein and functional networks and the intricate connections of biological pathways can be visualized and examined directly within the cellular context.
The aim of this lecture series is to build the basis to understand and perform cryo-electron tomography in both theory and practice. Our topics will cover:
1.	Essentials of the methodology, instrumentation and electron optics
2.	Contrast, dose and image formation
3.	A small excursion into reciprocal space - Mr. Tompkins meets Mr. Fourier
4.	Microscope operation, alignments, optical setups and image recording
5.	 “A picture is worth a thousand words” – basics of image analysis
6.	The nitty-gritty of specimen preparation (cells frozen in time)
7.	Micromachining with the focused ion beam – “cold cuts of cells”
8.	Markers, fiducials and tags – Useful little helpers
9.	Tomography – The best practice to get a tomogram
10.	Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction – Secrets and solutions
11.	3D image analysis – “Beating the noise, boosting the signal” – Sub-tomogram averaging and classification
12.	Segmentation and visualization – Mr. Tompkins in a 3D-Wonderland
13.	The lucky thirteen

Title: After Innovation
Description:
CONTENT:
This graduate seminar in Critical Innovation Studies examines what happens after the buzz of innovation has faded. We challenge the dominant pro-innovation bias by focusing on oft-neglected facets of technological life: the work of maintenance and repair, the realities of discontinuing technologies, the “dark side” of innovation (unintended consequences and inequalities), and visions of ruination and lost futures. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies (STS) and related fields, the course invites students to rethink innovation not as a one-time heroic act, but as an ongoing socio-technical process with a lifecycle that includes upkeep, failure, and even deliberate endings. We will explore how maintenance and care keep our world running long after the novelty of new tech fades, how and why certain innovations are phased out or abandoned (discontinuation), and how communities live amidst industrial decline and ruins, salvaging hope and new possibilities from “lost futures.”

By the end of the course, students will have a deep understanding of critical innovation studies perspectives. We will engage with key thinkers like David Edgerton, who urges attention to “technology-in-use” and the persistence of old but reliable artifacts; Anna Tsing, who illuminates life and survival in the ruins of capitalism; and Jaques Derrida, who theorizes how the unfulfilled promises of the past are shaping our vision of the present and future. Students from STS and other social sciences will find this course a critical complement to traditional innovation studies, as we highlight that success is entangled with failure, and creativity with maintenance. Through interactive discussions, in-class debates, and creative exercises, we will grapple with questions such as: What do we learn by “hailing the maintainers” instead of glorifying disruptors? How do discontinued or failed innovations shape the technological landscape? What social and environmental debts does the cult of innovation leave behind, and how might we reclaim those lost futures for more sustainable and just technological worlds?

OBJECTIVES:
Upon completing the course, students can identify, differentiate, and mobilize key concepts from Science and Technology Studies and Critical Innovation Studies to analyze maintenance, repair, discontinuation, ruination, dark innovation, and lost futures as integral parts of technological life. They are able to map technology lifecycles beyond novelty, tracing the sociomaterial co-production of infrastructures and artifacts with institutions, political histories, and collective imaginaries, and to interpret sites of decline and breakdown as dynamic processes rather than endpoints. Students can diagnose the distributive, ethical, and temporal politics of innovation and its afterlives, evaluate proposals for exits, phase-outs, and sunset clauses, and articulate when maintenance is preferable to replacement.
They are proficient in systematizing and comparing heterogeneous empirical cases across regions and sectors, crafting conceptually informed arguments that identify patterns of persistence and endings, and communicating findings clearly in debates, role-plays, and design-oriented exercises. Upon completion, participants can design and justify maintenance-centered and discontinuation-aware policy instruments, reconsider dominant metrics of success, assess the generalizability of purportedly universal solutions, and imagine viable alternatives that foreground stewardship, care, and repair. This reflexive perspective equips them to contribute to inclusive and democratic governance of socio-technical change in their academic work and professional practice.

Title: AI in and for Society
Description:
CONTENT:
Do you care about how ‘we’ can live together now and in the future? Do you sometimes get the feeling ‘we’ are headed in the wrong direction: not sustainable enough, too much of the wrong kind of machine learning, not enough innovation for the public good, too much hatred and fear and inequality?

This course is designed to address this unease. It is designed for everyone. It offers an introduction to understanding ‘the social’. ‘The social’ takes shape when ‘we’ live our everyday lives together and it shapes the possibilities for doing so. ‘The social’ is crucial in figuring out who is included in the ‘we’ and who is not. It organises what we expect from others and the future. It suggests to us what we might consider good and right. It helps us to know the world in different ways and navigate our own lives and our fate as a society.

‘The social’ is often overlooked. We know individuals, people, consumers, users, decision-makers etc. We also know values and ethics, but we are usually not quite sure what they are and where they come from. And some people have a sense that there might be such a thing as ‘society’, but then it is unclear what exactly that is beyond ‘many people’ in a country. 

This course is designed to introduce you to the idea of ‘the social’. What is it and how can we know and understand it? If we understand it, what does it mean and what follows from it? The course is about learning how to think about how we live together. That requires learning about and understanding a few social theories. Yet it is more about thinking for yourselves and developing a clear stance towards how you and others think about and want to live together.

This course can be unsettling for some who like their science to be clear cut truths to memorise. It can be politically provocative for those who like their politics to be outside of their science. And it can be fun for those who like their science to be serious. Some might take a liking to it and choose more options in this direction. Some will take from it the knowledge with whom to collaborate when their own work turns ‘social’ or ‘political’. And some will know that this really is not for them and that they want to spend their lives as deeply buried in a lab as possible without other people. All good.

It is a course based around an interactive lecture that works best when people bring to it their very different experiences and expectations about society, the social and how we should live together. So come along and bring your lives with you.

OBJECTIVES:
You will learn to think about and understand social phenomena. This involves understanding how ‘understanding’ is different from ‘explaining’ and, more generally, how the social sciences know. You will be introduced to some basic social theories and get a first idea how knowledge, infrastructure, politics and economics are social phenomena. You will come across some ‘truths’ from feminist and decolonial thinking that some of you might find ‘inconvenient’. And we will pay attention to some issues around data and ‘artificial’ ‘intelligence’ as this course is mandatory for AI&Society students.
Skills: ['Artificial intelligence', 'Machine learning', 'Ethics', 'Sustainability', 'Social impact', 'Innovation', 'Critical thinking and decision-making']

Title: Aircraft Performance
Description:
CONTENT:
The lecture Aircraft Performance gives an insight on flight performance calculations and explains the relations in flight dynamics based on analytical approximations of aerodynamic, thrust and gravitational forces. Based on the definition of a consistent nomenclature, the nonlinear equations of motion of aircraft are introduced that are used to derive stationary flight conditions. Based on these derivations, the optimal states for the individual conditions are derived – i.e. the flight performance parameters like for example the optimal glide angle or the maximum range of an aircraft.
Contents:

1. Introduction
2. Equations of Motion of the Aircraft
3. Glide
4. Straight and Level Flight
5. Climb and Descent
6. Turning Flight
7. Cruise
8. Acceleration / Deceleration
9. Combined Flight
10. Flight Envelope Limitations
11. Takeoff and Landing
12. High Speed Flight
13. Certification and Operational Requirements

OBJECTIVES:
After attendance of this lecture, the student is able to understand the relations of flight performance calculations and to apply this knowledge for flight performance calculations as they are common for the pre-design of aircraft.
Skills: ['Aircraft performance', 'Flight dynamics', 'Aerodynamic forces', 'Thrust forces', 'Gravitational forces', 'Equations of motion', 'Nomenclature']

-	Sensorik und Qualitätskontrolle: Geschmackswahrnehmung, Verkostungsschemata, Richtlinien, praktische Beispiele für Fehlaromen
-	Rechtliche Grundlagen und gesetzliche Anforderungen zu Getränkeinhaltsstoffen, Roh- und Hilfsstoffen, Wässer, Getränkegattungen (Erfrischungsgetränke, hochsafthaltige Getränke), Mischgetränke 
- Wasser: z. B. natürliches Mineralwasser, Quellwasser, Tafelwasser, Heilwasser Roh- und Hilfsstoffe sowie Getränkeinhaltsstoffe: z. B. Kohlensäure, Kohlenhydrate, Süßungsmittel, Aminosäuren, Aromen, Essenenzen, Zusatzstoffe
- Herstellung alkoholfreier Erfrischungsgetränke und grundlegende Aspekte der Produktentwicklung: Aromagewinnung, Konzentratherstellung, Grundstoffe, Ausmischung, Berechnungsgrundlagen 
- Fermentierte Getränke
-	Prozesstechnik: Anlagenbau im AfG-Bereich mit Fokus auf Abfülltechnik
-	Sensorik und Qualitätskontrolle alkoholfreier Getränke und Mischgetränke: Verkostungsschemata, Richtlinien, praktische Beispiele für Fehlaromen
-	Mischgetränke und innovative Getränke sowie Sportgetränke: Isotonie, Markttrends, Convenienceprodukte

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der erfolgreichen Teilnahme am Modul können die Studierenden die verfahrenstechnischen Grundlagen, die Technologie der Roh- und Hilfsstoffe und die rechtlichen Anforderungen der Getränkeherstellung benennen und beschreiben. 

Sie kennen die Anforderungen der analytischen, sensorischen und mikrobiologischen Qualitätssicherung und können diese beschreiben. Sie können die üblichen auf dem Markt erhältlichen Getränkegattungen und Wässer wiedergeben. Sie verstehen weiterhin deren Inhaltsstoffe, Roh- und Hilfsstoffe und können den Einfluss derer auf die Getränkematrix voraussagen. Die Studenten können anhand praktischer Beispiele die grundlegenden Getränkeparameter/-attribute selbstständig berechnen. Sie sind in der Lage, verschiedene Getränke aus dem nationalen Umfeld hinsichtlich der zum Einsatz kommenden Rohstoffe, technischen Herstellungsprozesse, rechtlichen Anforderungen und qualitätsbeurteilenden Analytik zu unterscheiden. Anhand der rechtlichen Rahmenverordnungen können sie Getränke diskutieren und auf Konformität überprüfen. Sie werden so in die Lage versetzt, einfache Getränkerezepturen eigenständig theoretisch zu konzipieren und Analysenergebnisse ganzheitlich zu diskutieren.

Title: Allgemeine Betriebswirtschaftslehre
Description:
CONTENT:
In der Lehrveranstaltung wird ein Überblick über die Betriebswirtschaftslehre gegeben. Zu Beginn wird die Betriebswirtschaftslehre als wissenschaftliche Disziplin mit verschiedenen Basiskonzepten vorgestellt. Dann werden die Subsysteme von Betrieben, die Ziele sowie Techniken des Managements behandelt. Anschließend werden die sogenannten konstitutiven Entscheidungsfelder dargestellt sowie die wichtigsten Teilgebiete der Betriebswirtschaftslehre.

OBJECTIVES:
Durch die Lehrveranstaltung sollen die Studenten in die Lage versetzt werden, die Inhalte folgender Lehrveranstaltungen leichter zu verstehen und einzuordnen. Sie sollen ein grundlegendes Verständnis für die wirtschaftlichen Probleme von Unternehmen, besonders aus dem Bereich des Agrarsektors i.w.S. und für betriebswirtschaftliche Analysemethoden und Entscheidungsunterstützung entwickeln.
Skills: ['Business software applications', 'Project planning and prioritization', 'Stakeholder and requirements management']

Title: Allgemeine Biologie
Description:
CONTENT:
Bau und Lebensweise von heterotrophen (freilebenden und parasitischen) Protisten (Amöben, Flagellaten, Ciliaten, Apicomplexa)
- Entwicklung, Baupläne und Lebensweisen von Tieren (Schwämme, Nesseltiere, Lophotrochozoa (z.B. Plattwürmer, Ringelwürmer, Weichtiere), Ecdysozoa (z.B. Fadenwürmer, Gliederfüßer), Deuterostomia (z.B. Stachelhäuter, Chordata inkl. Manteltiere
- Systematik der Wirbeltierklassen
- Evolution des Menschen

OBJECTIVES:
Die Studierenden sollen eine grundlegende Orientierung in der Zoologie erarbeiten und die Kompetenz erwerben, verschiedene Lösungsmöglichkeiten zu Fragen tierischen Lebens (Nahrungserwerb, Verdauung, Exkretion, sensorische Orientierung) als Anpassung an ökologische Nischen zu begreifen. Nach Abschluss der Veranstaltungen sollen Studierende in der Lage sein, diese Lösungsmöglichkeiten auf die zugrunde liegenden physikalischen Randbedingungen zurückzuführen.

Title: Allgemeine Botanik
Description:
CONTENT:
Im Rahmen des Moduls werden Grundkenntnisse der Biologie in den Bereichen der Zellbiologie, Botanik, Genetik und Zoologie vermittelt.
Vorlesungsthemen der Botanik sind: Kurzer Überblick zur Entstehung des Lebens, Stellung der Pflanze im Ökosystem und Beispiele verschiedener Organismengruppen des Pflanzenreiches. Gewebe der Pflanze, Anatomie und Morphologie des Vegetationskörpers der höheren Pflanze: Spross, Blatt, Wurzel, Metamorphosen, sek. Dickenwachstum, Fortpflanzung, Photosynthese, Wasserhaushalt der Pflanze, Transportvorgänge.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der erfolgreichen Teilnahme am Modul sind die Studierenden in der Lage:
- die Anatomie und Morphologie der Pflanzen zu erklären.
- die funktionalen Zusammenhänge im Bau pflanzlicher Strukturen zu verstehen, sowie den Zusammenhang verschiedener anatomischer Anpassungen ökologischen Faktoren gegenüberzustellen.
- die Grundlagen des Wasserhaushaltes zu verstehen.
- Abläufe und Zusammenhänge der Teilprozesse der Photosynthese zu erklären.
- den Aufbau und die Funktion von Zellen als elementare Einheiten des Lebens und die molekularen Strukturen und Prozessen, die die Grundlage des Lebens bilden zu verstehen.
- die wichtigsten molekularen Grundlagen der Vererbung zu verstehen und einfache Vererbungsmuster zu analysieren.
- die Grundlagen der Klassischen Genetik, der Populationsgenetik, der quantitativen Genetik und der Genomik zu verstehen und deren Bedeutung für die Pflanzen- und Tierzucht einzuschätzen.
- die Entwicklung vom Ei zum Organismus (Furchung, Gastrulation) und die Evolution, Taxonomie und Eigenschaften der für Agrarwissenschaftler relevanten Tiergruppen, anhand ihrer Grundbaupläne und ihrer biologischen Besonderheiten, zu verstehen.

Title: Allgemeine Mikrobiologie
Description:
CONTENT:
Im Rahmen der Vorlesung sollen Grundkenntnise über Mikroorganismen, im Besonderen über prokaryotische Mikroorganismen, vermittelt werden. Im Vergleich zu den Eukaryoten sollen die Vielfalt und besonderen Eigenschaften der Bakterien und Archaeen herausgearbeitet werden. Schwerpunkte  liegen im Bereich der Zytologie, Wachstums-, Ernährungs- und Stoffwechselphysiologie. Die zentrale Bedeutung der Mikroorganismen für bestimmte Stoffkreisläufe sowie ihre Wechselwirkung mit anderen Lebewesen (Symbiosen, Pathogenität) und ihre Anwendung in biotechnologischen Verfahren werden anhand von Beispielen ebenfalls behandelt.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme an dem Modul besitzen die Studierenden das grundlegende theoretische Verständnis und Fachwissen über prokaryontische und eukaryontische Mikroorganismen. 
Sie sollen in der Lage sein,
• mikrobiologische Fragestellungen und Arbeitstechniken zu verstehen und fachliche Fragen selbst zu entwickeln.
• Zusammenhänge zwischen Stoffwechselwegen und Stoffumsetzungen durch Mikroorganismen zu verstehen.
• das erworbene Wissen auf vertiefte Fragestellungen anzuwenden.
• Interesse an Mikrobiologie, mikrobiologischen Problemen und die Bedeutung von Mikroorganismen für Mensch und Umwelt zu fördern.

Title: Allgemeine Mikrobiologie 2
Description:
CONTENT:
This lecture course teaches advanced knowledge at the molecular level about the main steps of gene expression, including: transcription, translation, protein folding, chaperone function, membran integration of proteins, protein export and secretion, posttranslational modifications, anchoring of proteins to the cell surface.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing this module students have acquired extended theoretical knowledge and understanding at the molecular level about the processes involved in gene expression. 
Students should be able to
• acknowledge the importance and the interlinkage of the individual processes involved in gene expression.
• speicfy and explain differences between bakterien, archaea and eukaryotes and their impact.            
• transfer the acquired knowledge to similar cases.
A further objective is to awaken interest in microbiology and microbiological questions.
