Title: Dialogue Matters – A Difficult Conversation Lab
Description:
CONTENT:
Communication is essential, however not always easy. Sometimes dialogue seems to be impossible; we call this difference of opinion, disagreement or even conflict. However, there is more out there: mechanical engineers and economists, live scientists and mathematicians - just to name a few – speak “different languages” inside and outside their disciplines. To communicate effectively and overcome the challenges of looming quarrels or battles is the challenge. This course offers a dedicated, fun and teaching conversation lab, an efficient way to learn specific techniques and to construct your own consense oriented language, while exchanging experiences with peers.

This course assures insight on how common languages can be constructed between interlocutors from different fields, what difficult communication and conflict is like, how it escalates and how it can be mastered. Thus, it addresses a variety of communication models and techniques. Furthermore, we will look to types of difficult and toxic people and try out expert tactics to deal with them. And – last but not least – there will be room for self-reflection, recognition and management of one’s own communication and conflict resolution style(s).

OBJECTIVES:
Participants will get insight and acquire the following skills needed to communicate effectively and consensus oriented:
• application of communication models and techniques: the Communication Square, Non-Violent Communication, Neuro-Linguistic Programming, Active Listening and Establishing Rapport (among others)
• ability to analyse conflict and conflict escalation and to implement adequate conflict management, based on e.g. the Circle of Conflict, the Nine-Stage Model of Conflict Escalation, the Mediation Process and its phases
• awareness for and critical reflection of own communication and conflict management styles
• ability to learn from own and others' experience in order to speed up the capacity of ad hoc analysis in critical situations and - if necessary or advisable - to adapt critical behaviour.
Skills: ['Clear technical and non-technical communication', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Cross-functional collaboration', 'Negotiation']

Title: Digital Changemaker Course
Description:
CONTENT:
The students will join an interdisciplinary team and get matched with a real-world problem to work on. Each team of four to five students will collaborate with an existing company which is primarily an SME or NGO to develop a viable digitization concept for a company's internal process that includes an analysis of the ethical impact of the proposed concept. 
Within the 12 weeks, the students will receive input about the tools and methodologies they need to develop a digitization strategy as well as the impact assessment. 
The Digital Changemaker Course has 3 phases: 
-  The Problem Immersion Phase fosters a comprehensive understanding of the trends 
that will significantly impact the industry of the project partner in the coming years. This means that the students grasp the potential opportunities and risks arising from digitization. Building upon this, the objective of the Problem Immersion Phase is to shed light on the specific challenges faced by the project partner and to develop initial approaches for addressing them through digital technologies. 
- The Research Phase forms the foundation of the program. The objective of this phase is for the students to identify the existing technological, economic, and societal trends within the industry of their project partner for the next five years. Through this process, a shared understanding of the opportunities and risks of digitalization will be fostered among all participants. Furthermore, they will be introduced to concepts of project management and team communication. 
- The starting point of the Ideation Phase for the students is a prioritized list of project-partner-specific problems that can be addressed through digital technologies. The goal of this phase is for each team to develop a tailored solution concept for one of the problems, aligned with the project partner. In order to achieve this, different digital technologies should be compared and evaluated in terms of technological feasibility, as well as their economic and societal impacts.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the Digital Changemaker courses, students are able to apply innovation methodologies in a project team. Moreover, they are capable of coping with the challenges of working in interdisciplinary project teams. They are able to create and give presentations and gain experience in working on extensive real-world problems. 
Specific learning outcomes for the course are as follows. Students are able to: 
1. apply trend research methodology. 
2. identify problems that can be solved through digital technologies. 
3. evaluate technical and digital solution approaches from a multidisciplinary 
perspective, including assessing technological feasibility, economic benefits, and 
societal sustainability. 
4. develop a digitization concept and assess its ethical implications. 
5. plan, execute, and document expert and user research. 
6. apply the Design Thinking methodology to a digitization challenge. 
7. use story-telling tools to captivate an audience and present an idea. 
8. organize themselves in a team, communicate openly, and address problems in 
teamwork.
Skills: ['Project planning and prioritization', 'Cross-functional collaboration', 'Business software applications', 'Data analysis', 'Ethical awareness and data responsibility']

Title: Digital Ergonomics
Description:
CONTENT:
The exam of the module is a project work. This consists firstly of a 30-minute test (in writing), secondly, of the project and thirdly of a scientific article in the amount of max. 5 DIN A4 pages. In the test, the students demonstrate that they can work in limited time and without tools and that they can explain the possibilities of digital human modeling and apply the principles of ergonomic workplace assessment by various methods (e.g., LMM, MTM, EAWS, etc.). In the project, the students show that they can practically work on an ergonomic problem in a team and that they can use and apply the software ema Work Designer (ema = editor of human work) for the ergonomic planning of workplaces (production, office). Furthermore, they show that they can apply the methods and concepts of paper writing and assess the results obtained by evaluating and interpreting the collected data in the form of a (written) paper, they.

The grading is:
0.25 * test + 0.5 * paper + 0.25 * project (with software)
All parts must be passed with at least 4.0.
In the case of a repetition in the following summer semester, all parts must be provided again.

OBJECTIVES:
After the seminar the students will be able 
-	To explain the basics of ergonomic workplace design and assessment as well as the application of digital human models
-	To know the basics of using the software "ema Work Designer"
-	To apply the "ema Work Designer" software for ergonomic workplace design using an example for specific questions
-	To Assess a workplace using MTM, EAWS and the ema Work Designer software
-	To interpret the results obtained and to use information about paper writing.

Title: Digital Fabrication Research
Description:
CONTENT:
In this research-oriented course, students investigate contemporary and experimental topics in digital fabrication in architecture, focusing on theoretical frameworks or hands-on experimentation. The research aligns with active projects at the Professorship of Digital Fabrication and includes aspects of:
• Human-machine collaboration and co-design workflows.
• Robotic fabrication processes for architecture and construction (e.g., timber assembly, robotic bricklaying)
• Additive manufacturing (e.g., 3D printing with clay, earth, or concrete).
• Integration of computational design with digital fabrication.
• XR (Extended Reality) tools for design and assembly.
• Material-driven design and process-aware prototyping.
At the end of the course, students submit a comprehensive report that includes:
• An introduction to the research topic.
• A review of existing work and methods (state-of-the-art).
• A detailed description of their research process and outcomes.
• Critical reflections and recommendations for future research.

Title: Digital Responsibility for Information Engineering - lecture
Description:
CONTENT:
This course is part of the mandatory module Ethics in Information Engineering of the Master in Information Engineering (compulsory elective). This course introduces the essential theories, basic concepts, and common techniques of how private persons - in particular, people who work on generating, collecting, processing, and using data - and societal decision-makers decisions de-duce, make, and execute decisions. In addition, this course incorporates classical ethical theories, practical aspects of responsible decision-making, and applications of ethics-based decisions in the field of information engineering. The course captures the following topics:
- Classical ethical theories, paradigms, and approaches, including deontology and utilitarianism,
- Holistic and sustainability-oriented decision-making,
- Privacy, safety, and fairness of data gathering, collecting, and processing, and
- Regulations of data protection and requirements of ethical responsibility governance in companies and project teams, includ-ing the General Data Protection Regulation of the European Union.

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing the module, participants have gained the competence to:
- (Self-)critically reflect on classical ethical theories, paradigms, and approaches,
- Independently make holistic and sustainability-oriented decisions,
- Effectively consider privacy, safety, and fairness as major aspects of data gathering, collecting, and processing, and to
- Systematically evaluate and apply regulations of data protection.

Title: Digital Transformation and its Impact on Corporate Governance, Leadership, and Strategy
Description:
CONTENT:
This seminar is held by Dr. Ralf Wintergerst, CEO der Giesecke+Devrient GmbH Group and President of Bitkom.

In this seminar, some of the key ingredients of successfully leading a company and developing it along its strategy are being taught. The design of the seminar includes both theoretical frameworks and practical examples.

The content is structured into 3 modules: Corporate Governance, Strategy, and Leadership.

(1) Corporate Governance
Corporate Governance constitutes the legal and factual framework of a company and stipulates the legitimate interest of the various stakeholders in the company. Successful Corporate Governance supports companies to be well run. It can prevent companies from derailing from its strategy or drifting into scandals, which happens in companies of all sizes and in any industry.

(2) Strategy
Strategy and making choices are key to any company’s success or failure. When Companies create their strategy, the most important questions need an answer. But what are those most important questions? Therefore, this module captures the most important questions and the key management concepts behind those questions.

(3) Leadership
Leadership is the glue between Corporate Governance and Strategy. It makes Corporate Governance work, and so the implementation of the Corporate Strategy. Moreover, in a world that is ever changing, Leadership carries the responsibility for running the company well, but it also takes care of its employees and stakeholders to make a difference for both the company and also society.

In the final block, Corporate Governance, Strategy, and Leadership will be interlinked with one another to further rationalize what it takes to successfully run a company.

OBJECTIVES:
(1) Students will learn the main theories influencing today's Corporate Governance, so as the key principles on which Corporate Governance is based.
(2) Students will learn the difference between “good strategy and bad strategy” by asking the right questions and learning the most important strategic concepts in Strategy.
(3) Students will gain an understanding of how Supervisory Boards and Management Boards work, and what kind of instruments are being used.
(4) Students will learn why there is an (societal) interest in good leadership and what damage bad leadership can create to companies by learning the key concepts of leadership and ethics.
(5) Students will learn about the interlinkages of Corporate Governance, Strategy, and Leadership.
Skills: ['Business and product-oriented thinking', 'Project planning and prioritization', 'Strategy development', 'Leadership']

Description:
CONTENT:
Die Lehrveranstaltung vermittelt den Umgang mit digitalen Arbeitsmethoden zur Visualisierung von Entwurfsinhalten und gliedert sich in die Kursteile Grafik-Software und Layout. Die Schnittstellen zu CAD-Programmen im Entwurfsprozess und zur weiteren Bearbeitung in Grafik-Software werden exemplarisch erläutert.

Im Kursteil Grafik-Software lernen die Studierenden den Umgang mit pixel- und vektorbasierter Grafik-Software zur atmosphärischen Nachbearbeitung von CAD-Zeichnungen und Exporten aus 3D-Modellen sowie zur Erstellung einfacher Piktogramme. Der Fokus des Kurses liegt auf dem Kolorieren von Lageplänen und Erstellen von perspektivischen Collagen.

Der Kursteil Layout führt in die Verwendung professioneller Layout-Software ein. Der Fokus liegt auf dem Verständnis und der Anwendung von Formatvorlagen, dem Umgang mit Grafiken im Text, dem Arbeiten mit Verzeichnissen sowie der Vorbereitung von Dokumenten für den Druck.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme an den Modulveranstaltungen sind die Studierenden in der Lage, verschiedene digitale Methoden im Entwurfs- und Visualisierungsprozesses anzuwenden, in ihrer Bedeutung zu bewerten und eine adäquate eigene Arbeitsweise zu entwickeln. Die Studierenden sind ferner in der Lage, den richtigen Moment zu bestimmen, um von der Handzeichnung (Skizze) im Entwurfsprozess auf digitale Methoden umzusteigen, die ideale Entwicklungsumgebung für den digitalen Entwurfsprozess zu wählen und bereits erreichte digitale Entwurfsergebnisse einer weiteren Verwendung zuzuführen oder mit analogen Darstellungsmethoden zu kombinieren.

Title: Digitale Transformation von Berufs- und Arbeitswelt
Description:
CONTENT:
Im Rahmen eines Ansatzes problemlösenden, projektbasierten Lernens sind die Studierenden aller sechs Fachrichtungen gefordert, in Gruppen zusammenzuarbeiten, um Prototypen für die Verbesserung von Szenarien der digitalen Transformation zu entwickeln. Den Ausgangspunkt bilden physisch ausgestattete Szenarien im TUM-DigiLLab (Industrie 4.0, Gesundheit 4.0, Smart Home, Baker Space). Neben fachlichen Bewertungsdimensionen sind Innovativität, Nachhaltigkeit, Datenschutz und Datensicherheit zentrale Bewertungsdimensionen. Die Interdisziplinarität beinhaltet neben der Betreuung durch fachkompetente Dozierende eine informatische Betreuung und juristische Vorbereitung (Lehrstuhl für Recht und Sicherheit der Digitalisierung, Prof. Heckmann).

Stichwörter: Datenextraktion, Datenintegration, Datenanalysen, KI, Technologiekopplung, Personalisierung, Geschäftsprozessorganisation, Datenschutz und Datensicherheit aus Sicht der beruflichen Fachrichtung, Nachhaltigkeit in der Digitalisierung aus Sicht der beruflichen Fachrichtung, Werte und Rechtsgrundlagen der digitalen Transformation.

(3) Reflexivität und Bewertung: Lösungsräume und gefundene Lösungen sollen die Studierenden u.a. unter den Bewertungsdimensionen Innovativität, Datenschutz und Datensicherheit sowie Nachhaltigkeit bewerten.

Digitization is changing the professional world, especially with regard to communication and collaboration. As a result of this change, the vocational schools have to adapt their own vocational teaching-learning arrangements. Title: Digitaltechnik
Description:
CONTENT:
Fundamentals of digital information processing and storage: basic model for functional behavior of MOSFET transistors, current equations, delay time and dynamic power loss. Circuit-technical realization of arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication) as well as the synthesis of two- and multi-stage combinatorial operations (conjunction, disjunction, negation) and sequential switching operations from elementary basic components (logic gates, registers, MOSFET transistors). Logic optimization of combinatorial switching networks. Techniques for improving the information throughput of clocked, sequential switching devices by means of assembly line and parallel processing. Role and design of finite state machines as control units of various practical applications.

Further, the reasons and limitations of performance, timing, energy consumption and economical aspects of digital CMOS technology are covered in the context of communication and information technology.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the module, students will be able to understand basic circuit concepts of digital logic and function blocks, to analyze their interaction, to evaluate functionality and to develop simple blocks themselves. Performance-optimized implementations of multistage combinatorial logic blocks as well as finite state machines (FSMs) can be derived, evaluated and developed using the design principles of pipeline and parallel processing. Furthermore, the students acquire a basic understanding of the operation of MOS transistors and their application in CMOS circuits.In addition, students get a basic understanding in the functionality, composition and application of MOS transistors and CMOS circuitry.

Title: digi4all - Kompetenzen für das Unterrichten in einer digitalen Welt
Description:
CONTENT:
digi4all richtet sich an alle, die sich Kompetenzen für das Lehren und Lernen unter den Bedingungen der Digitalisierung selbstbestimmt aneignen möchten und die einen umfassenden Blick auf die Chancen und Herausforderungen der Digitalisierung für das Bildungssystem erhalten möchten. In 12 Modulen können informatische, mediendidaktische und medienpädagogische Grundlagen und Kompetenzen erworben werden. Hierbei werden die KMK-Standards für die Lehrerbildung adressiert, die den Umgang mit den Möglichkeiten und Herausforderungen der Digitalisierung betreffen. Hierzu gehören bspw. in den Standards der Bildungswissenschaften die „Gestaltung von Unterricht und Lernumgebungen einschließlich der Berücksichtigung digitaler Medien und Technologien“ und Konzepte der Medienbildung und informatischen Bildung zur Medienkompetenzförderung: „Lernen mit und über Medien; Umgang mit digitalen und analogen Medien unter konzeptionellen, didaktischen und praktischen Aspekten sowie kritische Reflexion aus technologischer, gesellschaftlicher und anwendungsbezogener Perspektive.

OBJECTIVES:
Alle Fächer und deren Fachdisziplinen erfahren starke Veränderungen durch die Digitalisierung. Innerhalb der Veranstaltung erwerben die Studierenden umfassende digitale Grundlagen-, Anwendungs- und Reflexionskompetenzen: Sie lernen mit digitalen Systemen selbstbestimmt umzugehen, diese zu verstehen, zu erklären und im Hinblick auf Wechselwirkungen mit Individuen, der Gesellschaft und dem Bildungssystem zu bewerten. Konzepte zum Transfer des Gelernten auf Lehr-Lern-Prozesse stellen den theoretisch fundierten Praxisbezug her und befähigen zu einem adäquaten Einsatz digitaler Medien sowie zur Gestaltung eines zeitgemäßen Unterrichts unter den Bedingungen der Digitalität.

Title: Dinge denken. Eine philosophische Projektwoche über die Technik im Alltag
Description:
CONTENT:
Staubsauger, Möbel, Bücher, Handys, Autos, Gummibärchen, Schuhe: überall sind Dinge. Menschliches Leben vollzieht sich in einer “Dingwelt” und wird von dieser konstant bedingt. Dennoch denken wir selten darüber nach. Was ist eigentlich ein Ding? Was macht es aus? Lassen sich Dinge systematisch einordnen? Inwiefern bestimmen die Dinge unser Leben - unser Verhalten, unser Denken, unsere Stimmungen, unsere Beziehungen zu anderen Lebewesen und zu uns selbst? Existieren die Dinge unabhängig von Menschen? Oder wie Ernst Bloch es formuliert: „Was ‚treiben‘ die Dinge ohne uns? wie sieht das Zimmer aus, das man verläßt?“  

Im Seminar besprechen wir philosophische Texte von verschiedenen Autoren, die aus unterschiedlichen Perspektiven über Dinge nachdenken. Ziel ist es, diverse Zugänge kennen zu lernen und auf konkrete Dinge anzuwenden. Dabei geht es insbesondere darum, soziale und politische Implikationen technischer Entwicklungen bewusst zu machen.

So lernen wir über alltägliche Dinge zu reflektieren, sie losgelöst von gewohnten Sichtweisen zu betrachten und in ihrer Bedingtheit und Mehrdeutigkeit zu erschließen.

Das Seminar findet als "Projektwoche" auf dem TUM Stammgelände statt.
Skills: ['Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Philosophy', 'Critical thinking and decision-making']

Title: Discovering Heritage
Description:
CONTENT:
Individual research on Architectural Heritage - 6 ECTS

“Discovering Heritage” aims at urging students to undertake individual researches on architectural heritage so to get an in-depth knowledge and understanding of what is standing behind the design of an architectural work in a specific shape and site and with respect to its original purpose and present understanding in contemporary societies.

Acquiring an in-depth knowledge meaning to discover and rediscover heritage by using different sources and investigation methods – thus, researching at the cross between the technical fields and the humanities by interdisciplinary linking the different aspects of conserving and restoring heritage buildings.
Because of this, a great deal of attention will be paid to the practical implications on architecture of the theoretical aspects of conserving and restoring buildings.
Then, the issue of a misinterpretation of historic findings with respect to the case studies chosen by students will also be illustrated by means of the case studies themselves, all the while watching at heritage as fragmented heritage in constant evolution.

Watching at heritage as a fragment of history in progress meaning to reconcile its historical recreations with new uses as well as their contemporary significance as an object of knowledge to be discovered by students and reinterpreted for assuring its survival for future while projecting heritage in the XXI century.

OBJECTIVES:
Following successful completion of this module students will be able to acquire a methodology suitable for undertaking individual researches in the conservation-restoration field.
Then,
- they will be able to analyse the historical aspects bond to the chosen case study.
- they will be able to clearly identify the connection between Architecture and the different architectural Languages and uses taking place within the space of the architectural heritage chosen, over time.
- Students will learn how to take the challenge of discovering Architectural heritage by using different sources and how to think interdisciplinary so to solve basic research questions on the individual research topic proposed.
Particularly, students will be able to:
- to recognize and clearly identify the different architectural elements and sites that are deemed to characterize their individual specific case study, along with the different functions alternating over time. Then, students are expected to be able to remember the different design configurations and redevelopments according to Eras and with respect to preservation theories.
Especially the implications of preservation theories into the practice are expected to be fully understood – thus, identified by students with respect to works of addition and the redevelopment of existing architectural features.
This critical assessment goes with a basic understanding of the interventions needed to preserve modern and historic architectural features while envisioning choices for novel solutions based on awareness.
- Finally, we expect students to be able to conceive novel solutions for the open challenge of transmitting heritage intact for future generations to be able to experience culture, all the while complying with the basic needs for use of spaces, along with their characteristic architectural features.

Title: Discrimination, Persecution and Extinction
Description:
CONTENT:
"Never again!" The crimes of the Nazi regime are one of the darkest chapters in German history. 
The Dachau Concentration Camp Memorial not only commemorates the inconceivable suffering of those persecuted and murdered as a result of the Nazi regime, but is also an appeal to the responsibility of future generations to prevent a repetition of any totalitarian-barbaric regime.

In cooperation with and under the direction of the Max Mannheimer Study Center in Dachau, the two-day event is dedicated to these tasks in the form of a guided tour and workshop. On the one hand, it shows the lives and work of people who, despite all their differences, have one thing in common: imprisonment in the Dachau concentration camp.
A wide variety of (historical) documents, such as autobiographical testimonies, photographs and film sequences, open up perspectives on people's lives during the Nazi period and beyond.On the other hand, it deals with the necessity of a culture of remembrance, with the different phases of confrontation with the time of National Socialism in the Federal Republic. 
On the basis of individual groups of former persecutees, it will be shown, among other things, how marginalization and discrimination continued to have an effect in the Federal Republic.

The event will take place on site in Dachau on the first day and will be continued on the second day at the TU Munich, Arcisstraße.

OBJECTIVES:
Students are able to identify the political-social contexts of specific historical events, to classify individual lives and statements of contemporary witnesses in relation to the events and their contexts, and to critically discuss aspects of memory culture.
Skills: ['Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Research-oriented mindset', 'Critical thinking and decision-making', 'Ethical awareness and data responsibility']

Title: Diskriminierung, Verfolgung und Vernichtung
Description:
CONTENT:
"Nie wieder!“ Die Verbrechen des Nazi-Regimes sind eines der dunkelsten Kapitel der deutschen Geschichte. Die KZ-Gedenkstätte Dachau erinnert nicht nur an das unfassbare Leid der Verfolgten und Ermordeten infolge des Nazi-Regimes, sondern ist auch Appell an die Verantwortung der nachfolgenden Generationen, eine Wiederholung eines jeglichen totalitär-barbarischen Regimes zu verhindern.

In Kooperation und unter Leitung des Max Mannheimer Studienzentrums in Dachau widmet sich die zweitägige Veranstaltung diesen Aufgaben in Form eines geführten Rundgangs und Workshop. Zum einen zeigt sie das Leben und Werk von Menschen, die, bei allen Differenzen, eines miteinander verbindet: die Gefangenschaft im Konzentrationslager Dachau. Unterschiedlichste (historische) Dokumente, wie autobiografische Zeugnisse, Fotografien und Filmsequenzen, eröffnen Perspektiven auf das Leben der Menschen während der Zeit des Nationalsozialismus und darüber hinaus. Zum anderen setzt sie sich mit der Notwendigkeit einer Erinnerungskultur, mit den unterschiedlichen Phasen der Konfrontation mit der Zeit des Nationalsozialismus in der Bundesrepublik auseinander. 
Anhand einzelner Gruppen ehem. Verfolgter wird u.a. aufgezeigt, wie Marginalisierung und Diskriminierung auch in der Bundesrepublik weiterwirkten.

OBJECTIVES:
Die Studierenden sind in der Lage, die politisch-sozialen Kontexte von spezifischen historischen Ereignisse zu identifizieren, individuelle Lebesläufe und Äußerungen von Zeitzeugen im Zusammenhang mit den Ereignissen und deren Kontexten einzuordnen sowie Aspekte von Erinnerungskultur und kollektiver Vergangenheitsbewältigung kritisch zu diskutieren.

Title: Diversität und Evolution der Moose
Description:
CONTENT:
Im Kurs werden die wichtigsten Moos-Gattungen anhand häufiger heimischer Vertreter vorgestellt. Ihre morphologischen Merkmale und Zeigerfunktion wird am Standort im Gelände besprochen. Das Bestimmen von Moosen auch mit dem Lichtmikroskop wird ausführlich geübt. Ausserdem werden evolutionäre Tendenzen und Verwandtschaftsverhältnisse innerhalb der Moose diskutiert. Es besteht die Möglichkeit, freiwillig ein Moos-Herbar anzulegen (unbenotet).
Blockkurs, voraussichtlich 23.03.-02.04.2026 (Achtung: inkl. Wochenende!)

OBJECTIVES:
In diesem Modul lernen die Studierenden häufige heimische Moosarten zu bestimmen und Standorte anhand der dort vorkommenden Moosen zu charakterisieren (Zeigerfunktion). Sie erwerben vertiefte theoretische Kenntnisse und ein erweitertes Verständnis über die Biologie und Systematik der Moose sowie die der Systematik zugrundeliegenden evolutionären Zusammenhänge.

Title: Diversität und Konfliktmanagement
Description:
CONTENT:
Im Seminar beschäftigen wir uns theoretisch mit der Rolle von Diversität in Konflikten und mit den Chancen und Risiken, die sich daraus ergeben. Wir werden uns dabei sowohl mit den Hintergründen von Konflikten und deren systematischen Kategorisierung als auch mit Lösungsansätzen und Konfliktstrategien beschäftigen. Theoretische Modelle werden anhand eigener Beispiele praktisch greifbar gemacht.
Die TeilnehmerInnen bekommen im Training praktische Methoden vermittelt, die sie im beruflichen und privaten Alltag bei der Lösung und Steuerung von Konfliktsituationen unterstützen.

OBJECTIVES:
Die Teilnehmer/innen sind sich über die Bedeutung von Diversität in Konflikten bewusst und haben Konfliktelemente und Konfliktlösungsmethoden theoretisch kennengelernt und praktisch ausprobiert. Die Reflexion des eigenen Konfliktverhaltens spielt dabei eine zentrale Rolle. Sie können Konflikte anhand verschiedener Schemata analysieren und zuordnen.

Title: Diversity in Music – Then and Now
Description:
CONTENT:
In this course, we explore the historical, cultural, and political dimensions of diversity in music from the 19th century to the present day. We’ll examine how questions of identity, inclusion, and representation play out across genres and cultures—with attention to race, gender, class, and power. Topics include the rediscovery of marginalized composers, the representation of women, members of the LGBTQ+ community, and people of color in both performance and behind-the-scenes roles, and how digital platforms and AI can reinforce or challenge systemic bias.
We’ll also engage with critical debates around respect versus appropriation—such as the legacy of white musicians in jazz—and examine how music can serve as a space of resistance, particularly under restrictive regimes. Through listening sessions, readings, and group discussion, students will develop gender and diversity competence, and gain tools to critically reflect on music’s social and political dimensions. Drawing on the TUM community's commitment to mutual respect and equal opportunity, they will also be encouraged to identify and articulate concrete ways to foster equity and inclusion—both within musical structures and in their own academic or creative spheres.
Case studies may include:
- 	Florence Price & Intersectionality: 20th century African American, mother, organist, composer
- Queer expression across centuries: Pyotr Tchaikovsky & Janelle Monáe
- From Jazz Roots to Trap Beats: Cultural Appropriation, Innovation, and the Legacy of Quincy Jones
- Woman, Life, Freedom: Singing as resistance in an oppressive regime

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the course students are able
- to understand of the role of diversity in music history and contemporary practice
- critically reflect on cultural and social contexts of musical works and performances
- to contribute to interdisciplinary dialogue and reflection on music’s power to shape identity, access, and community
- to envision and propose concrete strategies for promoting equity and inclusion in musical and broader social context

Title: Diversity Kompetenz
Description:
CONTENT:
Im beruflichen Alltag sind häufig vielfältige und widersprechende Interessen und persönliche Hintergründe von Mitarbeitenden, Kooperationspartner*innen wie Kund*innen in Einklang zu bringen. Der Aspekt der Diversity-Kompetenz stammt dabei eher aus der Menschenrechtsdebatte und diese hat sich im Laufe der Zeit verschärft: Cancel Culture, kulturelle Aneignung, Blackfishing oder Wokeness sind nur ein paar Themen, die derzeit im Diskurs sind.

In Firmen und Hochschulen gilt aber auch der Ansatz des Diversity-Managements: Wie kann ich mit der passenden Kombination von Vielfalt das Optimum für ein Projekt, eine Veranstaltung oder das Marketing herausholen? Unterschiedlichkeiten wie ethnische Herkunft, Hautfarbe, sexuelle Identität, Lebensalter, Geschlecht, Religion oder Behinderung benötigen passende Kompetenzen und methodische Herangehensweisen.
Der gute Umgang mit Diversity hängt aber nicht nur von persönlichen Fähigkeiten und Handlungsoptionen ab, sondern auch von institutionellen Voraussetzungen (AGBs, Personalmanagement, Willkommenskultur etc.). Hier setzt unser interaktiver Workshop an: 

• Diversity-Management-Theorie
• Beispiele für Rahmenbedingungen aus Unternehmen und Universitäten
• Reflexion eigener Vielfalt, Kooperations- und Abgrenzungsmechanismen
• Kennenlernen von Teamwork-Grundlagen, konstruktiven Strategien und Vernetzungsmethoden

OBJECTIVES:
Reflexion, Erarbeitung und Vermittlung von Grundlagen des Diversity Managements; Projektplanung und fallbezogene Rollenspiele in Teams und Organisationen, Konkretisierung der Erkenntnisse als Teamwork in Form von Diversity Papers als Hausarbeit auf der internen Moodle-Plattform.

Title: Drone Remote Sensing Meets AI
Description:
CONTENT:
This course introduces students to the rapidly evolving intersection of drone-based remote sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) for agricultural and environmental applications. Through lectures, hands-on exercises, and a drone image analysis competition, students learn how to preprocess drone imagery and apply AI techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNN) for crop and soil monitoring. The module emphasizes problem-based learning, teamwork, and practical implementation, enabling students to design data-driven workflows that integrate drone sensing with machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) for various applications such as biomass prediction and object detection in agriculture and vegetation systems.
Skills: ['Drone remote sensing', 'Artificial intelligence (AI)', 'Agricultural applications', 'Environmental applications', 'Image processing', 'Convolutions']

Title: Dynamics and Control of eVTOL Aircraft
Description:
CONTENT:
The lecture provides information on the novel field of electrical Vertical Take-Off- and Landing (eVTOL) aircraft in the following subfields:
- Dynamics & Modelling
- Performance & Control
- System Architecture and System Components
- Certification
Content:
1) Introduction: Market and Potential, Current Efforts, Rulemaking & Regulation Process
2) Equations of Motion: Frames, Definitions, Atmosphere, Kinematics, 12 degrees of Freedom, Equations of Motion
3) Aerodynamics: Basic Phenomena, Aerodynamic Modelling, Model Data Integration
4) Propellers and Rotors: Impusle Disc, Blade Element Theory, Geometry, Inflow, Slipstream, Nonlinearities, Transient effects, Performance Diagrams, Design Considerations, Inertia and Torques
5) Electric Motors and Motor Controllers: Principles of synchronous machines, physical modelling, equivalent block diagram, Sensoring, Back-EMF, PWM, Energy Considerations, Losses and efficiency, Performance, Control, Communication
6) Power Systems and Power Management: High Voltage Systems, Energy Management, Energy Storage, Batteries, Battery Management, Safety Considerations
7) Performance Analysis: Hover Performance, Cruise Performance, Climb and Descent, OEI Performance, Power and Energy Consumption (LTU and System Level), Maneuvering performance
8) Stability and Control Analysis: Static Stability / Trim, Linearisation, Modes, Transfer Functions, Controllability - all for hover, cruise and transition
9) Requirements & Certification: Handling Qualities, Response Dynamics, Disturbance Attenuation (Gust, Turbulence), Stability and Robustness, Performance requirements, OEI (LTU and PWR loss), maneuvers and margins
10) System Architectures and Topologies: General System Setup, Safety Analysis, Single Point of Failure, Energy Considerations, Data Flow, Latencies and Update Rates
11) Sensors & Actuators: Inertial, Airdata, GNSS, Data Fusion, Status Sensors, EMAs
12) Controllers for Hover: Control Allocation, Rate Control, Acceleration Control, Attitude Control, Velocity Control, Position Control
13) Controllers for Fixed-Wing-Flight: Control Allocation, Rate Control, Acceleration Control, Attitude Control, Velocity Control, Trajectory Control
14) Dynamics and Control of the Transion: Control Allocation, Effector Blending, Maneuver Design, Integrated Control, SVO Concepts
15) Controller Assessment: Stability and Robustness, Sensitivity, Control Power Utilisation, Failures,  Energy Consumption, OEI - Methods (Linear, Nonlinear, Mu-Analysis, MC, MCMC, Optimisation)
16) Presentation of examples

OBJECTIVES:
After the participation in the lecture students are able to understand the dynamics and the system of an electrical vertical Takeoff- and Landing (eVTOL) aircraft. Studenten can state and model the function of the subsystems, such as the power train - consisting of the energy storage, the motor controller, the engine and the propeller - as well as the flight control computers, sensors and actuators. Furthermore, they can understand kinematics and dynamic effects in every flight phase; namely in hover, transition and wingborne flight. Students can handle rigid body equations as well as aerodynamic effects. In addition, they are qualified for stating the functionality principles of controller systems in every flight phase and for analysing them with regards to defined criteria. Moreover, students are familiar with certification guidelines for eVTOL aircraft.

Title: Echtzeitfähige Geräte und Roboter
Description:
CONTENT:
Praktikum Echtzeitfähige Geräte und Roboter

In einer Vielzahl von Geräten befinden sich intelligente Steuerungssysteme um die zunehmend komplizierter werdenden Prozesse in Systemen zu kontrollieren. Bei zeitkritischen oder sicherheitskritischen Anwendungen steigen die Anforderungen an die Systemkomponenten und deren Zusammenwirken untereinander. In integrierten Systemen werden häufig Mikrocontroller eingesetzt. Diese bieten meist die Möglichkeit einer echtzeitfähigen Abarbeitung von Algorithmen.

Im Rahmen dieses Praktikums werden Sie einen solchen Mikrokontroller (STM32) programmieren lernen. Dazu steht jedem Studenten ein Roboter zur Verfügung, welcher über eine Vielzahl von Sensor- und Aktormodulen verfügt. 
Zunächst erlernen Sie die Ansteuerung einzelner Pins des Mikrokontrollers sowie die Einbindung verschiedener Sesnoren. Anschließend lernen Sie, die Motoren des Roboters anzusteuern und diesen fahren zu lassen. Sie werden ein eigenes Modul entwickeln, mit dem handelsübliche Servomotoren über Pulsweitenmodulation (PWM) angesteuert werden können. Sie lernen wichtige Kommunikationsprotokolle kennen und implementieren eine I2C Verbindung zur Ansteuerung eines Ultraschallsensors.
Den Abschluss des Praktikums bildet ein Rennen, bei dem die Teilnehmer gegeneinander antreten.
Skills: ['Real-time systems', 'Robotics', 'Embedded systems design', 'Control systems', 'System integration', 'Safety critical systems']

Title: Ecological Genomics
Description:
CONTENT:
This module provides an advanced introduction to ecological genomics, with a focus on how genome-wide data are used to understand evolutionary and ecological processes in natural populations. Emphasis is placed on empirical examples, interpretation of genomic data, and the integration of population, landscape, and functional perspectives.
1. Conceptual foundations of ecological genomics
– Definitions, scope, and interdisciplinary relevance across ecology, evolution, and genomics; contrasts with classical population genetics.

2. Principles of population genetics in the genomic era
– Key evolutionary forces (mutation, selection, drift, migration, recombination) revisited in a genome-wide context; genome-wide neutrality and background selection.

3. Genome-wide patterns of variation and structure
– Empirical exploration of genetic diversity, population structure, and genomic differentiation; application of summary statistics such as heterozygosity, Fst, Dxy, and linkage disequilibrium patterns.

4. Empirical case studies in population genomics
– Real-world examples illustrating adaptation, gene flow, and differentiation across genomes (e.g., temperature adaptation in insects, pesticide resistance in insects).

5. Detection of selection and signatures of adaptation
– Identification of selective sweeps, outlier loci, and polygenic adaptation using genome-wide data; interpretation of empirical signals of natural selection.

6. Landscape genomics and spatial population structure
– The role of geography and environment in shaping genomic patterns; concepts of isolation by distance and environment; examples include species in fragmented or heterogeneous habitats.

7. Genotype–environment associations
– Empirical approaches for detecting associations between genomic variants and environmental gradients (e.g., climate, altitude, soil); overview of statistical tools such as RDA, LFMM, and Bayenv.

8. Functional genomics in ecological contexts
– Introduction to gene expression and regulatory variation (e.g., transcriptomics, eQTL mapping); ecological relevance of stress responses, immune function, and phenotypic plasticity.

9. Linking genotype to phenotype in natural populations
– Conceptual challenges and empirical approaches in connecting genomic variation to ecologically important traits in both model and non-model organisms.

10. Integrative approaches in ecological genomics
– Combining population, landscape, and functional data to build a holistic understanding of adaptation and ecological differentiation.

11. Critical reading and interpretation of primary literature
– Structured discussion of case studies, focusing on study design, hypotheses, data interpretation, and the ecological significance of results.

12. Applications in conservation and biodiversity science
– Use of ecological genomic data to inform conservation management, define evolutionary significant units, and assess adaptive potential under global change.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module, students will be able to:
• Understand the foundational concepts, theoretical frameworks, and interdisciplinary scope of ecological genomics, including population, landscape, and functional genomic perspectives.
• Explain how genome-wide variation reflects ecological and evolutionary processes such as selection, drift, migration, and environmental heterogeneity.
• Interpret genomic data in light of population genetic theory, environmental gradients, and ecological context, using appropriate conceptual models.
• Analyze scientific literature in ecological genomics, critically assess different methodological approaches, and compare theoretical assumptions and interpretations across studies.
• Evaluate the relevance and limitations of various genomic frameworks (e.g., population genomics, landscape genomics, functional genomics) for addressing questions in ecology, evolution, and conservation biology.
• Develop coherent, theory-driven arguments about how genomic data can be used to understand organism–environment interactions and the genetic basis of adaptation in natural populations.

Title: Econometric Impact Analysis
Description:
CONTENT:
The course will introduce concepts and quantitative techniques
to evaluate impacts of conservation measures, such as payments for environmental services, integrated conservation and development projects, and the enforcement of regulatory policies. 
Role of impact evaluation in guiding the design of agri-environmental conservation measures, i.e., in the context of regional agri-environmental payments or in development project design, e.g. works of the J-Pal. 
Students will be familiarized with:
•	randomized experimental trials, 
•	instrumental variables, 
•	regression discontinuity design, 
•	difference-in-differences, 
•	different types of matching. 
Overview of methods and related debates will be given and discussed with the students: Topics like black-box versus theory-based impact evaluation; counterfactual analysis, experimental versus non-experimental design, selection bias, impact heterogeneity, and estimation methods will be discussed using different case studies of agri-environmental policies.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the course, students will be able to:
•	clean, organize and manipulate household datasets with Stata or R;
•	understand the assumptions required for different econometric impact evaluation technologies (including regression discontinuity, differences-in-differences, instrumental variables);
•	design an evaluation of a policy intervention or environmental/development project with at least one econometric impact evaluation technique;
•	judge the reliability of their own approach comared to those described in the literature;
•	describe their selected evaluation design, data and findings to their peers in a scientific presentation;
•	and summarize their research project in a term paper with appropriate use of tables and graphics.

Title: Economic History and Comparative Development
Description:
CONTENT:
Why, when and how did the world become rich/poor? Research of contemporary economic development has often neglected historical factors in explaining differences in inequality and wealth. The study of the past was usually delegated to the field of economic history, and connections between historical factors and present-day economic outcomes were seldom made. This course will cover the rapidly growing body of research within economics that takes a historical perspective into account.

The course uses a historical and comparative approach to understand the evolution and development of societies. In particular, we will examine research that asks whether differences in economic development, wealth and inequality today have historical roots. In addition, we will study different mechanisms and channels through which history matters. Particular attention will be paid to the role of institutions, geography and culture in explaining historical persistence. The course also covers important empirical methods to identify the causal effects of past historical events (e.g., the different types of colonial institutions) on current outcomes (e.g., GDP per capita in 2010).

While the material covered in the course is grounded in the field of economic history, there is a natural overlap with other fields in economics, particularly development economics, political economy, and cultural economics, as well as overlap with other disciplines, such as history, psychology, political science, anthropology, archaeology, and geography.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending the module, students will understand what historical factors influenced economic development and how persistent these factors are, i.e., how they still affect economic outcomes across countries today. Students can apply theories, concepts, and analytical techniques associated with economic history and microeconomics. Students will be also capable of using empirical methods to analyze persistent effects of historical data. In addition, students will learn to present scientific results and write a term paper according to scientific standards.

Title: Economics - Lecture
Description:
CONTENT:
This module provides an introduction to the basic concepts of economics. It is divided into two parts: micro- and macroeconomics.
Microeconomics deals with the behavior of individual agents, such as households, firms, and public institutions and with their interaction on markets. How can market demand be derived from the consumption choices of households? How can market supply be derived from the production decisions of firms? Which mechanisms give rise to an equalization of demand and supply? What are the consequences of market failure, and what can the state do about it?
Macroeconomics takes an aggregated perspective; it analyzes the economy as a whole. How can economic activity, inflation, and unemployment be measured? What are the factors that determine economic growth? Which mechanisms give rise to economic fluctuations, and how can these fluctuations be mitigated through fiscal and monetary policy?

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the module the students will be able to understand and explain the basic principles of economics. 
On the micro level, this includes consumer behavior as well as firms' production decisions. The students will be able to analyze basic mechanisms that give rise to the equalization of supply and demand in competitive markets. Having attended the module, the students will be able to understand the interrelation between market power and social welfare and will be able to explain market failures. On the macro level, students will be able to identify and explain the main sources of growth, unemployment and inflation. 
Moreover, they will be able to analyze the basic tools of monetary and fiscal policy.

Title: Economics I am Campus Straubing
Description:
CONTENT:
This course provides an introduction to basic concepts of microeconomics. It deals with the behaviour of individual economic units, such as households, business firms, and public institutions. Another concern is how these units interact to form markets and industries. How can consumer decisions be explained and how can aggregate demand be derived from consumer choice? Which are the factors that determine the production decisions of companies? How do equilibrium prices emerge in competitive markets, how in monopoly markets? What is the effect of government interventions in markets (e.g. taxes, price controls)? How does market power affect social welfare? Which factors lead to market failure?

OBJECTIVES:
After attending this module, students will be able to describe economic tradeoffs (particularly in choice under scarcity situations of consumers and firms). Moreover, they know strategies to solve those tradeoffs and are capable of applying them to new situations. Students are able to explain the fundamental economic mechanisms underlying specialisation and trade (particularly in view of technological progress). Students can predict how government interventions (e.g. taxes, price controls) will affect simple competitive markets. They are able to explain why certain industries are prone to market concentration and how market power affects social welfare. They can distinguish which types of goods are efficiently provided on free markets, and which not.
Skills: ['Microeconomics', 'Economic units', 'Households', 'Business firms', 'Public institutions', 'Market interaction', 'Industries', 'Consumer decisions', 'Aggregate demand']

• Policy measures, common agricultural policy of the EU, and agricultural policy around the world

• Emprical methods in the field of impact analysis / causal inference, such as:ä
- Difference-in-Differences
- Matching
- Instrumental variables

OBJECTIVES:
Upon completion of this module, the students will be able to:
• Describe basic concepts in production economics to model decision problems of agricultural producers,
• Understand the role of innovation and technology from an agricultural production perspective,
• Describe in economic terms the process of technology adoption and diffusion, including assumptions on the behaviour of relevant actors,
• Understand externalities associated with agricultural production and methods for their valuation,
• Describe policy measures aimed at adjusting market outcomes accordingly,
• Understand popular empirical methods to evaluate the effects of both new technologies and policy measures on production processes and outcomes,
• Critically evaluate methods and results from scientific articles on those topics.
Skills: ['Production economics', 'Production functions', 'Cost functions', 'Productivity', 'Efficiency', 'Innovation', 'Technological progress', 'Technology adoption', 'Diffusion process', 'Externalities', 'Ecology']

Title: Economics of Environmental and Climate Policy
Description:
CONTENT:
Evaluation criteria for environmental and climate policy measures based on welfare economics are used to derive a normatively optimal policy with regard to equity and temporal dimensions. We present economic cost-benefit analysis as a tool for the economic evaluation of environmental and climate protection measures. Subsequently, the suitability of environmental policy measures to overcome specific environmental problems is discussed. We compare a command and control approach with pollution taxes, pollution abatement subsidies and emissions trading. In addition to questions of allocation, the importance of transaction costs and technical progress is discussed. Against the background of environmental risks, the importance of property rights and liability rules is explained. An introduction to the public choice theory is given to explain the implementation of policy measures in practise. We discuss voter models for the analysis of political competition, decision-making rules and voting procedures, as well as the political influence of interest groups and bureaucracy. Against the background of global environmental and climate protection problems, game-theoretical explanations are presented.

OBJECTIVES:
In this course, policy measures for environmental and climate protection will be analysed theoretically based on welfare economic approaches whereas the implementation in practice will be discussed based on the public choice theory. The course attendees get to know valuation criteria for environmental and climate policy measures, which take into account temporal dimensions, risk considerations and aspects of equity. After successfully attending the module, the students are able to understand the effects of specific economic policy measures and to evaluate them in terms of welfare economics. With regard to the practical design of environmental and climate policy, the students acquire a comprehensive understanding of how political behaviour, collective decision-making processes and structures can be explained by using public choice theory. Attending the module enables the participants to analyse the individual and collective actions of political actors such as voters, administrations, parties and interest groups, as well as to apply game-theoretical explanations for international negotiations in the context of climate and global environmental problems.
Skills: ['Environmental economics', 'Climate policy', 'Welfare economics', 'Cost-benefit analysis', 'Economic evaluation', 'Equity', 'Temporal dimensions']

Title: Economics of Technology & Innovation - Lecture
Description:
CONTENT:
In this course, we will deal with some of the most pressing issues of innovation policy---why they matter, what their impacts are, and how we can analyze and address them.

We will ask questions like: Why does society value innovation, and what is the government's stake in it? Are we seeing enough innovative activity, and if not, what can be done? And how can we even begin to approach these complex questions?

The course also complements other offerings in the School of Management that explore innovation from a management perspective.

1. Introduction to Innovation Economics and Innovation Policy
What is innovation economics about, and what motivates policymakers to influence innovative activity?

2. Competition and Innovation
How does market competition impact technological progress and innovation? Does stronger competition always lead to better outcomes, or is the relationship more complex?

3. Mergers, Antitrust, and Collaborative Innovation
What happens to innovation when firms merge or collaborate, and why do competition authorities typically support partnerships over mergers?

4. Diffusion of Knowledge and Innovations
How do knowledge and innovations spread across industries and regions? What roles do networks, collaborations, and the efforts of individual firms play?

5. Appropriability of Innovation and Intellectual Property
What are the main types of intellectual property rights, and why is it so important for innovators to protect their ideas? How does having a "property right in an idea" connect to the motivation to keep creating new ideas?

6. Fiscal Policies and Innovation
How can fiscal tools like taxes and subsidies and financial incentives like prizes and research grants influence the incentive to innovative, and what role do they play in practice?

7. Regulation and Technical Standards
How do government regulations and agreements on technical standards shape the innovation landscape? In what ways can they encourage or possibly restrict technological progress?

8. Geographical Aspects of Innovation
How do geographical factors influence research and innovation? What role do regional clusters, knowledge spillovers, and geographical proximity play?

9. Science Policy, Idea Generation, and Entrepreneurship
How does science policy create a supportive environment for idea generation and entrepreneurship at universities, and how does this relate to universities'  more traditional role?

10. Social Consequences of Innovation
What are the wider social impacts of innovation, including its effects on inequality and lifestyle changes?

OBJECTIVES:
In this course, students will learn to identify and analyze key issues in innovation policy, gaining the knowledge and skills to understand their implications and explore solutions from economics, applied to the field of technology.

By completing this course, students will:

1. Gain an understanding of market dynamics and innovation:
-- Explain and critically assess how innovation affects market outcomes, from the growth of established firms to the emergence of new technologies and startups.
-- Understand the economic analysis of market failures and apply it in the context of innovation.

2. Understand policy analysis and its real-world impact:
-- Develop a thorough understanding of the economic principles governing the technology and innovation sector, with a focus on policy relevance and practical outcomes.
-- Examine the essential role of economic policy in driving innovation and critically assess key policy tools, including intellectual property rights, prizes, and R\&D subsidies.

3. Learn about the application of (micro-)economic analysis:
-- Build foundational knowledge of microeconomic models related to firm competition, using these models to explore different aspects of innovation.
-- Develop a basic understanding of methods for empirically testing hypotheses from theoretical models, promoting analytical approach to economic issues---no prior statistical knowledge required.
Skills: ['Economics of technology', 'Innovation policy', 'Innovation economics', 'Market analysis', 'Government policy']

Title: Edible Cities
Description:
CONTENT:
Urban agriculture has experienced a renaissance in recent decades. What are the possibilities for sustainable urban agriculture that supports multiple ecosystem services? This module explores ways in which urban agriculture can aid in the enhancement of food security, biodiversity, energy conservation, public health and well-being in cities. We will discuss the agro-ecological basis of urban horticultural production systems adapted for city environments. 

The seminar is highly interactive and combines lectures with field trips and presentations from guests and peers. In the seminars, we will 'see' cities as edible: in the present on field trips; in the past through films and advanced readings; and in the future through group presentations that design urban farming systems for future cities.
Skills: ['Urban agriculture', 'Sustainable agriculture', 'Food security', 'Biodiversity', 'Energy conservation', 'Public health', 'Urban planning']

Title: Eine psychologische Betrachtung von (generativer) KI
Description:
CONTENT:
Die jüngsten Errungenschaften im Bereich der generativen künstlichen Intelligenz (KI, z.B. ChatGPT) werfen vielfältige psychologische Fragestellungen auf. Deshalb widmet sich dieses Seminar, neben einer kurzen Einführung zur Funktion von Large Language Modellen, im Kern aktueller psychologischer Forschung zu generativer KI. Dazu zählen Chancen und Stärken, z.B. positive Arbeitsergebnisse wie Kreativität, Performanz und Produktivität, aber auch Risiken und Schwächen, wie Heuristiken und Biases der KI. Im Rahmen dessen werden verschiedene Anwendungsfelder, wie beispielsweise der organisationale Kontext, der Health Care Sektor sowie Wissenschaft und Forschung betrachtet.

OBJECTIVES:
Kritische Betrachtung von Large Language Modellen (z.B. ChatGPT) aus der Perspektive der psychologischen Forschung. Sie sind also unter anderem in der Lage, (a) generative künstliche Intelligenz anhand psychologischer Konstrukte und Merkmale zu beurteilen (b) das Erleben und Verhalten von Menschen im Umgang mit generativer künstlicher Intelligenz zu beschreiben, und (c) Chancen und Risiken der Technologie in verschiedenen Kontexten (z.B. Arbeit und Organisation, Health Care Sektor, Wissenschaft und Forschung, etc.) zu beurteilen.

Title: Einführung in aktuelle Forschungsthemen der Numerischen Mechanik

CONTENT:
Basierend auf ihrer aktuellen wissenschaftlichen Relevanz werden in jedem Wintersemester Forschungsthemen aus dem Gebiet der Numerischen Mechanik ausgewählt und den Studierenden vermittelt. Die ausgewählten Themen lassen sich typischerweise einem der folgenden übergeordneten Themenblöcke zuordnen:

1. Numerische Fluidmechanik
2. Numerische Festkörper-, Struktur- und Kontaktmechanik
3. Multiphysikalische, Mehrfeld- und gekoppelte Probleme
4. Mehrskalenprobleme
5. Dimensionsreduzierte Modellierung
6. Probabilistische Modellierung.

Welche Forschungsthemen im jeweiligen Semester behandelt werden, wird rechtzeitig vor Vorlesungsbeginn auf der Lernplattform Moodle sowie der Homepage des Lehrstuhls bekannt gegeben. Für jedes der Themen werden zuerst die notwendigen physikalischen und mathematischen Grundlagen vermittelt, um anschließend aktuelle und innovative wissenschaftliche Entwicklungen und Fragestellungen in diesem Bereich diskutieren zu können. Die behandelten Inhalte zu jedem Forschungsthema erstrecken sich dabei von den zugrundeliegenden Modellannahmen und den beschreibenden Differentialgleichungen bis hin zu geeigneten Diskretisierungsmethoden, Fragestellungen der algorithmischen Umsetzung und ausgewählten Simulationsergebnissen.

Title: Einführung in das rechnergestützte Werkstoffdesign
Description:
CONTENT:
Modeling and simulation are an important part of modern materials science. Computational methods and corresponding theories can be used to calculate the properties of materials from their fundamentals, enabling their development for future applications. The goal of this lecture series is to provide insight into the exciting world of computational materials science and an understanding of how it can be used for materials design. The entire course material is taught over two semesters: this course (winter semester) addresses the topics of nano-scale materials simulation: 
- Introduction to computational materials science, i.e. modeling over length scales. 
- Calculations of fundamental material properties (using density functional theory)
- Handling of material databases and basic principles of material informatics
- Thermodynamic modeling based on the CalPhaD approach

(Optionally, the follow-up course Introduction to Computational Materials Design 2 can be attended in the summer semester. During the summer course, the following topics are covered: Modeling and simulation of microstructure evolution in the solid state, linking simulations in the microstructural and macroscopic levels, and application of machine learning methods.) 

Guest lectures are planned to deepen the topics of materials informatics and data-driven materials modeling.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the lecture, students will be able to explain different methods and aspects of computational materials design. Among others, this includes  multi-scale materials modeling, materials informatics, and some of the common modeling theories based on the fundamentals of quantum chemistry, thermodynamics, solid state physics, and materials science. Students will be able to distinguish between the different modeling methods and apply them to a given problem. After completing the lecture, students will be able to perform simple calculations of basic material properties using the methods learned, identify important influencing parameters and evaluate the results.

Title: Einführung in das wissenschaftliche Arbeiten
Description:
CONTENT:
In diesem Kurs lernen Sie die Grundlagen des wissenschaftlichen Arbeitens kennen, indem Sie sich mit den Merkmalen, Zielen und Vorgehen der wissenschaftlichen Arbeitsweise befassen. Sie werden verschiedene Arten von wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten betrachten und die Qualitätsanforderungen an diese durch induktive Schlussfolgerungen ableiten.

Des Weiteren werden Sie sich mit ethischen Fragen des wissenschaftlichen Arbeitens bezüglich Suche, Auswahl und Verwendung von Informationen auseinandersetzen, mit besonderem Blick auf den Einsatz von KI-Tools wie ChatGPT, DeepL u.ä.

Zudem werden Sie auch pragmatisches Wissen erwerben, wobei Sie an die realistische Planung und eigenverantwortliche Umsetzung Ihres wissenschaftlichen Arbeitsprojekts herangeführt werden. Dabei lernen Sie, wie man eine systematische Recherche durchführt, korrekt zitiert und paraphrasiert und durch Vertiefung Ihres Wissens über den Aufbau schriftlicher wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten erlangen Sie Fertigkeiten in der Erstellung, Überarbeitung und Korrektur eigener Texte. Für Ihr Schreibportfolio werden Sie eine Diagrammbeschreibung und eine annotierte Bibliographie erstellen, was als Vorbereitung auf das Verfassen einer aktuellen Fachseminararbeit oder Ihrer Abschlussarbeit angesehen werden kann.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme sind die Studiereden in der Lage, ihren wissenschaftlichen Arbeitsprozess zu strukturieren, Informationen aus wissenschaftlichen Quellen inhaltlich zu erschließen und diese nach den erlernten ethischen und formalen Kriterien in die eigene Arbeit einzubinden.

Title: Einführung in die Bioprozesstechnik
Description:
CONTENT:

In ca. 1/3 dieses Moduls werden unterschiedliche biotechnologisch genutzte Systeme vorgestellt und deren biochemischen Hintergrund kurz erläutert. Der Schwerpunkt der Vorlesung liegt in der Beschreibung unterschiedlicher industrieller Prozesse und deren verfahrenstechnischen Umsetzung.    - Technological Overview: Description of the RNA-seq workflow, including library preparation, sequencing technologies, and data generation.
   - Applications: Insights into various applications such as identifying differentially expressed genes, alternative splicing, and discovering new transcripts.

2. Assessing Sequencing Data Quality Before Mapping
   - Pre-sequencing Quality Checks: Importance of sample quality and integrity.
   - Quality Control Metrics: Key metrics like base quality scores, GC content, and adapter contamination.
   - Quality Assessment Tools: Introduction to tools such as FastQC and MultiQC for evaluating raw sequencing data.

3. Trimming Sequencing Reads
   - Importance of Trimming: Explanation of why trimming is necessary to remove low-quality bases and adapter sequences.
   - Trimming Tools: Introduction to popular trimming software such as Trimmomatic, Cutadapt, and fastp.
   - Best Practices: Guidelines for setting trimming parameters and assessing the impact of trimming on data quality.

4. Mapping (RNA) Sequencing Data
   - Alignment Algorithms: Overview of algorithms and tools like STAR, HISAT2, and Kallisto.
   - Reference Genomes: Importance of using the correct reference genome and annotation files.
   - Post-Alignment Quality Checks: Evaluating the quality of aligned reads using metrics such as coverage uniformity and insert size distribution, mapping rate, unique alignments, and multi-mapping reads.
   - Biological Variation: Understanding sources of biological variation and technical variability in RNA-seq experiments.

5. Determining Gene Expression from RNA-seq Data
   - Counting Strategies: Methods for counting reads mapped to individual genes using tools like HTSeq, featureCounts, and Kallisto.
   - Normalization Techniques: Importance of normalizing count data for library size and sequencing depth with methods like TPM, FPKM, and RPKM.

6. Handling Outliers
   - Identifying Outliers: Techniques for detecting outlier samples and genes in RNA-seq data.
   - Managing Outliers: Strategies for addressing outliers, including filtering, transformation, and robust statistical methods.

7. Differential Gene Expression Analysis with R and DESeq2
   - Experimental Design: Importance of proper experimental design and replication.
   - DESeq2 Workflow: Step-by-step guide for using DESeq2 for differential gene expression analysis, including input preparation, model fitting, and result interpretation.
   - Visualization: Creating visualizations such as MA-plots, heatmaps, and volcano plots to represent differential expression results.

8. Functional and Pathway Enrichment Analysis
   - Gene Set Enrichment Analysis: Overview of tools and techniques for functional enrichment analysis.
   - Pathway Analysis: Understanding biological pathways using tools like KEGG and Reactome.
   - Result Interpretation: Integrating enrichment results with biological knowledge to gain meaningful insights.

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing the module, students will be able to:
•	Apply knowledge and methods for bioinformatics data analysis
•	Develop an understanding of the analysis of high-throughput RNA sequencing data
•	Understand the biological fundamentals of RNA sequencing projects
•	Learn and apply tools and methods for RNA sequencing data analysis
•	Independently conduct a project for comparative analysis of RNA sequencing data
•	Use the command line and bioinformatics tools for RNA sequencing data proficiently
•	Apply basic statistical concepts in RNA sequencing data analysis

Title: Einführung in die Dauerüberwachung von Tragwerken
Description:
CONTENT:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) describes the automated and continuous monitoring of engineering structures, including high-rises, bridges, offshore platforms, and power plants. In contrast to non-destructive testing, permanently installed sensors are used and no personnel is required on site. Moreover, the objective is different, as the aim is not to analyze pre-existing damage scenarios but to diagnose future damages that occur during monitoring, for example, due to gradually developing damages (corrosion, support settlements) and extreme events (impacts of any sort, floods, storms, earthquakes).

OBJECTIVES:
During the course, the attendees will acquire the following competencies:
- The ability to distinguish SHM from non-destructive testing, and to evaluate which approach is most suitable to the specific monitoring application 
- Internalize the basic assumptions and limitations of SHM
- Avoid common mistakes related to instrumenting engineering structures
- Learn how to preprocess data, extract damage-sensitive features, and detect, localize and quantify damages
- Become acquired with established machine learning approaches to evaluate damage-sensitive features
- Develop a basic understanding of digital twins and their application in SHM
- Improve basic coding skills in MATLAB, and access pre-coded SHM packages in MATLAB

Title: Einführung in die Intuitionistische Logik
Description:
CONTENT:
Dieser Kurs ist für Studierende aus allen Fachrichtungen geöffnet, die sich für die logisch-formale Charakterisierung von Konstruktions- und Argumentationsverfahren interessieren (Philosophie, Mathematik, Informatik, Ingenieurwissenschaften). 

Die intuitionistische Logik ist eine Abschwächung der klassischen Logik. Sie entstand als ein Versuch, der anti-platonistischen, konstruktivistischen Auffassung der Mathematik gerecht zu werden, die gegen 1911 von dem holländischen Mathematiker und Philosophen L. E. J. Brouwer ausgearbeitet wurde und „Intuitionismus“ genannt wurde. Charakteristisch für die intuitionistische Logik ist eine radikal epistemische Auffassung der Wahrheit, der zufolge etwas genau dann wahr ist, wenn es rational akzeptierbar oder gerechtfertigt behauptbar ist – was im Falle mathematischer Sätze so viel heißt wie: Wenn es beweisbar ist. Diese konstruktivistische Auffassung von Wahrheit entspricht auch den Ingenieurwissenschaften und der Informatik: Es reicht nicht zu behaupten, dass eine Aussage wahr ist, sondern z.B. in der Geometrie oder Mechanik muss ein Beweis mit einem geometrischen oder mechanischem Konstruktionsverfahren vorliegen, in der Arithmetik ein Beweis mit einem Berechnungsverfahren, in der Informatik ein Beweis mit einem Computerprogramm. Aber auch bei Gericht reicht eine Anklage nicht aus, sondern es muss ein Beweisverfahren für die Anklage vorgelegt werden.

Der Kurs ist folgendermaßen aufgebaut:
1. Historische und Philosophische Hinweise auf die intuitionistische Auffassung der Mathematik
2. Klassische vs. Intuitionistische Logik; realistische vs. Epistemische Auffassung der Wahrheit. Die “Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov” Erklärung der intuitionistisch verstandenen logischen Operatoren.
3. Semantische Charakterisierung der intuitionistischen Aussagenlogik via Kripke-Modelle.
4. Syntaktische Charakterisierung der intuitionistischen Aussagen- und Prädikatenlogik
(Hinweise).
5. Beziehungen zwischen modalen und intuitionistischen Logik: Gödels modale Übersetzung der intuitionistischen Logik.

OBJECTIVES:
Tiefes Verständnis der intuitionistischen Aussagenlogik.

Title: Einführung in die Methoden der Aquatischen Systembiologie
Description:
CONTENT:
The excercise offers a broad overview of the research in aquatic systems biology. The focus lies on the introduction to different methods for assessment and evaluation of aquatic systems. The methods are introduced for several focus topics (habitat structure, water chemistry, sediment quality, macroinvertebrates, periphyton and macrophytes, fishes, bioindication) in theory and impelmented in a consecutive exercise. The content of the excercise covers: sampling design and sampling methods (abiotic); habitat structure analysis, sediment analysis,  physikochemical parameters; sampling design and sampling methods (biotic); species determination and taxonomy (phytobenthos, makrophytes, macroinvertebrates, fish); data management and statistics.

OBJECTIVES:
After attendance of the course the students possess deep practical knowledge of ecological assessments. They learn essential methods for planning, setup, procedure and analysis of assessments in aquatic ecology and are able to apply them. They aquire taxonomic knowledge (fish, macroinvertebrates, periphyton, macrophytes) and are able to conduct qualitative and quantitative analysis. the students also get introduced into statistical analysis (multivariate and univariate).

Title: Einführung in die Modallogik
Description:
CONTENT:
Die Modallogik ist der Zweig der Logik, der sich mit dem logischen Verhalten von Aussagen befasst, in denen Ausdrücke wie „möglich“, „unmöglich“, „notwendig“ oder „kontingent“ vorkommen. Der Kurs richtet sich an Studierende aller Fachrichtungen, die sich für die formale Charakterisierung von Argumentationsverfahren interessieren (Philosophie, Mathematik, Informatik). 

Der Aufbau des Kurses ist wie folgt:
i) Historische Einführung (mit Verweisen auf die klassische Aussagenlogik)
ii) Arten von Modalitäten: alethische, deontische, temporale, epistemische usw.
iii) Monomodale und multimodale aussagenlogische Sprachen
iv) Kripkes Semantik für modale aussagenlogische Sprachen: Rahmen, Bewertungen und Modelle.
vi) Wichtige Beziehungen zwischen Eigenschaften von Rahmen (Reflexivität, Transitivität,
Serialität …) und modalen Schemata (T, 4, D …)
vii) Modale axiomatische- und Tableaux- Kalküle für die Systeme K, T, D, K4, S4, S5
viii) Korrektheit und Vollständigkeit: Beweis des Korrektheits- und des Vollständigkeitssatzes)

OBJECTIVES:
Tiefes Verständnis der modalen Aussagenlogik.
Skills: ['Logic', 'Formal methods', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving']

Title: Einführung in die nukleare Sicherheitsanalyse von Kernreaktoren mit Reaktorsicherheitssoftware
Description:
CONTENT:
The course aims at giving the participants a full and comprehensive overview of: 

- The principles of nuclear reactor safety and system behaviour from the point of view of nuclear safety. 

- The principles of uncertainty and sensitivity analysis applied to nuclear reactor simulations and their importance in the evaluation of the simulations’ results.

Main topics:

- Introduction to the basic layout of modern light water reactors

- Understand the fundamentals of nuclear reactor safety evaluations and the role of regulations. 

- Carry out simulations of relevant safety scenarios with state-of-the-art system analysis codes. 

- Understand the basis of uncertainty propagation and sensitivity determination in the results of safety simulations. 

- Carry out uncertainty and sensitivity calculations using system analysis codes.

OBJECTIVES:
- steady-state model simulation

- transient simulation

- live-visualisation of simulations

- simualtion results analysis and interpretation  

- uncertainty and sensitivity safety analysis

The simulation programs including ATHLET, ATLAS and SUSA from GRS gGmbH (Gesellschaft für Reaktorsicherheit) will be used on the computers in the department's PC-pool.
Skills: ['Nuclear reactor safety', 'Simulation software', 'Uncertainty analysis', 'Sensitivity analysis', 'Risk assessment']
