Title: Model Reference Adaptive Control
Description:
CONTENT:
The Model Reference Adaptive Control (MRAC) design strategy offers various methods to design controllers for systems with inherent uncertainties and/or nonlinearities while maintaining superior reliability and performance compared to classical design strategies.
Significant progress in the fields of stability and robustness analysis for adaptive systems enabled the use of these techniques in flight control applications, which were also successfully demonstrated in various flight tests.


Specifically the following topics will be addressed:
- Mathematical Preliminaries
- Classical Model Reference Adaptive Control (direct and indirect)
- MRAC with Closed-Loop Reference Models
- Neural Networks
- Concurrent Learning Adaptive Control
- GP MRAC
- Command Governor Based Adaptive Control
- L1 Adaptive Control

In each chapter the presented theory is demonstrated using aerial applications.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module, the student have the capabilities to
- understand the mathematical background of adaptive control theory
- understand the conceptual differences of direct and indirect model reference adaptive control frameworks
- understand the effects of reference model modifications such as hedging, closed-loop reference models or command governor modification
- understand the universal function approximation using neural networks
- understand the learning characteristics of concurrent learning and GP MRAC
- understand the filtering aspects of L1 and command governor based adaptive control
- apply the theory of various adaptive control architectures to appropriate examples
- analyze robustness and stability of a variety of adaptive control schemes
- evaluate benefits and drawbacks of adaptive control frameworks
- create their own adaptive control architectures, both theoretically and in Matlab / Simulink

Title: Modeling, Control and Design of Wind Energy Systems
Description:
CONTENT:
The course offers a broad introduction to the engineering principles underlying the operation of wind turbines, as well as their design. The course is organized in the following five main modules:
• Introduction: introduction to wind energy, and overview of wind energy systems and wind turbines; the wind resource and its characteristics; anatomy of a modern wind turbine; wind turbine components; electrical aspects.
• Wind turbine aerodynamics: overview of rotor aerodynamics; one-dimensional momentum theory and Betz limit; wake swirl; airfoils; blade element momentum theory, dynamic inflow; unsteady corrections, blade tip and hub losses, dynamic stall, stall delay and three-dimensional effects; deterministic and stochastic wind models.
• Dynamics and aeroservoelasticity: rigid and elastic flapping and lagging blade; the rotor as a filter, aerodynamic damping, flutter, limit cycle oscillations; loads; stability analysis; aeroservoelastic models of wind turbines; aeroservohydroelastic models for off-shore applications.
• Wind turbine control: overview and architecture of wind turbine control systems; on-board sensors; supervisory control; regulation strategies; trimmers, load-reducing control, dampers; load and wind observers.
• Wind turbine design: overview of design criteria and certification guidelines; aerodynamic design; structural design; design and choice of sub-systems and components.

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing the course, students will have an understanding of the physical processes underlying the energy conversion process from wind. They will have a solid basic knowledge of wind turbine aerodynamics and structural dynamics, and they will understand the main strategies used for controlling these machines over their complete operating range. A specific goal of the course is to provide students with a multidisciplinary vision on the physics of wind energy systems, and an understanding of the methods used for their modeling and simulation. A particular emphasis will be placed on design, and on the effects of design choices on the cost of energy.
Skills: ['Control systems', 'Renewable energy systems', 'Mechanical design', 'Thermodynamics', 'Fluid mechanics', 'Simulation software', 'MATLAB']

Title: Modeling Future Mobility Systems
Description:
CONTENT:
Transportation systems are seen as some of the most pervasive and influential systems in any society or economy as they are key enablers for significant achievements, e.g., individual mobility, trade, globalization, and wealth. Hence, transportation systems have a substantial socio-economic impact but also face tremendous challenges as transportation must (in a best-case scenario) meet the triple bottom line, fulfilling economic, ecological, and social requirements. To achieve this goal, today's and future transportation systems for freight and passenger transportation become more complex, especially with respect to intermodal freight transportation, autonomous driving, shared mobility, and the physical internet. Enormous challenges but also significant benefits for both society and investors remain in the next decade.

This course combines specific lecture parts with seminar elements. In the seminar part, teams of 2-3 students will analyze a novel transportation concept using operations research methods. Students learn how to develop and implement an appropriate mathematical model and solution methodology to solve the respective planning problem in a manner that is sufficient to allow for applied managerial analyses.

Title: Modellierung komplexer soziotechnischer Systeme
Description:
CONTENT:
The seminar provides basic and advanced knowledge of modeling complex socio-technical systems with a focus on Safety-II approaches and systemic human factors methods. In addition to a theoretical overview of Safety-I and Safety-II and the paradigm shift in safety research towards resilience engineering, the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) according to Hollnagel is introduced, practically applied and critically reflected upon.
The aim is to acquire the ability to independently model, analyze and reflect on dynamic work contexts in terms of functional interaction and emergent system behavior.

The seminar can be roughly divided into the following three sections and their contents:

Frontal teaching theoretical part
•	Historical overview, Safety I vs. Safety II, basics of complex systems & socio-technical perspectives, systems theory, emergence and feedback
•	Overview of various systemic HFE methods

Interactive practical part
•	Theoretical and practical basics of FRAM, case studies
•	Introduction to software tools (FMV, FRAMalyse)
•	Guest lecture by an international FRAM expert

Project work
•	Presentation and discussion Topic selection/case study
•	Application to case study 
•	Iterative consultations with lecturer
•	Project presentation & discussion

OBJECTIVES:
After participating in the module, participants will be able to:

Theoretical Understanding and Basics in Safety Science
1.	explain the paradigm shift from Safety-I to Safety-II theoretically and classify it in terms of safety science,
2.	differentiate between classic and modern safety analysis methods in terms of objectives, underlying system assumptions and application contexts,
3.	name systemic Human Factors and Ergonomics (HFE) methods and describe their strengths and limitations.

Method Application and Analysis Skills
4.	apply the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) methodically correct,
5.	master the use of software tools such as FMV and FRAMalyse for functional modeling,
6.	independently select a proper case study and model and analyze it using FRAM based on a self-developed research question
7.	systemically describe complex interactions in sociotechnical systems and derive potential emergent risks.

Reflexion, Evaluation and Communication
8.	critically assess technology impacts in complex human-machine systems considering systemic perspectives
9.	communicate constructively in interdisciplinary tandems, reflect together, and work on problems with methodological support
10.	present own results scientifically sound and discuss critically in academic discourse
Skills: ['System modeling software', 'Resilience engineering', 'Human factors', 'Safety engineering and risk assessment', 'Simulation software']

Title: Modellierung von Unsicherheit in den Ingenieurwissenschaften
Description:
CONTENT:
Engineers are constantly faced with the task of producing quantitative estimates and making decisions regarding the safety, reliability and performance of various systems. More often than not, these tasks must be carried out under limited information and significant uncertainty. Despite the progress in mathematical modeling and advances in numerical simulation techniques, our actual predictive ability has not commensurately increased. Engineers must account for the various sources of uncertainty (e.g. environmental effects, physical properties, model parameters) in order to reach rational conclusions. This course presents the necessary tools and methodological framework for dealing with uncertainty including basic elements of probabilistic machine learning.

OBJECTIVES:
Students will learn the basic mathematical framework of probability theory and to a lesser extent of statistics. Students will get exposed to modeling engineering problems that are characterized by random variability and uncertainty using the tools of probability theory. Students will learn the basic elements and  properties of the Monte Carlo method and will be able to apply it in solving problems modeled with multiple random variables. Students will be able to estimate model parameters with the help of data by using methods such as maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation. Special attention will be paid to problems of probabilistic regression and classification (i.e. probabilistic machine learning).  Students will get exposed to the basic concepts of decision-making and design in the presence of uncertainty and will be able to solve pertinent problems.

Title: Modellierung von Unsicherheiten und Daten im Maschinenwesen

4) Uncertainty modeling
5) Monte Carlo
6) Estimation and model building

   - Regression/Classification
   - Dimensionality reduction

OBJECTIVES:

Title: Models in the study of human behavior
Description:
CONTENT:
Formal models (in mathematical or programming language) figure prominently in the natural science (e.g., physics), but less so in the behavioral sciences (e.g., behavioral economics, psychology). The lack of models – particularly of those that attempt to explain the cognitive processes underlying human behavior – led to the emergence of distracting labels and narratives (e.g., “biases”, “thinking fast and slow”). These distractors are remarkably popular in behavioral sciences as well as in business and society, yet they have done so little to advance our understanding of why people behave the way they do. This course shows how modeling is invaluable for gaining genuine insights into human behavior and how it can drive empirical research and real-world applications (e.g., policy-making). Some state-of-the-art examples are presented by the students in the mock conferences.


Some guiding questions and discussion points are:

- What the behavioral sciences want and where they have gone astray? 
- Why the behavioral sciences cannot help but to model? 
- What are scientific models of human behavior? 
- What can the behavioral sciences learn from the natural sciences and their models? What not?
- Which role do cognition and the environment play in the explanation of human behavior?
- Case studies in decision making under risk and uncertainty (descriptive, predictive, process/cognitive models)
- Relations among and integration of models within and across model classes
-  Modeling and the construction, development, and testing of theories about human behavior and cognition
- Real-world applications of models of human behavior and cognition

OBJECTIVES:
Upon completion of the module, students possess profound knowledge about the utility and limitations of formal modeling approaches to the study of human behavior. Specifically, students are familiar with the goals and problems of the behavioral sciences and understand how they can be addressed through formal modeling. They know different model classes – including some state-of-the-art models in decision making – and which research question and inferences they are appropriate for. Based on this knowledge, students are able to interpret and evaluate models in the relevant literature and to make reasonable modeling choices for future research or applied projects. In addition, students improved their ability to effectively communicate the main ideas and results of a published paper or a broader research project in concise scientific talks.

Title: Moderne Gesellschaften im Zeitalter der Digitalisierung
Description:
CONTENT:
Gesellschaften sind grundlegend von Wandel, Umbrüchen und Transformationen geprägt (z.B. aus historischer Perspektive durch die französische oder die industrielle Revolution), welche oftmals unter dem Begriff der „gesellschaftlichen Modernisierung“ firmieren. Die Digitalisierung kann als eine weitere grundlegende Veränderung gesellschaftlicher Beziehungen, Verhältnisse und Strukturen als Teil der Modernisierung gelesen werden. Die digitale Transformation kann zum Beispiel die Organisation von Arbeit (z.B. Nutzung digitaler Infrastrukturen für das Arbeiten im Home-Office), den Wandel der Medienlandschaft (Zunahme der Nutzung und Vielfalt digitaler Plattformen und sozialer Netzwerke) oder auch unsere basalen, alltäglichen Handlungen (Nutzung von Smartphones, Messaging-Diensten, Liefer-Apps) betreffen. Jedoch gilt es trotz der Innovationspotentiale der Digitalisierung, diese nicht nur als eine weitere Form von „Fortschritt“ einer sich immer weiter modernisierenden Gesellschaft zu begreifen. Vielmehr sollen aus soziologischer Perspektive, wie auch schon bei anderen tiefgreifenden gesellschaftlichen Umbrüchen, die Wechselwirkungen, Herausforderungen und Spannungsverhältnisse einer solchen „digitalen Moderne“ ergründet werden. 
Das Seminar richtet sich an ein interdisziplinäres Publikum und soll eine Einführung in zentrale Begriffe, Themen und Theorieansätze der Soziologie bieten, welche gerade im Zuge der Digitalisierung der Gesellschaft vor neue Herausforderungen gestellt werden. Den Teilnehmer:innen soll dahingehend ein Einblick gegeben werden, wie die Digitalisierung soziologische Perspektiven, Fragestellungen und Erklärungen verändert, neue Sichtweisen ermöglicht und notwendig macht.

OBJECTIVES:
Das Lernziel des Seminars besteht darin, dass die Studierenden ein Gefühl für soziologisches Denken entwickeln und soziologische Theorien und Ansätze auf aktuelle Phänomene der digitalen Transformation anwenden können, sowohl hinsichtlich der Einordnung der Digitalisierung in den Kontext gesellschaftlicher Modernisierung als auch der Entwicklung analytischer Perspektiven auf die Gegenstände einer soziologischen Erforschung digitaler Phänomene.

Title: Moderne Methoden der Mikrobiellen Ökologie
Description:
CONTENT:
Molekulare Methoden spielen in der mikrobiellen Ökologie eine sehr wichtige Rolle, um die Vielfalt der Mikroorganismen in der Umwelt zu erfassen. Aber auch neue Ansätze zur Isolierung bisher ungekannter Prokaryonten sind für das Verständnis über das Funktionieren von Ökosystemen von grosser Bedeutung. Entsprechend wird in dem Modul auf ein breites Spektrum von Methoden eingegangen, die in der modernen mikrobiellen Ökologie genutzt werden. Hierzuzählen neben PCR basierten Verfahren auch Hochdurchsatzsequenziertechniken aber auch der Einsatz stabiler Isotope. Aber auch klassische Verfahren die in der Routineanalytik eine wichtige Rolle spielen wie Biomassemessungen oder Enzymaktivitätsbestimmungen werden vorgestellt und in der Praxis erlernt. Abschliessend werden auch zukünftige Ausrichtungen, insbesondere im Bezug auf Proteomic und Metabolomic diskutiert

OBJECTIVES:
Nach Abschluss der Lehrveranstaltung soll der Student in der Lage sein, selbstständig eine Auswahl aus der "Methodenbox" zu treffen, die für seine Fragestellung am Besten passen. Der Student soll vertraut mit den Vor- und Nachteilen einzelner Methoden sein und so die Komplimentarität und Synergien von einzelnen Ansätzen zu erkennen. Ferner soll der Student in der Lage sein entsprechende Methoden selbstständig zu nutzen, Z.B. im Rahmen einer Masterarbeit oder Promotion. Durch das Seminar sollen Kenntnisse aus der aktuellen Forschung genutzt werden um Perspektiven der mikrobiellen Ökologie für die Zukunft zu erarbeiten

Title: Molekularbiologie der Pflanzen
Description:
CONTENT:
This lecture series examines plant based solutions to global challenges—especially climate mitigation, adaptation, and resilience—while building a molecular understanding of how plants work. Using Arabidopsis thaliana as the central model, the course connects gene function and genome analysis with functional genomics and systems biology, and develops core concepts in photomorphogenesis, proteolysis, and membrane trafficking. A guest session with the TUM Venture Lab spotlights innovation and start up perspectives on food security and climate solutions. 
Each topic begins with a short conceptual primer followed by recent examples and guided discussion.
•	Plant based solutions to global crises; frameworks for mitigation/adaptation/resilience; guest lecture with TUM Venture Lab/start ups. 
•	Gene function and genome analysis in Arabidopsis; from sequencing/annotation to genotype to phenotype logic. 
•	Functional genomics & systems biology: tools, data types, and integrative network thinking. 
•	Mutant analysis strategies and genetic approaches in plants. 
•	Photomorphogenesis & light perception: molecular circuits and developmental outcomes. 
•	Proteolysis & the ubiquitin–proteasome system: from tags to turnover. 
•	Membrane trafficking & transport: endomembrane system, vesicle routes, transporters.  
•	Targets for engineering and nature based solutions for sustainability and food security.

OBJECTIVES:
Intended Learning Outcomes. 
By the end of the module, students will be able to:
•	Explain regulation of gene expression and genome organization in plants and interpret functional genomics readouts (e.g., transcriptomics). 
•	Compare plant based options for climate mitigation/adaptation/resilience using mechanistic reasoning and case studies. 
•	Analyze experiments in photomorphogenesis, proteolysis, and membrane transport and link them to development/physiology. 
•	Interpret Arabidopsis mutant/phenotype evidence and formulate predictions for genetic tests or engineering targets.  
•	Develop a working understanding of systems biology in Arabidopsis.
Skills: ['Molecular plant sciences', 'Genomics', 'Systems biology', 'Functional genomics', 'Arabidopsis thaliana', 'Gene function analysis']

Title: Molekulare Biologie biotechnologisch relevanter Pilze
Description:
CONTENT:
In this course, you will learn about the diversity, physiology and biotechnological applicabilities of fungi. A focus will be the unique capability of fungi to degrade and convert plant biomass. Exemplary contents that will be discussed are: gene technology (bio-engineering), plant cell walls as substrate and their degradation, signaling pathways of substrate perception, biotechnological applications of enzyme and small-molecule production, as well as application of fungi in the agricultural industry. 
In the practical/seminar part of the course, selected topics will be discussed in more detail by student presentations and/or with the help of practical examples. In addition, an excursion (e.g. to the Clariant Sunliquid demonstration plant in Straubing) is planned, to showcase fungi in action.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful participation in the module, the students will have advanced knowledge of the biology, genetics and biotechnological applications of fungi for the production and development of natural and artificial biocompounds. 
They will be able to: 
• recapitulate the fungal metabolic capabilities
• comprehend and name the fundamental signaling pathways for metabolic adaptation
• using selected examples, classify the respective enzyme systems and their functions in anabolic/catabolic reactions
• understand the molecular techniques for genome manipulation and strain development and discuss them
• critically assess the pros and cons of the presented production systems. 
Moreover, the module is intended to help develop problem-solving skills as well as to foster the interest for eukaryotic microbiology, it's advantages and disadvantages, and the importance particularly of filamentous fungi for environment and industry.

Title: Molekulare Biotechnologie
Description:
CONTENT:
In this lecture we will address the use of genetically modified microbes, plants and animals for the production of proteins and low molecular weight substances. We will explain the basics of laboratory methods necessary for genetic modifications to achieve high level expression of foreign genes. The basics of fermentation and protein purification will be shown as well as immunological tests. Methods of genetical modifications of higher animals and plants as well as their metabolic engeneering will be an issue.

OBJECTIVES:
After this lecture students will be able to understand how genetically modified organisms are produced and how they can be used for production of commercial products.

Sie besitzen ein grundlegendes Verständnis für Methoden der Genom-Modifizierung und können die praktischen und ethischen Pro- und Cons dieser Technologien bei Säugetieren bewerten. Die Studierenden können die physiologischen Regelkreise beschreiben und bewerten und moderne quantitativen Messverfahren sowie molekulare Schlüsseltechnologien erklären und illustrieren. Sie bekommen zudem einen Einblick in Einsatzmöglichkeiten als Biomarker oder in Therapien. Title: Molekülspektroskopie
Description:
CONTENT:
In the course of the lecture the basics of the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter will be worked out, especially the time-dependent perturbation theory will be derived and important terms of spectroscopy will be introduced, e.g. the transition dipole moment, resonant transitions, Raman scattering or term symbols. These fundamentals are used to discuss rotational, vibrational and electronic spectroscopy, as well as nuclear spin and electron spin resonance. One focus is the interpretation of experimental spectroscopic investigations.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending the lecture, students will be able to assign spectra of different energy ranges of individual degrees of freedom in molecules, to understand and interpret the spectra, and to derive important physico-chemical quantities from them.
Skills: ['Spectroscopy', 'Quantum mechanics', 'Mathematical and statistical reasoning', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Research-oriented mindset']

Title: Molekülspektroskopie und Quantenmechanik für LAG
Description:
CONTENT:
Einführung in die quantenmechanischen Grundlagen der Molekülspektroskopie sowie zum Aufbau der Materie; Beschreibung der molekularen Bewegung: Rotation, Schwingung, Elektronische Anregung, Elektronenspin; Spektroskopische Methoden zur Beobachtung dieser Bewegungen: Mikrowellen-, Infrarot, Raman, UV-Spektrokopie. Der Einfluss von molekularer Symmetrie auf die Spektroskopie; Instrumentelle Grundlagen: Spektrometer und Lichtquellen, ausgewählte Beispiele der Anwendung von Spektroskopie in der chemischen Analyse.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme an der Modulveranstaltung Molekülspektroskopie und Quantenmechanik für LAG sollen die Studenten den Aufbau der Materie unter dem Gesichtspunkt einer modernen quantenmechanischen Beschreibung verstehen. Sie sind mit dem Konzept der Elektronenkonfiguration vertraut und kennen die Bildungsprinzipien für Mehrelektronensysteme sowie die Konzepte der chemischen Bindung. Weiterhin lernen die Studenten die Operatorschreibweise in der Quantenmechanik kennen und sind mit Größen wie den Eigenwerten zum Drehimpuls- und Spinoperator vertraut. Sie sind in der Lage, diese Größen für die Beschreibung der Molekülrotation und der Kernspin- sowie der Elektronenspinresonanz einzusetzen. Sie kennen die quantenmechanische Beschreibung von harmonischen und anharmonischen Schwingungen und können die Konzepte zur Analyse von Molekülschwingungen anwenden. Insgesamt lernen die Studenten folgende Spektroskopien kennen: µ-Wellen-, IR-, Raman- und UV-Vis-Spektroskopie. Sie sind in der Lage, Spektren der aufgelisteten Spektroskopiearten zu verstehen und diese kritisch zu bewerten. Die Studenten lernen zudem, Informationen über Moleküle aus den jeweiligen Spektren zu extrahieren. Dabei wird den Studenten die Bedeutung in der chemischen Analytik vermittelt.
Skills: ['Spectroscopy', 'Quantum mechanics', 'Molecular spectroscopy', 'Mathematical and statistical reasoning', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Research-oriented mindset']

Title: Motivation to Go! - Stagnation überwinden und loslegen
Description:
CONTENT:
Kennst du das? Du nimmst dir fest vor, regelmäßig in die Vorlesungen zu gehen, doch deine Vorsätze verpuffen schnell im Alltag. Studienaufgaben wandern von To-Do-Liste zu To-Do-Liste. Die Prüfungsvorbereitung oder die Abschlussarbeit kommen nur schleppend voran.
In diesem Kurzworkshop schauen wir uns an, warum das so ist und wie du das ändern kannst. Wir beleuchten, was hinter Aufschieberitis steckt und wie du deine Motivation gezielt stärken kannst. Mit einer Mischung aus kurzen Inputs und coachenden Methoden entwickelst du Ideen für Lösungen, die wirklich zu dir passen. Dabei geht es nicht um Patentrezepte, sondern darum herauszufinden, was du selbst bewegen kannst.

OBJECTIVES:
Die Studierenden sind in der Lage,
- ihre eigene Motivationslage zu reflektieren.
- die Gründe für das Aufschieben von Aufgaben zu erkennen.
- zu erklären, was Motivation ausmacht.
- konkrete Maßnahmen zu entwickeln, um ihre Motivation im Studium zu steigern.

Title: Multilinear Algebra
Description:
CONTENT:
Multilinear algebra provides a basic set of tools used in various areas of theoretical physics (quantum physics and general relativity) and mathematics (representation theory, differential geometry & topology, algebraic geometry & topology). At its core are variations on the theme of the tensor product. Tensors, in turn, also play an increasingly important role in computer science and numerics.

The course will provide a thorough introduction and overview and cover:
* Modules as generalizations of vector spaces
* Tensor products and tensor powers of modules
* Tensor algebras
* Tensor ranks
* Symmetric and exterior algebras
* Compound matrices
* Hodge star operator
* Noncommutative multilinear polynomials
Skills: ['Multilinear algebra', 'Tensor products', 'Quantum physics', 'General relativity', 'Representation theory', 'Differential geometry', 'Algebraic topology', 'Mathematical and statistical reasoning']

Title: Multiphase flow in engineering systems
Description:
CONTENT:
is an essential course to equip students with the knowledge and dedicated practical skills modern fluidic processes demand. Throughout the lecture, complex interactions of co-existing same or different material phases —liquids, gases, solids are elucidated; thus, the course will be of interest to all students targeting a broad variety of industries, including energy, thermal, chemical, textiles, food, pharmaceutical, etc. where multiphase flows are indispensable. The very fundamentals, such as void fraction concepts, types of flow (two-phase, three-phase, single component, multicomponent) are depicted. Quantities characterizing multiphase flows, governing equations, phenomenological modeling, experimental techniques, to the more advanced and specialized topics including multi-material models, tracking sharp interface, adaptive meshing, porous media flows and applications of multiphase flow are addressed.
Particularly, the prediction of multiphase systems applying computational means and a variety of advanced solution strategies provide competencies and skills to existing courses.
Skills: ['Multiphase flow', 'Fluid mechanics', 'Thermodynamics', 'Heat transfer', 'Engineering systems', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving']

Title: Multiphysikalische Interaktion in mechanischen Systemen
Description:
CONTENT:
The module is aimed at students of all technical disciplines (e.g. mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, physics, etc.). The most important methods in engineering dynamics are derived before multi-physical effects are considered. The lecture is structured as follows:
1. Elements of analytical dynamics (Principle of virtual work und Lagrange formalism)
2. Linearization and stability
3. Vibration modes and mode superposition
4. Introduction to rotor dynamics
5. Continuous systems: linear dynamics and discretization
6. Multifield coupling: Vibro-acoustics
7. Multifield coupling: Elastohydrodynamics
8. Multifield coupling: Electromechanics
9. Multifield coupling: Electromagnetics
10. Multifield coupling: Thermo-elastic coupling

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the module, students will be able to,
- apply the fundamental ideas of analytical mechanics to simple systems,
- linearize simple mechanical systems and analyze them with regard to stability, vibration and transfer behavior,
- apply the key fundamental ideas of the discretization of mechanical systems (e.g. Rayleigh-Ritz, FEM),
- apply the equations of motion of simple rotor systems and evaluate the stability and resonance for such systems,
- analyze the dynamic behavior of multiphysically coupled systems (e.g. electrostatic, piezoelectric, electromagnetic, acoustic and thermal) and understand the principles of discretizing such systems,
- understand selected software to solve simple, multiphysically coupled systems.
Skills: ['Analytical dynamics', 'Multiphysics', 'Mechanical systems', 'Engineering dynamics', 'Virtual work', 'Mechanical design', 'Simulation software']

Title: Munich - 'The Capital of the Movement'
Description:
CONTENT:
The seminar analyses Munich’s importance for the history of National Socialism. Participants get to know the permanent exhibition of the Munich Documentation Center. It traces the path from the founding of the Nazi Party in 1919 through to the elaborate staging of power in Munich as the ‘capital of the movement’ during the regime phase. The seminar looks at the majority society, at structures and individuals, but also considers the repercussions for the persecuted.

Furthermore participants can search for selected topics on their own at an interactive Learning Centre.
Afterwards there will be a city tour to some places of particular importance for the National Socialism - the former 'Parteiviertel'.

Please bring your own pen and writing paper.

OBJECTIVES:
Afterwards participants are aware about the importance of Munich during the National Socialism as a place of foundation of NSDAP.  In addition they will be able to relate to the change of topography of the former district 'Parteiviertel'.
Skills: ['Historical analysis', 'Research-oriented mindset', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Critical thinking and decision-making']

Title: Munich Plan I

-	A capability to draw with precision, skill and care

Title: Myths, Machines, and Futures
Description:
CONTENT:
Myths, Machines, and Futures: Speculative Fiction Across Cultures is a creative writing course that explores speculative storytelling across multiple genres, including science fiction, and hybrid genres that blend elements of the surreal, the futuristic, and the mythic. Students will develop their own original stories while engaging with ideas of alternative futures, technological evolution, and environmental transformation.

The course draws on global speculative traditions, introducing Afrofuturism, South Asian speculative fiction, Latin American magical realism and solarpunk, encouraging students to explore how speculative fiction challenges dominant narratives and imagines new possibilities for the future. 

With a focus on the intersection of science, technology, and society, students will craft narratives that engage with futuristic innovations, ecological sustainability, and cultural change. Whether envisioning utopian green cities, exploring the ethics of AI, or blending mythology with cutting-edge science, this course encourages bold, imaginative storytelling.

OBJECTIVES:
By the end of the course, students will have improved their ability to craft compelling speculative fiction narratives. They will develop critical storytelling skills, including world-building, character development, and thematic exploration whilst gaining insight into the intersection of speculative fiction and global perspectives.

Title: Nachhaltige Architektur, Stadt- und Landschaftsplanung
Description:
CONTENT:
The module consists of a lecture series in which the main approaches to sustainable architecture, urban and landscape planning are presented and the interfaces and interactions of the subject areas within the overall system are analyzed and evaluated.

In the lecture, technical experts convey the basics of planning in the areas of landscape architecture/public space, interactions between spatial and transportation planning, sustainable urban development, accessibility as a basis for designing sustainable mobility, electromobility, renewable energy systems/energy management, climate responsive building, energy use, resource-efficient construction, building materials and materials, construction technology and life cycle engineering, real estate development as well as digital tools for early design planning.

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the module, students will be able to 

- understand general sustainability criteria in architecture, urban and landscape planning in existing and new buildings and groups of buildings and the associated systems in the areas of materials, building concepts, energy supply and integration of renewable energies as well as in urban development, spatial planning, accessibility and mobility. 
- understand the relationships between the consumption of resources (energy, materials, water). 
- analyze issues relating to the use of energy and resources in the building sector with regard to the potential for sustainable planning. 
- evaluate the interrelationships and systemic interaction of the individual planning components to achieve sustainable planning approaches. 
- independently analyse current political and regulatory framework conditions and the issues involved based on the characterized system effects. 
- evaluate the effects of planning decisions on the overall system. 
- independently scrutinize current issues and develop appropriate strategies and solutions. 
- summarize the topics they have learned
Skills: ['Sustainable architecture', 'Urban planning', 'Landscape planning', 'Environmental impact assessment', 'Sustainable design', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving']

Title: Nachhaltige Gebäudeplanung im urbanen Kontext
Description:
CONTENT:
As a supplement to the lecture "Sustainable Architecture, Urban and Landscape Planning", this seminar focuses on cities around the world. Each team of students analyse the level of sustainability of one city and propose improvements with a vision in mind: how to achieve sustainable development that provides both quality of life for all and a positive ecological footprint.

The lecture series presents the essential approaches of sustainable architecture, urban and landscape planning. Different topics are introduced by expert guest lecturers, which form a holistic view of planning sustainable environments. 
During the seminar, this knowledge is applied to the specific case of each city. The selected cities present a variety of conditions such as different climate zones, level of exposure to disasters, population sizes, governmental regimes, and level of income, which provided a comprehensive view of our built environment on a global scale. 

With the help of key performance indicators, each team researches the status quo of one city in different sectors: urban planning, green infrastructure, mobility, energy, water, and waste. Besides those criteria, they also look into crucial aspects such as environmental quality, climate hazards and disaster risk, health, education, happiness, equality, or governance. Through research and critical evaluation, each team assesses the present situation and formulates a vision for their city. With the help of other cases studies, they propose strategies and solutions to improve the current status quo and transform their cities into sustainable urban environments. In short, the course intends to discover what it takes to create a sustainable city of the future.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending the module, the students will be able to:
>>> Identify the interdependencies of relevant topics within a city ecosystem (urban planning, green and blue infrastructure, mobility...)
>>> Assess through given indicators and data research the current sustainability of a city and its present and future challenges to achieve meaningful improvements.
>>> Compare the balance between ecological footprint vs. quality of life in a worldwide view.
>>> Formulate objectives and subsequent activities to achieve sustainability and quality of life in a city.
>>> Plan comprehensive strategies for a city towards its vision for sustainability as a result of the research, assessment and formulated steps in a team-based environment.
>>> Enhance highly collaborative and visual representation skills.
Skills: ['Sustainable architecture', 'Urban planning', 'Urban development', 'Sustainability assessment', 'Quality of life', 'Environmental planning', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving']

Title: Nano- and Microrobotics
Description:
CONTENT:
This course focuses on nano- and microrobotics for biomedical applications. We will first cover key definitions and discuss the basic concepts related to engineering nano- and microrobots. We will discuss physics at the sub-millimeter scale and how scaling laws influence microrobot design. We will then cover materials, fabrication approaches, and power sources for nano- and microrobots. In particular, we will draw attention to stimuli-responsive materials and their applications in engineering wireless, small-scale machines. We will study different types of microrobots based on their functions, specifically actuation, sensing, and locomotion. Within the context of biomedical nanorobotics, we will cover in vivo and in vitro applications of small-scale robotic systems. We will discuss the integration of nano- and microrobots in biological systems, focusing on biocompatibility, and provide examples of bio-applications, including drug delivery, biomolecule sensing, biomanipulation, and microsurgery. Finally, we will address current challenges in the field and take a critical look at potential solutions.

Course topics:
•	Introduction to nano/microrobotics
•	Physics at the sub-millimeter scale
•	Stimuli-responsive materials 
•	Powering small-scale robots
•	Magnetic and optical control 
•	Fabrication methods
•	Actuation 
•	Sensing 
•	Locomotion 
•	Biological applications 
•	Biocompatibility 
•	In vivo integration for drug delivery and microsurgery
•	In vitro implementations for sensing and cell manipulation

OBJECTIVES:
After participating in this course, the student is able to:
1.	Understand the physical working principles of small-scale robotics 
2.	Analyze different power sources for nano/microrobots and explain their limitations
3.	Apply knowledge on material and fabrication approaches for nano/microrobots to solve design problems
4.	Evaluate important criteria for smooth device integration with cells and tissue
5.	Understand and critically analyze research papers in nano/microrobotics and related disciplines 
6.	Apply generated nano/microrobotics knowledge to create ideas for new types of devices

Title: Nanomechanical Systems
Description:
CONTENT:
The module consists of a lecture and accompanying exercises. The lecture deals with the fundamentals of nanomechanical systems. These include the fabrication of freely suspended nanostructures, their vibrational behavior in the linear and nonlinear response regime, actuation and detection mechanisms, damping and Q-factor. Both the classical and quantum mechanical regimes of nanomechanics are covered. Modern applications in sensing or quantum technologies are also discussed.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module, students will acquire knowledge of nanomechanical systems and be able to evaluate developments in this area. In particular, an understanding of the following fundamental concepts will be obtained:
- Vibrational behavior and important characteristics of nanomechanical resonators.
- Behavior in the classical and quantum mechanical regimes
- Applications of nanomechanical systems

Title: Nanomechanical Systems Lab
Description:
CONTENT:
The module is focussing on the experimental investigation of simple nanomechanical systems such as nanostring or membrane resonators. It comprises the experimental characterization and, if possible, the fabrication of the underlying nanomechanical sample, as well as the evaluation of the obtained measurement data, comparison with theory or numerical simulation, and interpretation of the results.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module, students gain practical laboratory experience in working with nanomechanical systems. This includes learning the general basics of laboratory work, the handling of the measurement equipment, as well as the characterization of nanostructured samples. In addition to the experimental part, students acquire knowledge in the computer-aided analysis of measurement data and in the oral as well as written presentation of research results.

Title: Nanotechnologie
Description:
CONTENT:
The lecture focuses on various methods of nanofabrication (optical, electron beam lithography, focused ion beam) and newer emerging techniques (x-ray lithography, nanoimprint, etc.). In particular the physical principles are discussed and limitations for the various methods given. Various synthesis and crystal growth methods for advanced semiconductor nanostructures will be further introduced such as chemical and physical vapor phase epitaxial techniques (MOVPE, MBE, etc.) and the physical growth principles of 0D,1D, and 2D materials highlighted. Examples will be given where these low-dimensional nanostructures are implemented into cutting-edge technological applications. The second part of this lecture deals with specific nanoanalytical methods required for characterization of structural, surface and atomic properties of nanofabricated and synthesized materials. These include electron microscopy, surface analytical methods, ion beam analytical techniques, x-ray techniques, and some new sophisticated techniques, such as atom probe tomography, etc.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful participation and engagement in the module "Nanotechnologies" students will have gained:

1) basic knowledge in nanofabrication and analysis of semiconductor-based devices,
2) the capability to select and evaluate specific nanofabrication methods relevant for nanotechnological applications,
3)  the possibility to explore the limits of the various methodologies,
    the capability for structural, atomic and interface specific analysis of nanostructured  
    materials, and
4)   the important knowledge in understanding the complex interplay between material synthesis, structural and electronic properties of materials, and their effect on functionalities in cutting-edge device applications.

Title: Natur im modernen Kapitalismus
Description:
CONTENT:
The aim of the lecture series is to give participants the opportunity to engage with fundamental questions concerning "impact" and "progress" orientation in society, and, specifically, in the development of entrepreneurial innovations.

Throughout the lecture series, we not only impart specialist expertise from a range of related professional fields, but also give students the opportunity to ask critical and practical questions, exchange ideas and discuss key social issues relating to technology development with renowned academics and practitioners.

The lecture series is divided roughly into 4 blocks that build on each other:

The first part deals with the question of what social progress actually means and how new developments might relate to it. The second part takes a critical look at the question of the extent to which the naturalisation of capitalism can lead to social progress. The third part deals with the potential of nature for entrepreneurial opportunities. Finally, the last part deals with the extent to which cross-species perspectives can meaningfully drive design and innovation processes in practice.

OBJECTIVES:
- Learn important fundamentals of the issues and meaning of societal "impact", societal “progress", and the increasingly debated "more-than-human" turn in the design and management of innovation.

- Develop a better understanding of the key themes, and challenges for impact-oriented entrepreneurs in pursuing ideals of naturalizing capitalism, and shaping society-oriented innovation processes.

- Critically analyze the "impact" of new developments that rely on "nature" as an asset for entrepreneurial opportunity, and how such narratives contribute to the creation of a particular social reality.

- Explore the ways in which 'nature' can inspire and inform entrepreneurial efforts to address social, environmental and economic challenges, and contribute to social progress in the design and development of innovations.

- Build skills in critical analysis, written communication and creative thinking with the goal of critically evaluating and actively shaping issues of progress in society.

After the course, students will be able to:

Define, explain, critically discuss, and apply key perspectives related to impact, progress and nature.

- Interpret, classify and evaluate the conduct and performance of any organized efforts aimed to create a society “living in harmony with nature”.

- Describe, compare, and evaluate entrepreneurial strategies and innovation concepts with regard to their potential for social progress; in particular, assess how impact-oriented entrepreneurship can contribute to societal progress.

- Differentiate the newly learned perspectives and innovation strategies from previously learned management perspectives.

Title: Navigating Difficult Conversations with Empathy and Ease
Description:
CONTENT:
Whether in group projects, interactions with professors, personal relationships, or later in professional life – difficult conversations are inevitable. Many people either avoid them or approach them in an emotionally charged way. 
This seminar equips both local and international students with the skills to handle challenging discussions with greater empathy, confidence, and clarity. Through practical exercises and reflection, participants develop emotional self-regulation skills and learn to approach conflicts constructively. These competencies are valuable during studies and for future professional life. 
  
We will focus on the following aspects: 
•	Perception & Unconscious Patterns (unconscious bias, tools for irritating intercultural situations) 
•	Emotional Intelligence & Self-Regulation (emotional triggers, emotions and needs, “amygdala hijack”) 
•	Preparing and conducting difficult conversations (clear language, paraphrasing, constructive communication, 4-step model)

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the course, participants will be able to… 
•	reflect on their own perception and recognize unconscious biases 
•	understand and manage emotional reactions in difficult conversations 
•	apply constructive communication techniques with confidence 
•	prepare for and conduct difficult conversations effectively 
•	gain practical experience through simulations and individualized feedback

Title: Navigation and Data Fusion
Description:
CONTENT:
Navigation is the highly accurate, continuous determination of position, velocity and orientation of a vehicle from sensor measurements. Knowledge of the kinematic states of a platform is essential for all guidance and control in air, sea and space applications. By fusing complementary navigation methods in a so called integrated navigation system, the advantages of different technologies can be unified into a single system, while their individual disadvantages can be avoided. A MATLAB toolbox for an integrated IMU/GPS navigation system will be developed within the execises to illustrate the results of the lecture.

Lecture topics:
    - Introduction & Geodesy
    - Inertial Navigation Sensors
    - Inertial Navigation Algorithms
    - Integrating IMU Algorithms
    - Navigation Error Propagation
    - Stochastic Sensor Error Processes
    - Satellite Navigation
    - Navigation System Theory
    - Multi-Sensor Multi-Frequency Data Fusion
    - Integrated Navigation Systems

OBJECTIVES:
After participating in the module, students will be able to understand both the mathematical theory and the operational algorithms needed to develop highly accurate integrated navigation systems. After attending the course, the students gained an insight into how data from various sensors (accelerometers, gyros, GPS, barometers, magnetometers, optical sensors,...) are merged to calculate position, speed and position in modern navigation systems and get a feeling for the difficulties involved.

Title: Netzsicherheit
Description:
CONTENT:
The course provides an introduction to the field of network security. Starting 
with possible threats and attack scenarios, requirements for providing 
specific security services are derived. After introducing the basic concepts 
of security mechanisms, the integration of security mechanisms into network 
architectures and network protocols are discussed. Security vulnerabilities of 
existing network architectures are also discussed. As a basis for the 
realization of security mechanisms, cryptographic algorithms (in particular 
symmetric cryptography, public key cryptography and cryptographic hash 
functions) are presented. Afterwards, the basics and methods for security 
protocols for authentication, authorization, access control, message 
integrity, confidentiality and non-repudiation are discussed. Subsequent 
sections present specific security mechanisms, in particular of the TCP/IP 
protocol family. The standard examples include PKI, Kerberos, IPSec, and TLS, 
Firewall-architectures and Intrusion Detection Systems.

Title: Neuroimaging of Aspects of Consciousness with Reference to Clinical Applications
Description:
CONTENT:
Short abstract:
The lecture approaches the topic of consciousness via the two neuroimaging techniques of functional MRI and EEG. Basic selected models of consciousness or conscious perception will be introduced. State of the art analysis methodologies will be explained which aim at detecting signatures of consciousness. The lecture will take a clinical perspective on consciousness. In that regard anesthesia as well as pathologies affecting consciousness like coma or psychiatric diseases up to the effect of hallucinogenic drugs will be discussed.

Contents and educational objectives:
The lecture introduces neuroimaging perspectives on the broad and diverse field of consciousness with a bias on the clinical context. Concepts of consciousness are elusive and multi-faceted. They range from loss of consciousness in anesthesia to conscious perception in the awake state, potentially altered in disease. Here, we will take a focus on the clinical context. Imaging methods help assess the state of consciousness of patients. They also elucidate how brain activity changes in altered states of consciousness found in disease or actively modified for patient benefit. 
Within the lecture series, we start by defining the scope of the lecture. We then lay the ground by introducing relevant established theoretical models. A primer each on fMRI and on EEG for the purpose of the lecture series will be given. During the lecture series, we layout and discuss the imaging relevance of two concepts of consciousness referring to i) brain criticality and ii) a predictive coding account. The scope of different states of consciousness on an axis from coma to hallucinations will be discussed in dedicated lectures on: Coma, anesthesia, sleep, schizophrenia, and evoked hallucinations. In a practical session visual hallucinations can be experienced which are caused by flicker light stimulation. Clinical relevance of the neuroimaging assessments will be emphasized.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the module, students are able 
- To explain and understand basic principles of EEG and fMRI imaging techniques
- To explain and understand relevant analysis techniques
- To explain and understand most relevant concepts of consciousness
- To explain and understand models of how consciousness can arise from features of brain function
- To know clinical conditions which can affect consciousness and how they impact aspects of consciousness

Title: Neuromorphic Electronic Devices

Title: Neuroprosthetics
Description:
CONTENT:
The lecture covers the theoretical foundations of neuroprostheses. 
As the underlying principle of all neuroprostheses is the electrical excitation of neurons, we will cover this topic in depth using cochlea implants as an example.

In the practical computer laboratory (2SWS), which complements the lecture (2SWS), we will program a solver for the cable equation of an active axon and implement a computer model of a cochlea implant. The practical part is obligatory, it will be graded and you have to pass with at least 4.0. 

Topcis:
- Overview neuroimplants
- numerical solution of linear and nonlinear differential equations
- electrical models of cells and neurons
- derivation and solution of the cable equation for nerve fibers (axons)
- simulation of the electrical excitation of nerve fibers (axons)
- simulation of electrical field spread in the body
- anatomy and function of the hearing organ
- coding of sound in the auditory nerve
- implementation of a coding strategy for a cochlear implant
- electrochemistry of electrodes, biocompatibility and foreign body reactions

OBJECTIVES:
After this course, the particitants will have:
- ability to analyze nonlinear systems (neurons) and solve nonlinear differential equations
- knowledge how neuroprostheses work
- understanding of the underlying principles of electrical stimulation of neurons
- ability to model electrically evoked neuronal excitation
- ability to analyze and evaluate contemporary neuroprostheses and novel developments
- ability to implement models of new neuroprostheses and their coding strategies

Title: Neutronen- und Röntgenstreuung an kondensierter Materie
Description:
CONTENT:
This lecture provides a comprehensive introduction to neutron, electron, and X-ray scattering as experimental probes of condensed matter. Students will learn how structural and magnetic properties of matter can be explored using modern scattering techniques, from crystalline order to disordered systems and large-scale structures. The course combines theoretical foundations with practical exercises, including lab work and simulation, preparing students for applications in contemporary condensed matter research. The winter term will cover mainly probing static properties of matter probed by neutrons and x-rays while the summer term focuses on measurements using electron scattering and the role of excitations and dynamic processes.

•	General introduction to scattering methods (neutrons, X-rays, electrons)

•	Structure of condensed matter: from amorphous to crystalline; real and reciprocal space

•	Mathematical foundations of scattering, with a focus on elastic processes

•	Neutron scattering: history, cross sections, sources and facilities, scattering theory, diffraction (coherent, incoherent, magnetic), diffuse scattering in liquids and disordered systems, large-scale structures (reflectometry, SANS), instrumentation and optics, McStas simulations

•	X-ray scattering: theory of interaction with matter, X-ray sources and optics, diffraction, absorption spectroscopy, resonant elastic scattering (REXS), laboratory exercises (Laue and XRD)

The lecture combines theoretical foundations, experimental methods, and practical exercises, offering students a comprehensive introduction to scattering techniques widely used in condensed matter research

OBJECTIVES:
By the end of the course, the student will be able to:

    Plan, predict and interpret neutron and X-ray scattering experiments.
    Read and evaluate articles containing neutron and X-ray scattering results
Skills: ['Neutron scattering', 'X-ray scattering', 'Condensed matter physics', 'Magnetic properties', 'Structural properties']

Title: New emerging topics in Soil Biophysics
Description:
CONTENT:
The scope of this module is to learn fundamental biophysical processes taking place at the root zone and particularly at the root-soil interface and their emerging impacts on water and nutrient exchange between the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. In this module, we will discuss the basic principles of soil physics in the context of water and nutrient transport within soils and plant roots. The particular attention is to learn why, when, and where soil physics plays an important role in water and nutrients transport across the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.

This module is graded and its examination consists of two assignments: 
1)	An oral exam targeting the learning outcomes of the lecture of Soil Biophysics. This exam serves to assess students understating of the governing principle of water and nutrient retention and transport across the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. In particular, students will be asked to mechanistically discuss the potential roles of different belowground traits in improving plant access to limited soil resources under different conditions. 
The oral exam will be around 30-45 min and will be graded as “pass” or “fail.” This exam will be scheduled within the last 3 weeks of the semester, and a successful evaluation (passed) is a prerequisite to taking part in the second assignment. 
2)	A seminar presentation followed by submission of an extended summary on a selected topic. Students are asked to give a presentation and write an extended summary to demonstrate a solid understanding of a given topic. In both cases, students are asked to use their own wordings and structure within the entire report rather than the style and sentences used in the main selected articles/reviews. 
The oral presentation is expected to be 15 min presentation followed by a subsequent 30 min discussion. The extended summary is expected to be a minimum of 5 pages and will be graded. Students will be informed about the grading criteria of their extended summary during the lecture via a template. The presentation will be scheduled within the last 3 weeks of the semester. The extended summary should be submitted by the end of the semester.The final grade for students who successfully passed the oral exam (not graded) is an averaged grade from the oral presentation (30%) and the extended summary (70%).

OBJECTIVES:
This module aims to enable students: 
1)	To mechanistically describe the theories of water and nutrients retention and transport across soil-plant-atmosphere continuum
2)	To mechanistically discuss why and when plant access to soil resources is limited in different soils and how plants may deal with these limitations
3)	To evaluate the potential roles of different belowground traits (soil and plants) in improving plant access to limited soil resources under different conditions
4)	To explore the state-of-the-art search in the field of soil-plant interactions and rhizosphere

Title: Nonlinear Continuum Mechanics
Description:
CONTENT:
This course deals with the mathematical description of the mechanics of material bodies, which can be modeled as continuously distributed in space. It builds upon basic principles of Newtonian mechanics as well as thermodynamics and extends them by mathematical models that are able to realize those principles on space and time resolved material bodies. In more detail throughout the course:
(1) the term “continuum“ is explained.
(2) the mathematical description of large space and time resolved deformation (kinematics) is introduced.
(3) the concept of stress is reviewed and extended.
(4) balance principles of Newtonian mechanics and thermodynamics are derived based on kinematics and the concept of stress. 
(5) common material laws (constitutive laws) are introduced in order to relate stress and strain, in particular laws for the macroscopic description of plasticity and (visco-)hyperelasticity.
Skills: ['Thermodynamics', 'Fluid mechanics', 'Heat transfer', 'Mechanics of materials', 'Machine design', 'Finite element analysis', 'Material science', 'Structural analysis', 'Dynamics and kinematics', 'Simulation software']

Title: Numerische Algorithmen im Hochleistungsrechnen
Description:
CONTENT:
The lecture discusses selected algorithms from the following classical problem settings in scientific computing ("the seven dwarfs of HPC"), in particular:
- Solvers for partial differential equations (and related problems) on structured and unstructured grids (e.g. domain decomposition methods)
- Algorithms in numerical linear algebra on sparse and dense matrices (direct and iterative solution of linear systems on HPC architectures, eigenvalue problems, etc.)

A particular focus is on situations, where parallelisation of sequential algorithms is not sufficient, but algorithmic improvements are required to reach best-possible performance.

In that context, the following approaches for optimisation and analysis of algorithms will be discussed:
- Performance analysis and performance models (Roofline, Cache, Bulk Synchronous Parallelism) 
- Shared-memory parallelism (data dependencies, parallel loop, tasking)
- Distributed-memory parallelism (MPI; tiling, blocking and partitioning methods)

OBJECTIVES:
Participants know important algorithms from various representative problems in parallel and high performance computing, in particular motivated by applications in scientific computing. They can evaluate their range of application in standard scenarios, are familiar with their basic performance features, and can also evaluate their parallel scalability. 
Students are able to decide whether a numerical algorithm is parallelizable in an efficient way and to analyze internal data dependencies and the runtime of parallel algorithms. They understand the different ways of parallelism and are able to exploit them when writing numerical code for different architectures. 
Participants know different parallelization strategies for solving linear systems and partial differential equations and are able to implement and evaluate them.
Skills: ['Solvers for partial differential equations', 'Domain decomposition methods', 'Numerical linear algebra', 'High-performance computing', 'Structured grids', 'Unstructured grids']

Title: Numerische Festkörpermechanik
Description:
CONTENT:
Inhalt der Veranstaltung ist die Modellierung und numerische Lösung von mechanischen Festkörper- und Strukturproblemen, wie sie im Ingenieurwesen Verwendung finden. Während eingangs ein Überblick über verschiedene Methoden der numerischen Festkörpermechanik gegeben wird, wird im weiteren Verlauf der Vorlesung der Fokus auf der Finite-Element-Methode (FEM) liegen. Dabei wird die FEM anfangs am einfachen Beispiel des 1D-Dehnstabes eingeführt, bevor anschließend die Theorie und mathematischen Grundlagen der Methode, z.B. die zugrundeliegende schwache Form der mechanischen Bilanzgleichungen oder das Konzept von Ansatzfunktionsräumen, für den allgemeinsten Fall von 3D-Kontinua hergeleitet wird. Darauf aufbauend werden numerische Aspekte der FEM, z.B. das isoparametrische Konzept, Aspekte der numerischen Integration, Konvergenz der Methode oder sogenannte Locking-Effekte, vermittelt. Abschließend wird das bislang für statische Systeme eingeführte Konzept der FEM auf dynamische Probleme erweitert.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der erfolgreichen Teilnahme am Modul Numerische Festkörpermechanik sind die Studierenden in der Lage, diskrete Modellierungen von mechanischen Festkörpersystemen zu erstellen und zu lösen. Dabei können sie aus verschiedenen Theorien für das jeweilige Problem passende Modelle und Elemente auswählen. Ebenso können sie die numerischen Ergebnisse kritisch hinterfragen und Einschränkungen durch die vereinfachende Modellierung erkennen.
Skills: ['Finite element method', 'Mechanical engineering', 'Structural analysis', 'Simulation software', 'Material science']

Title: Numerische Methoden der Elektrotechnik
Description:
CONTENT:
- methods for solving linear equation systems, e.g. Gaussian elimination, cholesky decomposition, SVD, conjugated gradients method, relaxation

- methods for finding the root of a real-valued function, e.g. Newton-Raphson method, interval section
- numerical methods for integration of differential equation systems, e.g. explicit and implicit Euler method, trapezoidal method, Gear method

The named methods are developed in context of their application area in electrical engineering. One famous example is electronic circuit simulation - a time-saving key technique that allows to design large circuits and systems without loss of material. Numerical methods and algorithm are the main part of modern simulation processes.
The following simulation types are used to explain the named numerical methods:
- linear small-signal frequency domain analysis (AC analysis)
- nonlinear quiescent point calculation (DC analysis)
- transient analysis
- nonlinear frequency analysis (Harmonic Balance, shooting methods)

OBJECTIVES:
After passing this course the student is able to use basic numerical methods in fundamental tasks of electrical engineering, e.g. numerical simulation processes.
Skills: ['Linear equation systems', 'Gaussian elimination', 'Cholesky decomposition', 'SVD', 'Conjugated gradients method', 'Model order reduction', 'Arnoldi-iteration', 'Lanczos method', 'Newton-Raphson method']

Title: Nutzen der Raumfahrt
Description:
CONTENT:
Spaceflight is fascinating for many people. But is this enough to justify the enormous efforts which are necessary? After a historical introduction which includes different justifications and motivations for spaceflight, the basic technological and economical boundary conditions for conducting transportation and activities in space are described, as well as the cost-benefit ratio for estimating the utility. Four different areas of the utility of spaceflight are presented: Subjective utility, quantifiable utility, utility as a byproduct and potential utility as the biggest and most important area. The lecture finishes with two topics: What is the way to a successful hi-tech domain and how does spaceflight fit into this pattern?

OBJECTIVES:
After participation the students are capable of understanding the enormous difficulties of spaceflight and the necessity to have a valid justification. They are able to remember different areas of utility and the importance of each area. They are able to use this knowledge to search for new applications for activities in space and are capable to convince institutions of the necessity of these applications.

Title: Ökobilanzierung
Description:
CONTENT:
The module 'Life Cycle Assessment' is offered in the winter semester. The main content of the module is understanding and applying the method of life cycle assessment as well as networked thinking in relation to ecological decision criteria and their dependencies and interpretation.

The course provides an overview of the context of life cycle assessment and alternative assessment methods. On the one hand, the processes and procedures of life cycle assessments and analyses in general are considered, and on the other hand, the approaches of life cycle assessments in the construction industry are analyzed and conclusions are drawn regarding decision criteria and approaches for planning sustainable buildings. The course is based on national and international standardization. The necessary basic knowledge for creating a life cycle assessment/analysis is taught.

OBJECTIVES:
After participating in the module ‘Life-Cycle-Assessment’, students will be able to understand and apply the method of lifecycle assessment as well as to make use of the principal of cross-linked thinking regarding environmental aspects, interdependencies and the interpretation of these. This includes the basics of an environmental assessment, as well as the understanding and application of the functional principles considering the content, processes and methods of LCA. The can describe and understand the regulation background of LCA on an international and national basis. The participants will be able to design a goal and scope definition for the LCA of products and buildings and to develop and perform the calculation. The students can master the application and interpretation of datasets and databases (like oköbau.dat, ecoinvent etc.) quantitatively and understand the principle of operation of different LCA-tools (like eLCA, LEGEP, GaBi etc.). The will also be able to interpret the results appropriately.
Skills: ['Life Cycle Assessment', 'Environmental impact assessment', 'Networked thinking', 'Ecological decision criteria']

Title: Ökologie und Evolution von pathogenen Bakterien
Description:
CONTENT:
Teil 1: Einführung in die Evolutionsbiologie: Methoden der Evolutionsforschung, Entstehung komplexer Strukturen, Entstehung von Variabilität in Individuen, Fixierung von Allelen in Populationen.
Teil 2: Bakterielle Genome und Populationsstrukturen: Bakterielle Genome als Ergebnis fixierter Mutationen, Typisierung bakterieller Populationen, Infraspezifische phylogenetische Populationsanalyse.
Teil 3: Evolution von Antibiotikaresistenzen: Wirkungen von Antibiotika, Ökologie des mikrobiellen Resistoms, Mechanismen der Antibiotikaresistenz, Evolution von Antibiotikaresistenzen.
Teil 4: Ökologie als angewandte Evolutionsbiologie: Ökologische Rahmenbedingungen, Invertebraten und Vertebraten als Wirte, Wirtswechsel, Populationsökologie, Virulenzgentransfer und Pathogenitätsinseln, Ökologie intrazellulärer Pathogene, Reduktive Evolution bei Pathogenen und Symbionten.

OBJECTIVES:
Die Hörer sollen die grundlegenden Methoden der Evolutionsforschung sowie experimentell belegten Evolutionsprozesse bei Prokaryonten kennenlernen. Das erworbene Wissen soll auf molekularbiologische und epidemiologische Daten (Populationen von Pathogenen, Antibiotikaresistenzen) angewendet werden. Darüber hinaus die Fähigkeit erworben werden, experimentell nicht reproduzierbare Daten aus der vergleichenden Biologie (Pathogenitätsinseln, reduzierte Genome) vor dem Hintergrund der experimentell verifizierten Evolutionsprozesse zu interpretieren.

Title: Ökologische Stadtentwicklung
Description:
CONTENT:
Cities are good for people - but are they also good for the planet? What possibilities exist for sustainable, environmentally sound urban development and what role can the development of green infrastructure play in this? The module provides knowledge and methods of urban ecology and presents innovative approaches to ecologically-oriented urban development. The focus is on the conversion of existing urban structures. Topics include: Environmental impacts and challenges of global urbanisation, theory and principles for ecologically-oriented urban development; management of urban metabolism (material and energy flows, greenhouse gas emissions) and natural resources (urban climate, water, soil and biodiversity), cultural ecosystem services and citizen involvement, adaptation to climate change, strategies for multifunctional green infrastructure.

OBJECTIVES:
On successful completion of the module, participants should: 
1. understand core theories and methods of urban ecology  
2. understand and have acquired knowledge on important tasks for urban ecology in urban development such as planning for urban climates, local stormwater management, soil protection, biodiversity, and climate change adaptation 
3. be able to analyse and assess strategies for urban ecological planning 
4. be able to transfer and apply ecological theories and methods in a project excerxise for developing a strategy for urban ecological development

Description:
CONTENT:
Topic of the seminar are current issues and questions of restoration ecology and ecosystem management for specific ecosystems and habitats in a global context. The seminar covers basic ecological aspects, processes and dynamics of the respective system,  biotic, abiotic and anthropogenic factors as well as possible approaches and measures for protection and management. All topics are closely linked to current
research projects of the institute.

Topic WS2014: Encroachment
Many grassland communities worldwide show a massive increase of native, mostly woody legumes. Associated with this encroachment is an decrease in plant biodiversity and the repression of fodder grasses, leading to a reduced pastoral production. Causative is a shift in the competitive balance between perennial grasses and the legume. Despite intensive research, the factors and processes causing this shift are still not entirely understood, With the winter term 2014 seminar the current state of research on encroachment will be discussed. 

---

OBJECTIVES:
