Title: Psychoregulation und Entspannungsverfahren
Description:
CONTENT:
Mit der Neufassung des Sozialgesetzbuch V im Jahr 2000 hat der Bereich der Primärprävention eine hohe Bedeutung erhalten, ein Schwerpunkt darin bildet das Präventionsprinzip „Förderung individueller Kompetenzen der Belastungsverarbeitung zur Vermeidung stressbedingter Gesundheitsrisiken“ (AG Spitzenverbände, 2006). Neben theoretischen Grundlagen zu Wirkung und Wirksamkeit von Entspannungsverfahren wird in der Veranstaltung ein Einblick in deren Anwendung und Durchführung vermittelt.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach erfolgreicher Teilnahme am Modul sind die Studierenden in der Lage:
* Die psycho-physiologischen Grundlagen von Psychoregulation zu beschreiben
* Die Ebenen der Wirkungen von Entspannungsverfahren darzustellen sowie die jeweils wichtigsten psychophysiologischen Methoden zur Messung dieser Wirkung zu nennen
* Entspannungsverfahren als Form der Psychoregulation nach unterschiedlichen Gesichtspunkten zu klassifizieren,
* Das Handlungsfeld „Entspannung“ im Leitfaden Prävention zu erklären,
* Verschiedene Entspannungsverfahren zu demonstrieren und bzgl. ihrer Eignung in der Prävention und für unterschiedliche Zielgruppen zu bewerten.

Title: Python and Advanced Data Science
Description:
CONTENT:
Data Science and Machine Learning are the major technologies and have a huge impact for large private businesses, public institutions, and research. With technological developments, globalization and dynamic environment in every industry, the amount of generated data is growing exponentially. Data science therefore is crucial and deals with the methods and tools needed to analyze (large amounts of) data and draw actionable conclusions from the results gained in the process.

The lecture covers the Python programming and applying advanced Data Science concepts with Python implementations. The module covers the following topics:
1. Introduction and Organization
2. Python Data Structures
a. Lists
b. Dictionaries
c. Tuples
d. Sets
e. Numpy & Pandas
3. Working with files and databases, SQL
a. Working with different file types
b. Database Management System (DBMS)
c. SQL
4. Data Analysis & Visualization
a. Data understanding and analysis
b. Data visualization
5. Data Wrangling & Manipulation
a. Data Cleaning & Preparation
b. Exploraty Data Analysis (EDA) techniques
c. Hands-on exercises
6. Building Machine Learning Models & advanced techniques-I
a. Bias-variance Trade-off
b. Regression and regularizations
c. Multicollinearity, VIF, Heteroscedasticy
d. Ensemble models, Random Forest, Bagging, Boosting, tunning parameters
7. Building Machine Learning Models & advanced techniques-II
a. Logistic Regression, Sigmoid, AUC-ROC, precision-recall
b. Unsupervised learning
c. Hands-on exercises
8. New Technologies & ML Models
a. AutoML, H20
b. More new ML technologies
c. Hands-on exercises
9. Deep Learning-1
a. Neural Networks
c. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
10. Deep Learning-2
a. CNN
11. Natural Language Processing-1
a. NLP pipelines
b. TF-IDF
12. Natural Language Processing-2
a. Sentiment Analysis
b. Hands-on Exercises
13. Project

OBJECTIVES:
Upon the completion of this course, students will acquire knowledge of advanced Data Science concepts and learn how Python can be used in this context.
Students will also learn about data structures in Python and how to write programs/scripts using Python data structures. They will learn how relational databases and SQL can be used for data analysis and storage. They also develop skills on using Python libraries for data analysis, dealing with raw data, data pre-processing and visualization methods. Through exercises and projects, they will gain hands-on experience and solve data analysis problems.
They will gain theoretical knowledge of advanced techniques for Machine Learning (ML) models and their applications. Students will also learn how to choose ML models and then build them with hands-on examples. In the projects, they will be able to build advanced models through interactive exercises and real-world examples through projects, which use a variety of data sources, project scenarios, data analysis tools and advanced ML techniques. They will also learn how to evaluate their models and improve them by tunning.
Students will gain knowledge about new technologies and applications in ML and Data Science fields. Moreover, Deep Learning topics will be introduced. Moreover, students will learn about Natural Languages Processing and its pipelines with some hands-on exercises.
Finally, students will be able to communicate their findings behind the data to relevant audiences by visualizing and presenting their idea through presentations and reports.

Title: Python for Engineering Data Analysis - From Machine Learning to Visualization
Description:
CONTENT:
With the success of data-driven business models often built around machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), data science and modeling have been pushed into the focal point of various disciplines, reaching from factory automation through business analytics to materials science.
Today, data science paradigms are introduced as "the new way to do things" in all scientific and engineering domains. Unfortunately, often the sizable heritage of the "new" methods in engineering (see Forrester et al., 2008) is overlooked and new methods are applied uncritically.

This module aims to introduce the Python programming language as a tool for engineers and scientists to perform data analysis tasks typically arising in a lab (e.g., data cleaning, computing statistical measures, data visualization, and linear modeling). In addition, the relation between simple statistical modeling and machine learning methods and their inherent capabilities and limits will be discussed.

The content is organized in five parts:
- Introduction to the Python programming language.
- Accessing data - interacting with lab equipment, text files, or databases.
- Data visualization - do’s and don’t’s.
- Data modeling - simple, statistical techniques to create a data model.
- Introduction to machine learning methods.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of the module, students are able to
- solve algorithmic problems in Python.
- perform basic data analysis and statistics tasks on datasets.
- use the available python tools for 2D and 3D data visualization.
- understand various methods to model data (e.g., linear regression, neural networks).
- remember the capabilities and limits of these methods.

Title: Python-Kurs für IngenieurInnen und WissenschaftlerInnen
Description:
CONTENT:
This course provides Python programming skills for engineers and scientists in a simple and structured way to perform tasks such as data processing, simulation and visualisation. The contents of the course are as follows:
1. Introduction to python (data types, data structures, control flow (loops, if-else, while), functions, objects and classes).
2. Essential scientific python tools (numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib, sklearn)
3. Application examples with Python (curve fitting, solving equations, machine learning, mechanics).

OBJECTIVES:
The aim of this course is to provide participants with basic programming skills to solve scientific and technical tasks using the Python programming language. After successful participation in the course, participants should be able to perform a data analysis, model simple systems, solve differential equations and use machine learning for a specific task.

Title: Quanten-Computing mit supraleitenden Qubits
Description:
CONTENT:
Quantum computing is transitioning from small noisy prototypes toward architectures capable of fault-tolerant operation. Current research focuses on scaling systems, improving coherence and control, and implementing quantum error correction (QEC) with concrete codes and fault-tolerant gate sets. The central questions are how to realize scalable hardware, how to map algorithms efficiently to specific platforms, and how to meet the thresholds required for error-corrected computation.

This course covers the physical operation of quantum processors, the algorithmic landscape that motivates fault tolerance, and the hardware–software stack linking control, readout, and characterization. Emphasis is on superconducting qubits, which short comparisons to other platforms (e.g., neutral atoms, trapped ions, spin qubits).

Topics covered:

* Qubits and quantum gates (physical principles).
* Quantum algorithms: from core protocols (teleportation, Grover, QFT) to hardware-aware mappings.
* Quantum error correction and fault tolerance (codes, decoding, thresholds, logical operations).
* Superconducting quantum circuits (qubits: transmons, fluxoniums, couplers).
* Control and readout of superconducting qubits.
* Characterization of qubits, gates, and processors.
* Overview and comparison with other platforms (trapped ions, spin qubits).
Skills: ['Quantum computing', 'Superconducting qubits', 'Quantum error correction', 'Fault-tolerant quantum computation']

Title: Quantensensorik
Description:
CONTENT:
Amongst the various quantum technologies being developed, quantum sensing stands out: It has become a real-world application operating at room temperature and is being used to measure magnetic and electric fields, temperature, pressure and, yes, gravitation. This module will introduce you to the basic physics behind this exciting technology, will demonstrate a specific realisation based on so-called color centers in considerable detail and will discuss how to push the limits of quantum sensing. We will start by reviewing quantum mechanical two-level systems and their representation in the Bloch sphere, spins and their dynamics including relaxation and decoherence as well as magnetic resonance and the pulse sequences used to study it. We will introduce the nitrogen-vacancy complex in diamond and will learn how to measure dc and ac magnetometry using this atomic scale sensor to realise, e.g., NMR spectrometers capable of analysing minute samples. In the second part of the module, we will take a step back and look at the fundamentals of the quantum mechanical measurements process including the standard quantum limit, quantum non-demolition measurements as well as squeezed states and present examples from solid state physics for the field of quantum or cavity optomechanics as well as spin ensembles where these concepts are put to practice.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of the module the students are able to:
· Describe a two-level system in the Bloch sphere
· Calculate spin dynamics
· Explain magnetic resonance, dephasing, relaxation and decoherence
· Describe the electronic levels and dynamics of color centers such as the NV complex
· Develop the major pulse sequences used for quantum sensing
· Discuss the sensitivity limits reached so far for NV-based magnetometry
· Derive the standard quantum limit
· Discuss quantum non-demolition measurements
· Depict quantum states in the Wigner representation
· Introduce cavity optomechanics
· Judge new concepts for quantum sensing
Skills: ['Quantum Sensing', 'Sensing technologies', 'Magnetic field measurement', 'Electric field measurement', 'Temperature measurement', 'Gravitation measurement', 'Physics']

Title: Quantifying Earth system resilience from space
Description:
CONTENT:
!!! NEW DATE for intro session: Friday, October 24, 4-6pm !!!

Given the significant impact of human activity on Earth's climate, an important question emerges: how resilient are key components of the Earth system, i.e., to what extent can natural stabilizing mechanisms still compensate for disturbances? This seminar explores methods for assessing system resilience and applies these approaches to observations of critical Earth system components with a focus on satellite remote sensing as the primary data source.


Topics covered with regard to the quantification of resilience are
- Theory of dynamical systems, linear stability and bifurcation theory
- “Critical slowing down” in dynamical systems as a proxy of changing resilience
- Advances in resilience estimation
- The compartments and phenomena of the earth system covered are
- Land vegetation, tropical rainforests, drylands,
- (Sub)tropical monsoon systems
- Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation


Intended learning outcomes: After completing the module, students will be able to
- describe the most important methods for quantifying the resilience of components of the Earth system
- explain the main theoretical background of these methods, as well as their main advantages and limitations
- critically evaluate common hypotheses discussed in science and/or the media, especially against the background of observations
- read and critically discuss scientific literature in the context of tipping points
- present scientific literature appropriate for the target group

This seminar will take place online and as a Block seminar. The first session will be held on Friday, October 24, 4-6pm, during which we will give an introduction into the topic as well as explain the overall intended learning outcomes and structure of the seminar. During this time slot, we will open a poll for finding the best dates for the other block sessions, during which the participants will present their chosen topics. During these presentation session, we will not only focus on the single topics, but in particular on understanding, interpreting, and discussing similarities, differences, and implications of various research.

OBJECTIVES:
- Capability for statistical analysis of remote sensing data
- Ability to quantify resilience and its changes from time series
- Mastering methods for trend detection and attribution

Title: Quantitative Genetics and Selection
Description:
CONTENT:
Participants learn the basic principles of quantitative genetics and their relevance in the context of plant breeding. Essential concepts of population genetics, such as the genetic composition of populations and the effects of natural selection and mutations are taught. Quantitative genetics concepts important to plant breeding such as inbreeding and heterosis, epistasis, phenotypic and genotypic variances, resemblance between relatives, heritability, and genotype-environment interactions are introduced. It is shown how these concepts can be used to calculate selection success and optimize breeding programs.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of the module, students are able to understand the basic concepts of quantitative genetics and to evaluate their relevance for problems in plant breeding. They can explain important population genetic concepts such as the Hardy-Weinberg Law, understand the concepts of linkage and linkage disequilibrium and how they can be estimated in experimental populations. The students become familiar with the theoretical concepts underlying breeding values and combining ability and their application in estimating heritability. They can identify and quantify resemblance between relatives. They are able to apply these concepts to selection theory for the optimization of breeding programs.

Regarding the choice of topics treated as well as the methodological approach pursued, the module is intended as a continuation of the corresponding modules covering classical information theory .
Topics covered in the lecture are

Title: R for crop modelling
Description:
CONTENT:
The module includes aspects of the yield physiology of crops: C-balance (photosynthesis, respiration, C-allocation), water balance, light uptake, growth and development and model representations of these components in a cropping system with numerical solutions, crop models and coding in R. The course will contain two components. First, students will be exposed to basic concepts of systems analysis, modeling and computer simulation of agricultural and biological systems. Emphasis will be placed on continuous simulation of dynamic models with examples that give students a broad exposure to dynamic simulation models. An overview of applications of models in agricultural and biological systems will be given. Basics of working with R and a simple crop model developed in R will be taught via e-learning tools and seminars during this first half of the semester. The second part of the course will introduce students to a simple dynamic crop simulation model. They will apply their knowledge of R and the simple crop model in R, to modify the model and apply it for a class projects. Lectures will expose the students to various methods for working with dynamic models, including parameter estimation, model evaluation, and sensitivity analysis which they will apply in a project work. Students will also be exposed to uncertainties in models associated with uncertainties in model parameters, inputs, and structure.

OBJECTIVES:
The basic modeling approaches of cropping systems processes are presented and supplemented in the lectures by example from different models and recent research. In the accompanying exercises, parallel to lecture material, student will individually read scientific literature and carry out exercises on methods of model development, parameterization, evaluation, sensitivity analysis and uncertainty analysis. In a seminar setting, the first part of the semester will be accompanied with e-learning developed for this module, they will learn the basics of R and how a simple model is applied in R (1SWS for first half of semester). Students will prepare homework exercises on model creation and discuss these and literature in class. The lectures will be accompanied with regular brief quizzes to test their comprehension of new definitions and concepts. Students are encouraged to assist each other in homework (understanding reading material and in performing specific modeling tasks) and during discussion in class.
Skills: ['R', 'Crop Modelling', 'Yield Physiology', 'Photosynthesis', 'Water Balance', 'Growth Models', 'Cropping Systems', 'Coding', 'Numerical Solutions']

Title: Radar Signals and Systems
Description:
CONTENT:
1. Basics of Radar

– Pulse modulated Radar

2. Components of Radar Systems

– Antennas and phased array techniques

3. Target Detection

– Detection theory
– Matched filter
– Ambiguity function
– Pulse compression
– Clutter
– Moving target indication (MTI)
– PRF staggering

– Target tracking

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing this module, students will be able to professionally explain the physical principles of radar technology, including the propagation and scattering of electromagnetic waves, the Doppler effect, and the significance of the radar cross-section. They will be able to describe and differentiate between the various operating modes and functional principles of modern radar systems such as CW, FMCW, and pulse modulation. They will be able to calculate typical radar system parameters such as range, resolution, and SNR and apply them to practical examples. Students will master fundamental signal processing methods such as matched filtering, pulse compression, CFAR, and tracking for evaluating radar signals and will be able to implement them. They will also acquire the ability to break down complex radar system architectures into functional units and analyze the interrelationships between transmitter, receiver, antenna, and signal processing. Factors that influence radar system performance, such as frequency selection, antenna characteristics, clutter, and noise interference, can be systematically evaluated. They are able to critically compare different radar methods with regard to their suitability for specific applications and also assess the performance of a radar system based on simulation data or measured values, identifying weaknesses. Finally, they are also able to design concepts for modern or future radar systems based on the SAR principle or MIMO technology, taking technical aspects into account.

Title: Reaktionsthermodynamische Grundlagen für Energiesysteme
Description:
CONTENT:
At the beginning, the basics known from the Thermodynamik I lecture will be revised shortly. The functional dependence of the state variables will be pointed out and real gas effects are introduced and discussed on the basis of the thermal state equation for ideal gases. The first and second law of thermodynamics are presented shortly, with it introducing the exergy.
Using these basics, the real behavior of substances will be depicted by deducing the real change of enthalpy and accordingly internal energy during state changes. The differences to the ideal gas behavior are highlighted. 
Further topics under consideration are:
Introduction of thermodynamics of mixed phases – ideal mixtures – real mixtures –thermodynamic treatment of mixtures
state variables of chemical reactions – the stoichiometric conversion equation – the extent of reaction – reaction rate – kinetic considerations of equilibrium
enthalpy of reaction – absolute enthalpy – temperature dependence of the reaction enthalpy 
equilibrium of chemical reactions: Gibbs free energy – reaction equilibrium – temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant – exergy of the chemical reaction – introduction of the chemical potential
phase equilibria of single component systems and ideal mixtures 
chemical and phase equilibrium of real substances - fugacity

OBJECTIVES:
Premising on basic thermodynamic knowledge the students shall acquire the following competences: 
Application of thermodynamics on practice-oriented multicomponent systems with and without chemical reaction. 
Calculation of chemical equilibria from thermodynamic data.
Understanding of the connection between chemical reaction and thermodynamic variables

Title: Rechnergestützte Entwicklung, Konstruktion und Fertigung - CAE/CAD/CAM
Description:
CONTENT:
Continuous use of different software tools is an inherent part of today’s product development and production process everywhere. During the course “CAD/CAM“ participants will be given an overview over the application of modern software tools for product development and production.
The course is split into two parts: The CAD part is to be held at the Institute of Materials Handling, Material Flow and Logistics (Professor Fottner), while the CAM part is to be held at the institute for Machine Tools and Industrial Management (Professor Reinhart). 
During the CAD part of the course a parametric 3D-CAD software tool (Inventor CAD) will be used to demonstrate the systematic structure and methodical use of 3D-CAD models. Participants will, under supervision, study different technics for the modelling of parts in a CAD system. Basic methods such as feature based modelling and free-form surface modelling will be taught as well as the usage of components for modelling of complex parts. Emphasis will be placed on the systematic and logic structure of the models. Finally deriving technical drawings for manufacturing from 3D-models and kinematic analysis of assemblies will be taught. 
During the CAM part of the course several aspects of computer aided production are considered. After an introduction to production planning participants will develop programs for milling, turning and drilling operations both manually and computer aided. Complex processing operations for milling are taught, as well as the usage of software for quality assessments. Real-time Demonstrations in the iwb machine park are included to expand the course from theory to practice.

OBJECTIVES:
During this course the following objectives are taught:
•	Systematic analysis of the structure of designed parts 
•	Understanding and developing technical drawings for manufacture
•	Parametric construction of parts and assemblies
•	Management of product-specific design data
•	Analysis of kinematic degrees of freedom in assemblies
•	Defining the machine setup for CAM operations
•	Defining bodies for collision tests, raw material, part clamping, tools and tool clamping for CAM operations
•	Developing plans for work and inspection
•	Planning CAM operations for simple and complex geometric features
•	Generating machine code to carry out the programed CAM operations

They understand the architecture and implementation of basic encryption algorithms and protocols and their application in computer networking.
Participants can determine the performance of selected networks and security implementations, and can implement specific protocol mechanisms.

Title: Rechtliche Aspekte in der Bauwerkserhaltung
Description:
CONTENT:
In the eyes of many technicians building maintenance is carried out in the law-free, unregulated area, although there are a number of practice-relevant legal regulations, both in public building and monument and building protection law as well as in private building contract and architects law, as well as in “housing law” and tenancy law. Following these regulations is absolutely necessary to successfully finish construction projects. The module answers questions such as:
-	Public building law: Do you need a building permit for a repair? How long does it last? To what extent is the “Guideline for the protection and repair of concrete components” as a technical building design also introduced by the building authorities? What does this mean for the need for consent in the individual case, for example, PPS?
-	Housing tenancy: What technical standards apply to the construction of the building at the time the building was built or at the time of repair? What applies to the unworked stock? Do tenants have to tolerate construction-related measures, if so, under which conditions?
-	Housing law: Building maintenance - "structural alteration" or "modernizing repair"?
-	Private construction law: Which technical standards apply to the construction work, which is at the time of the construction of the building or at the time of the repair? What applies to the unworked stock? What is the responsibility of a property developer who has promised a white tub to his buyers? Does this also apply to the entrepreneur who carries out the repair work?
-	Architectural and engineering law: What is the obligation to provide information and clarify the technical and / or economic compromises? Building management in the HOAI (Fee structure for architects and engineers), where can you find them? "

OBJECTIVES:
Knowlege of practically relevant public and private building rights with building in existing buildings.

Title: Reden und Schreiben über Architektur
Description:
CONTENT:
Die Veranstaltung ist als Vortragsreihe mit ausführlicher Diskussionsgelegenheit angelegt, an der mehrere Professuren des Departements Architektur beteiligt sind. Das Modul ergänzt und erweitert die Studienangebote der Entwurfsstudios auf der einen Seite und des wissenschaftlichen Arbeitens auf der anderen Seite. Ausgangsüberlegung für das Angebot des Moduls ist es, dass sich Architektur zwar in Entwürfen bildlich und in mündlichen Kommentierungen darstellt, dass ArchitektInnen aber sowohl im Studium als auch in ihrer späteren Berufspraxis in umfangreichem Maß auf mündliche und schriftliche Mitteilungen angewiesen sind. Die Veranstaltung soll sich mit dieser Rede- und Textproduktion reflektierend auseinandersetzen: Die Veranstaltung widmet sich der kritischen Analyse von unterschiedlichen Texten (Wettbewerbsausschreibungen, Architekturkritik und Architekturgeschichte, Ausstellungstexte, Entwurfserläuterungen, Homepages von Büros etc.). Die fast ausschließlich mündliche Vermittlung in den Entwurfsstudios und die im engeren Sinn wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten im Studium werden mit dem Modul ein drittes Format an die Seite gestellt, das dem Nachdenken über die mündliche Vermittlung und die Textproduktion in der Architektur und der Vorbereitung in die schriftliche Praxis der Architekturvermittlung dient.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme an dem Modul sind die Studierenden in der Lage
- ein Verständnis für die Textproduktionen in den verschiedenen Architekturinstitutionen zu entwickeln (u.a. Architekturbüros, Wettbewerbe, Ausstellungswesen, Architekturkritik)
- Texte aus den Bereichen Architekturkritik/Architekturgeschichte kritisch zu analysieren, und u.a. Darstellungsabsichten, Argumentation, Zielpublikum zu erkennen
- in eigenen Textproben von Architekturkritiken, Wettbewerbstexten und Büromitteilungen die Kenntnisse aus Institutionen- und Textkenntnis selbständig anzuwenden

Title: Reflexion
Description:
CONTENT:

Im Dialog mit der ganzen Gruppe wird die eigene Aufgabenstellung erarbeitet. Das Thema ist in Absprache mit der Professur frei wählbar. Es sollte aber möglichst in einem der Forschungsschwerpunkte angesiedelt sein und einen klaren Entwurfsfokus haben. In der Regel findet die Masterthesis als Einzelarbeit statt, Gruppenarbeiten sind aber auch möglich. Es wird begrüsst, wenn sich Masterthesen auf aktuelle Forschungsprojekte (z.B. im Cluster M-Cube oder im Kontext des New European Bauhaus) beziehen, da sich Lehre und Forschung hier optimal ergänzen können.

Title: Regelung elektrischer Antriebe Teil I - Modellierung der Antriebskomponenten
Description:
CONTENT:
The module covers the following topics:
- Physical operation principle of electric machines (Maxwell's equations, physical principle of torque generation in rotating electric machines),
- Modelling of AC machines for controlled drives (space vector representation, fundamental wave model of induction machines),
- Control strategies for AC drives (primarily field-oriented control),
- Sensors for controlled drives (current, position and speed sensors),
- Applications of controlled electrical drives,
- Further perspectives (innovative control methods for AC machines, challenging aspects of current measurement in electrical drives)

OBJECTIVES:

- understand the electromagnetic energy conversion process in rotating electrical machines,
- remember the assumptions underlying the fundamental wave model and understand their meaning,
- use space vectors,
- derive the fundamental wave models of induction and synchronous machines and determine their parameters,
- implement the presented control strategies for AC drives,
- remember the properties of different machine types and sensors as well as their areas of application in drive control,
- be aware of the current developments in the field of electric drives.

Title: Regenerative Energiesysteme I
Description:
CONTENT:
The objective of this lecture is provide an overview on the current state and application of renewable energy technology. The lecture not only focuses on technologies but also on environmental, social and economical factors that lead to the intensivied world wide harvesting of CO2-neutral energy sources as well as their potentials and limitations.

The course RENEWABLE ENERGY TECHNOLOGY (taught in English) is split into two modules 3 ECTS each (one per semester), beginning with “RET I” in the Winter Semester. The attached module “RET II” will be offered in the Summer Semester.
The course is supported by various institutions of the TUM: The Institute for Energy Systems, The Institute for Fluid Mechanics, The Institute for Energy Economics and Application Technology, The Institute for Wind Energy as well as the “Laboratory of Steam Boilers and Thermal Plants” from the National Technical University of Athens.
The module “RET I” covers the following topics:
•            Fundamentals (historical overview, power plant fundamentals, climate, energy consumptions and forecasts, energy economics, electricity control, fossil and nuclear energy)
•            Energy from Biomass (properties of biomass, biomass potentials, fuel properties, heat production, power production by means of combustion, power production by means of gasification, biogas production by means of anaerobic fermentation)
•            Geothermal Energy (potential, exploitation, direct utilization, central heating, district heating, deep geothermal systems, power generation, combined heat and power, economic aspects, risks)
•            Wind Energy (basic facts, introduction to wind turbine aerodynamics, the wind resource, wind turbine types, configurations, components)

•            Wednesday 16:10 / 17:40 pm MW 0350 
•            2 hours (90 min) lecture per week; no exercise course/ tutorial
•            Dates / room for RET II (summer term) to be announced at a future date
•            Please register in TUMonline (campus.tum.de) for this course 
•            Lecture Renewable Energy Technology consists of two semesters: 
              Renewable Energy Technology I: winter term
              Renewable Energy Technology II: summer term
•            3 ECTS per semester
•            One written exam after each term (60 min)
•            Re-examination in the following term on the topics of both terms

Title: Reinforcement Learning für Optimierungen in Biomechanik
Description:
CONTENT:
The course provides a comprehensive introduction to state-of-the-art optimization methods and cutting-edge reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms for the analysis and estimation of human body dynamics. It includes:
1. methods for collecting and processing movement data, using gait data as a case study
2. classical optimization methods and their limitations
3. the main concepts of RL algorithms
4. the application of RL algorithms to predict joint torques, muscle forces and muscle activations
5. guest lectures by experts from clinical and scientific practice
The focus is more on the systematic variation of parameters and less on a realistic modeling. Students should adapt and apply various RL algorithms and examine their plausibility and sensitivity by varying parameters.

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing the module course, students will be able to formulate various problems in biomechanics as optimization problems and solve them with the help of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. They are able to:
1. model various problems in biomechanics as optimization problems.
2. develop problem specific multi-body systems (MBS) models in the open-source physics engine MuJoCo and analyze their advantages and limitations.
3. adapt RL algorithms from the open-source library stable-baselines3 to make use of these models.
4. develop extensions for the RL algorithms to improve the quality of the solutions they find.
5. evaluate the solutions obtained in terms of their scientific and practical relevance.

Title: Remote Machine Intelligence Lab
Description:
CONTENT:
●	Overview of robotics and control
o	Introduction to robotics and control of robotic systems: a general overview of kinematics, dynamics and control of the robotic systems are given.
o	Motion control: Decentralized control, PD plus gravity and inverse dynamics controller and their closed-loop dynamics are illustrated.
o	Force/impedance control: The impedance control in task space and joint space is shown is reviewed.
●	Telerobotic systems and applications
o	Overview of telerobotics: the importance of telerobotics and different examples are reviewed.
o	Control architectures: different control architecture used in teleoperation is introduced.
▪	Direct control
▪	Shared control
 
▪	Supervisory control
o	Stability and transparency in tele-manipulations: the importance of stability and transparency is shown in illustrative example scenario.
o	Telepresence reference platform at MIRMI: our telepresence setup with different protocols is introduced, and the performance of the system in contact with different environments is presented.
o	Clear intensive guidance for programming with haptic devices
o	Designing a teleoperation system for remote interaction and skill transfer
●	Teleoperation with haptic devices
o	Intensive guidance for programming with haptic devices and designing teleoperation system for remote interaction and skill transfer.
o	Making students user-ready to haptic technology and challenges for teleoperation systems over real communication networks (e.g. system stability, communication load, etc.).
o	Working with haptic devices and remote robot in virtual reality, introduction to ROS, Chai3D, and then a quick overview about available examples.
o	Overview of teleoperation design in real environment and corresponding stability issues, and remote learning from demonstration technologies.
o	Writing codes and programming the teleoperation system either in virtual or real environments to perform a certain number of tasks that are ranging from simple to complex.
●	Drone and its application
o	Simulation (Gazebo) and a real one that has basic semi-automatic control already implemented, including on-board localization.
o	Students will implement is on-board occupancy mapping using the mounted depth camera, as well as (local) planning to avoid collisions with the environment.
o	Develop a final demo, in which the drone can be steered intuitively with a keyboard, while the drone is inherently safe and will only ever move as far as safe to avoid colliding with the environment.

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of the course, students have understood the working principles of teleoperation systems with haptic feedback. They are ready to write code to connect haptic devices with remote robots, manipulate the robots and interact with remote objects while perceiving stable force feedback. Moreover, the students are also able to program and remotely transfer necessary knowledge to the robot for executing complex tasks at full autonomy. Besides, the students will be able to explain the main components of autonomous drones, i.e. state estimation, mapping, motion planning and control. In addition, they will know in detail the working principles of 3D occupancy mapping and planning, and be able to implement them as a real-time ROS/C++ application. Title: Renaturierungsökologie-Projekt
Description:
CONTENT:
(1) Wie gut sind die Kopien? Die Garchinger Heide und ihre Ausgleichsflächen. Problemstellung 
Die Garchinger Heide ist eine Spenderfläche für zahlreiche Ausgleichsflächen in der nördlichen Münchner Schotterebene. Auf den Ausgleichsflächen wurde Mähgut oder Druschgut der Garchinger Heide ausgebracht und in der Folge gepflegt. Projektarbeit Ziel der Arbeit ist eine GIS-Datenbank zu erstellen mit Angaben zur Lage, zum Status und zu den Monitoringergebnisse zu erstellen. Zudem soll nach Möglichkeit der Renaturierungserfolg bewertet werden und Verbesserungsvorschläge erarbeitet werden. Dazu muss Kontakt mit den unterschiedlichen Projektträgern aufgenommen werden. Das Projekt findet in Kooperation mit dem Heideflächenverein Münchner Norden e.V. statt. Voraussetzungen: Die Arbeit richtet sich an Studierende der Bachelorstudiengänge Landschaftsarchitektur und Landschaftsplanung und Biologie sowie den Master Ingenieurökologie und Naturschutz und Landschaftsplanung. Für das Projekt werden Kenntnisse bei der Pflanzenbestimmung und in R benötigt. Für die Anfahrt zu den Vegetationsflächen wird ein Auto benötigt. Kontakt: Dr. Markus Bauer (markus1.bauer@tum.de) 

(2) Eschen im Naturwald an der Isar: Lokalisierung, Mortalität, Prognose
In einem Transsekt entlang der Isar zwischen Ismaning und Landshut sollen stichprobenartig 100 einheimische Eschen (BHD > 30 cm) markiert werden (GPS-Koordinaten) und umgefallene Alteschen in der Umgebung erfasst werden. Ferner soll an den Stichprobenpunkten über Knospenmerkmale kontrolliert werden, ob fremdländische Eschenarten im Baumbestand oder Jungwuchs vorkommen. Von Vorteil wäre eigenes Fahrzeug. Kontakt: Dr. Karl-Heinz Häberle (haeberle@tum.de)

(3) Kartierung und räumliche Analyse von künstlichen Offenstandorten in Bayern. 
Die Fläche natürlicher Sand- und Kiesbänke hat im letzten Jahrhundert massiv abgenommen. Durch Verlust dieser wertvollen Habitate sind heute viele auf solche Standorte spezialisierte Tier- und Pflanzenarten gefährdet. Anthropogen bedingte Sonderstandorte wie Kies- oder Sandwerke, Steinbrüche oder Ruderalflächen bieten teilweise vergleichbare Standortbedingungen und werden von verschiedenen Arten auch als Ersatzhabitate angenommen. Allerdings sind diese Standorte oft nur kleinräumig und weit voneinander entfernt. Genetischer Austausch zwischen diesen Standorten ist daher oft eingeschränkt. Mit der ausgeschriebenen Arbeit sollen anthropogen bedingte Offenstandorte in Bayern anhand von Luftbildern kartiert und kategorisiert werden. Anschließend soll untersucht werden wie sich die räumliche Verteilung dieser Standorte in Bezug auf Genfluss ausgewählter Arten verhält und welche Möglichkeiten zum Schutz dieser Arten sich ergeben. Voraussetzungen: Die Arbeiten erfolgen ausschließlich mit QGIS oder R; Feldarbeit ist nicht erforderlich. Kontakt: Dr. Thomas Wagner (wagner@tum.de)

OBJECTIVES:
Die Themen fördern das Verständnis ökologischer Prozesse als Basis für naturschutzfachliches Management. Methodisch lernen die Bearbeiter die selbstständige Literaturrecherche und -auswertung sowie experimentelles Arbeiten im Freiland und im Labor bzw. Gewächshaus.

Title: Research in Action
Description:
CONTENT:
To prepare students for their master thesis and any empirical research projects, this course covers both theoretical foundations of management science as well as empirical research methods.

In particular, this seminar introduces students to every step in the empirical research process from generating a research question via developing an appropriate research design to data analysis and interpretation. All steps will be taught in an applied manner and students have the chance to develop and discuss their own research agendas.

OBJECTIVES:
After students have taken this course, they
…understand the empirical research process
…understand what makes a good research question
…have knowledge of basic and advanced methods of data collection and data analysis
…have the ability to conduct a systematic literature review for a scientific topic and judge the scientific quality of knowledge
…have the ability to design appropriate research designs for a variety of research questions
…can apply their empirical knowledge in statistical analyses.
Skills: ['Research-oriented mindset', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving', 'Project planning and prioritization']

Title: Research Methods in Business Psychology
Description:
CONTENT:
The course covers key methodological principles in business psychology. Topics include scientific reasoning, hypothesis development and study design (e.g., experiments, field studies). Students will learn how to operationalize constructs such as work motivation and design empirical studies using surveys, interviews, observation and implicit measures (e.g., IAT). Data analysis focuses on descriptive and inferential statistics (e.g., t-tests, ANOVA, regression) with introduction to tools like R or SoSci Survey. Applications in organizational and consumer psychology are discussed, including employee surveys, leadership evaluation, and advertising research. The course also addresses quality criteria (objectivity, reliability, validity) and ethical standards in psychological research.

Title: Research Methods in Landscape Architecture
Description:
CONTENT:
Research through Design
The seminar Research through Design (RtD) addresses the theory of designing research, quality criteria of scientific knowledge and their application in the method of designing research (Entwerfendes Forschen).

Mapping 
The Mapping seminar focuses on a scientific method for the analysis of physical and non-physical spatial phenomena in cartographic maps; the production of maps that, as well as containing topographical data, also spatially communicates non-physical, e.g. psychological or cultural, information, in map-like images. Objects or situations are selected, sorted and grouped, and usually shown within categories or types.

Topics: https://www.arc.ed.tum.de/en/lareg/teaching/research-methods/

OBJECTIVES:
After participating in the module, students will be able to distinguish between empirical, hermeneutic and design-based methods in spatial sciences and understand general criteria for scientific quality. They will also be able to use this knowledge of criteria to overcome theoretical and experimental methodological limitations in spatial practice and to develop and work on a simple research question of their own design using the method of design-based research (RtD).
Constituting on present skills in planning and designing and on the specific methods introduced by the lecture, students are able to develop a landscape architectural or urbanistic task at the regional scale by means of a spatial-structural analysis and design concept. In addition, they will be able to understand the scientific-design method of mapping and apply it to a topic of their own choosing or one specified in the seminar.

Title: Research Methods in Psychological Prevention
Description:
CONTENT:
The module consists of 1 lecture with blended learning components, and 1 practical seminar. The content of the module is conveyed through lectures, presentations and discussions. In the lecture the students will read relevant and current literature. In the seminar, the students will apply the six steps of the Intervention Mapping Framework to create their own health promotion program. The seminar involves discussions, group work as well as feedback on planning a health promotion program.

- Differentiation of prevention and (mental) health promotion in the field of psychology
- Differentiation of mental illness and mental health
- Models of attitude and behavior change in general and in health-related behavior
- Essentials of effective behavior change methods
- Application of the Intervention Mapping Framework: 6 steps of program planning: deed assessment, program objectives, program methods and strategies, program production, program adoption and implementation and program evaluation.

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing the module, students will be able:
- to understand and describe the major psychological problems in prevention
- to understand and describe main methods and approaches in the psychology of prevention
- to discuss and evaluate approaches in health promotion and the prevention of disease from a psychological perspective
- to understand, communicate and design target-group-specific prevention strategies in health- related issues
- to apply the Intervention Mapping Framework within program planning.

Title: Research Project
Description:
CONTENT:
The following points provide an overview of the topics and methods covered in the research internship. Depending on the individual research questions of the students, some but not all of these topics will be practically addressed.

1. Practical Work with Linux and High-Performance Computing (HPC) Clusters  
   - Application of Linux commands and scripts for efficient analysis of large datasets.  
   - Use of HPC clusters to perform computationally intensive bioinformatics processes.

2. Data Preparation, Research, and Quality Control  
   - Independent research of relevant sequencing and reference datasets for analysis.  
   - Application of tools like FastQC and MultiQC to assess the quality of sequencing data.  
   - Practical trimming of sequencing reads using tools such as Trimmomatic to improve data quality.

3. Mapping and Alignment of Sequencing Data  
   - Use of mapping tools like HISAT2, STAR, or BWA to align (RNA or DNA) sequencing data to plant reference genomes.  
   - Evaluation of alignment quality using various metrics, such as mapping rate and coverage uniformity.

4. Phylogenomic Analyses  
   - Independent use of tools like OrthoFinder to identify orthologous genes and generate phylogenomic trees.  
   - Comparison of phylogenetic relationships across different plant varieties and species and interpretation of results.

5. SNP Calling and Variant Analysis  
   - Use of SNP-calling tools like GATK or SAMtools to identify genetic variants in plant data.  
   - Interpretation and annotation of SNPs to understand their biological relevance.

6. Gene Expression and Transcriptome Analyses  
   - Analysis of RNA sequencing data using tools like HTSeq, featureCounts, or Kallisto to quantify gene expression.  
   - Application of normalization techniques and conducting differential gene expression analyses with DESeq2.

7. Functional Enrichment Analyses  
   - Performing gene set enrichment analysis to identify biological processes using tools like KEGG and Reactome.  
   - Analysis and interpretation of biological pathways in plant genomes and transcriptomes.

8. Development and Application of Bioinformatics Pipelines  
   - Independent development and adaptation of bioinformatics workflows for the analysis of plant data.  
   - Application of specific pipelines for NGS data analysis or phylogenomic studies.

9. Benchmarking of Tools  
   - Comparison of the performance of various bioinformatics tools in terms of speed, accuracy, and suitability for specific questions.  
   - Documentation and interpretation of benchmarking results to select optimal tools for future projects.

10. Independent Research Project  
    - Planning and execution of an individual project in the field of plant research, based on a specific scientific question.  
    - Application of research strategies to efficiently use scientific literature and databases.

11. Documentation and Presentation of Results  
    - Structured documentation of conducted analyses and results.  
    - Presentation of research findings in a scientific context, e.g., through reports or presentations.

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing the module, students will be able to:
•	Work confidently with Linux and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters.
•	Deepen and apply their existing knowledge of plant genomic data, such as NGS data and phylogenomic analyses.
•	Learn and proficiently apply bioinformatics tools and methods for the analysis of genomic data.
•	Learn, develop, and independently apply bioinformatics pipelines for specific use cases.
•	Apply research strategies to efficiently utilize scientific literature and relevant data sources.
•	Independently plan and execute their own project, selecting and applying appropriate analysis tools and methods.
•	Critically interpret the results of plant genomic analyses and develop problem-solving strategies.
•	Clearly document and present their research findings.

Title: Research Project on Mechanisms of Microbiota-Pathogen interaction
Description:
CONTENT:
You will be part of a larger research project aimed at understanding how the gut microbiome protects against enteric pathogen infections. Our lab focuses on the concept that complex microbial communities confer protection by nutrient blocking—consuming substrates that would otherwise support pathogen growth within a nutrient network. However, the specific nutrients (eg carbohydrates, amino acids, ions) involved and the microbes that utilize them remain unknown. To address this, we employ synthetic microbial communities to investigate these mechanisms in detail, with the ultimate goal of informing the development of next-generation probiotics.
Your research may focus on various aspects of microbiota-pathogen interactions, particularly nutrient competition and the production of inhibitory compounds. Additionally, your work may involve developing and optimizing cutting-edge methods and assays, isolating microbes, and conducting studies on microbial growth, nutrient consumption, and metabolic networks.

OBJECTIVES:
This module is designed to equip you with the skills to design and conduct independent research within a supportive lab environment. You will formulate a hypothesis-driven research question based on existing literature or data and attempt to answer it through experimental work. The project will be a combination of supervised and self-guided lab work, following good scientific practice.
Skills: ['Research-oriented mindset', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving']

Title: Research Project on Phages in the gut microbiome
Description:
CONTENT:
You will be part of a larger research project exploring how phages interact with their bacterial hosts within host-associated microbial communities. Despite their lytic potential, phages can stably coexist with their host bacteria in the human gut over extended periods without eliminating them or being lost. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood but may involve bacterial resistance factors, as well as spatial and functional separation between phages and their hosts. Ultimately, uncovering the mechanisms of phage-bacteria coexistence will contribute to the advancement of phage therapies for gastrointestinal infections.

OBJECTIVES:
This module is designed to equip you with the skills to design and conduct independent research within a supportive lab environment. You will formulate a hypothesis-driven research question based on existing literature or data and attempt to answer it through experimental work.
Skills: ['Research-oriented mindset', 'Analytical thinking and structured problem solving']

Title: Research Project on Plant Cell Biology
Description:
CONTENT:
Participants in this module will actively engage in an ongoing research project, gaining direct insight into the processof scientific discovery. They will acquire hands-on experience with experimental work, learning to plan, conduct, andtroubleshoot laboratory procedures. A central focus will be the introduction to, and practical application of, modernmethods in Plant Cell Biology, enabling students to become familiar with state-of-the-art experimental approaches.
Students will be guided in designing and performing their own experiments, moving from the formulation of a researchquestion to the execution of targeted investigations. Emphasis will be placed on the critical interpretation of researchdata, including the evaluation of experimental outcomes and their relevance within a broader biological context. 
In addition, participants will practice rigorous documentation of both experimental procedures and datasets, followingFAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles to ensure scientific transparency andreproducibility. They will develop the ability to formulate sound scientific rationales and hypotheses as the foundationfor experimental inquiry. Finally, students will train in scientific presentation, learning how to communicate theirfindings clearly and effectively in both oral and written formats.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module, students are able to:
-Carry out basic and/or advanced biochemical and/or cell biological and/or computing and/or genetic approaches.
-Explain and apply key experimental techniques used during their internship.
-Design and perform experiments independently.
-Integrate findings from orthogonal approaches to draw coherent biological conclusions.
-Document scientific procedures and outcomes following the FAIR principles.
-Discuss scientific procedures and outcomes in a structured scientific presentation.

Title: Research Project Soil-Plant-Atmosphere Continuum
Description:
CONTENT:
This module introduces students to current topics and experimental methodologies related to soil-plant-atmosphere interactions, with a particular focus on water and carbon flux dynamics. The specific research project for each student is tailored according to the ongoing research within the group and the student's individual interests.
Typical topics covered in the module include:
•Soil-plant hydraulic dynamics and their role in water transport within ecosystems
•Carbon allocation processes within plants and soils, emphasizing storage and movement of carbon
•Root exudation and its impact on soil microbial communities and nutrient cycling
•Effects of drought and heat stress on soil health and plant physiological responses
•Soil amendments and their role in enhancing soil fertility and structure
•Regenerative farming techniques aimed at improving soil and ecosystem resilience
•Soil contamination and remediation, exploring approaches to mitigate and repair environmental damage
•Root anatomy and morphology and their influence on plant performance and soil interaction
•Root-mycorrhizae interactions and their contribution to nutrient uptake and plant health

•Soil hydrophobicity and its implications for water infiltration and retention
Students will gain hands-on experience with a variety of standard soil and plant physiology techniques. In addition, students will be introduced to data analysis tools commonly used in research, such as R,  Python, and MATLAB, to handle and interpret experimental results.
A list of current projects is available at https://www.lss.ls.tum.de/sbe/offered-projects-theses-positions/, and students are encouraged to propose their own topics within the group’s research focus.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module, students will have acquired the following knowledge and skills:
•Comprehensive understanding of current challenges in research related to soil-plant-atmosphere interactions.
•Practical proficiency in advanced methodologies for investigating the dynamics within the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.
•Ability to design, execute, and critically evaluate research studies, drawing connections between experimental results and existing scientific literature.
•Competence in effectively communicating research findings through both oral presentations and written reports, tailored for a scientific audience.
•Apply cutting-edge techniques in soil and plant ecology to solve complex, research-driven questions within the soil-plant-atmosphere system.

Title: Responsible AI
Description:
CONTENT:
1.	Introduction to Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI)
a.	Motivation for responsible AI
b.	Definition and core principles of responsible AI
c.	Application areas of responsible AI
d.	Introduction to Human-AI collaboration

2.	Tradeoffs between different principles of responsible AI
a.	Typical principles such as fairness, accountability, transparency, explainability, privacy, anti-bias, and societal impact
b.	Different uses and definitions of AI principles in practice

3.	Introduction to Explainable AI (XAI)
a.	Difference between interpretability vs. explainability
b.	Effects of XAI on AI transparency and trust
c.	Collaborative Distributed Machine Learning

4.	Introduction to Accountable AI
a.	Accountability facets for AI systems
b.	Difference between accountability and responsibility, transparency, and auditability
c.	Effects of the accountability mechanism 

5.	Motivating Research on Responsible AI
a.	Scientific problematization
b.	Argumentation strategies
c.	Foundations of academic writing

OBJECTIVES:
In the seminar “Responsible AI”, students will learn the foundations of what makes an AI responsible and how social and technical factors drive or hinder responsible AI. Moreover, the students will learn the most common responsible AI principles and how different AI developers employ them. Students will learn to apply this knowledge to answer a specific research question regarding responsible AI and how to conduct a scientific project. Lastly, students will harness the skills necessary to write a scientific paper about their research project.


After successful completion of the course, students are able to:
1.	Understand and explain the core aspects of responsible AI
2.	Differentiate between the different principles of responsible AI
3.	Understand the trade-offs between different responsible AI principles and how to address them
4.	Conduct a basic scientific research project independently and as a group
5.	Write a scientific (seminar) paper for a given research question
6.	Elaborate and present research on a specific responsible AI related topic and research question

Description:
CONTENT:
The module focuses on analyzing regional innovation cultures and the associated socio-technical challenges. Students examine how responsibility is embedded in technological development and identify key influencing factors. Using selected case studies from science, politics, and industry, they explore different strategies for fostering responsible innovation. Additionally, methodological approaches from STS research and ethnographic fieldwork are practically applied to contemporary developments in quantum computing.

Title: Responsible, Sustainable and Inclusive Digital Product Creation
Description:
CONTENT:
"The module teaches key concepts and methods for  responsible, sustainable and inclusive digital product creation. The content is organised along four thematic focal points:

1. Responsibility: responsible digital design. Reflection on privileges, responsibility and social impact.
1. Sustainability: analysing the ecological impact of digital products. Development of sustainable concepts.
2. Diversity: addressing discrimination and bias in digital products. Developing ideas that are sensitive to discrimination.
3. Inclusion: Recognising and designing accessible and inclusive digital products. Reflection on accessibility and participation."

OBJECTIVES:
As part of the module, students develop concepts for digital products that systematically take social responsibility, ecological sustainability and inclusion into account. Through project-based learning, interdisciplinary teams work on real or self-chosen challenges and apply methods of Conscious Design. The focus is on reflecting on privileges and social power relations, analysing digital products and developing their own ideas that are both socially and ecologically sustainable. The practice-orientated work is supplemented by accompanying inputs, methodological exercises and feedback phases. The aim of the module is to promote the ability to consciously and responsibly design digital products and to develop creative interdisciplinary solutions.

Title: Ressourcentraining
Description:
CONTENT:
Im Prinzip spricht nichts gegen interessante Herausforderungen und Abwechslung. Manchmal aber kommt man an den Punkt, an dem man befürchtet, den Anforderungen nicht gerecht werden oder die Erwartungen nicht erfüllen zu können. Und auch sonst wäre es schön, wenn die Dinge leichter von der Hand gingen. Glücklicherweise haben wir stets die Möglichkeit, auf unsere Talente, Stärken und Ressourcen zurückzugreifen – wenn es uns gelingt, diese bewusst wahrzunehmen und zu aktivieren.

Themenschwerpunkte
- Eigene Stärken kennen - Selbstwert stärken
- Wichtige Ressourcen für Erfolg im Studium und beruflichen Erfolg definieren und entdecken
- Eigene "Schwächen" akzeptieren oder konstruktiv nutzen
- Eigene Werte, Prägungen und die inneren Antreiber reflektieren
- Die sieben Säulen und sieben Schlüssel der Resilienz (Widerstandsfähigkeit) kennenlernen und ausbauen
- Blick auf das Wesentliche – Was ist für mich, meine Aufgabe, meine Ziele wichtig, dringlich und hilfreich? 
- Networking

OBJECTIVES:
Nach der Teilnahme sind die Studierenden in der Lage ihre eigenen bereits vorhandenen Ressourcen, Talente und Fähigkeiten bewusst zu sehen, neue Ressourcen zu entdecken und die eigene Resilienz zu stärken. Sie entwickeln ein Gespür für förderliche Kontakte und Netzwerke. Die Studierenden werden bestärkt, neuen Herausforderungen mutig und zuversichtlich entgegen zu sehen.

Title: Rhetoric and Argumentation. An Academic Talking Lab
Description:
CONTENT:
This course tackles three questions: 
1.	How does a convincing argument look like?
2.	What is the main structure of a convincing argument? 
3.	Why is the way of speaking or writing crucial to build up a convincing argument?                     
Picture this: You go on a Saturday morning to Marienplatz. You want to get fresh air, to have a nice walk and eventually to get a hot chocolate at the Café Glockenspiel. You stop by at this Café and you order an exquisite hot chocolate. You take the menu in your hands and notice that the food is not named. Each dish has a list of all the ingredients and a detailed chart with nutritional information: calories, protein, sugar. 
Ask yourself this: Would you order a dish just by seeing the nutritional facts of it? Or would you rather buy a dish because it has a nice name and the description of the ingredients is full of positive features? If you say yes to the last question, then you are not giving attention to the actual content of the dish but rather you are deciding based on its appearance. 
That is exactly what this laboratory is about: How the appearance of an idea - or a dish - changes its content. We want to sell other people our own ideas. We want to convince them.
Our mean to do so is really simple:  argumentation. On the one side, it is about looking good. So get dressed because we are going to a fancy bal. You are probably not getting in if you wear dirty sneakers, a shirt and training pants. This is called Rhetoric. 
On the other side, it is about being good. So we are not just wearing a nice suit for the bal but also we know that behind that suit there is a good person. A good argument is made of logical relations between sentences. Does it make sense to say that water is not wet? Probably not. That is called Logic. 
Our ideas work exactly like that: How you present them is how people are going to take them. If you want a person to believe in your idea, you need to make it as if you were going to the bal: Your idea needs a nice fancy suit.
Some topics we are going to address are these:
-	Truth theories;
-	Rational Thinking;
-	Deduction and Induction;
-	Types of arguments;
-	Eloquence Vs Rhetoric;
-	Emotional language.
-	Language and Society.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the workshop, students will be able to:
1.	identify a good argument from a bad one;
2.	build up a good argument and therefore apply basic rules of Rational Thinking. 
3.	evaluate how wording has positive and negative emotional responses on the approached person.

Title: Ring 1
Description:
CONTENT:
The lecture series provides insights into contemporary positions of the TUM in the topic area of „Urban and Landscape Transformation“.
The topic area investigates complex and networked urban landscapes and systems in times of global transformation. Urban hinterlands are reservoirs or vital resources that have increasingly become exposed to global ecological, economic and social challenges and have become the focus of environmental and sustainability debates. Whilst global transformation processes are difficult to influence let alone control with the classic tools of the designer, architecture, urban design and landscape architecture do offer a repertoire of possibilities to integrate complex spatial, aesthetic, social, cultural, ecological and sustainable qualities into contemporary living environments. 
The lecture shows examples of projects and approaches from TUM, on how to conceptualise and strengthen such urban and landscape transformation areas.

Further Information:
https://www.arc.ed.tum.de/en/lareg/teaching/lecture-series-1-urban-and-landscape-transformation/

Title: Ringvorlesung

Title: Risk & Society
Description:
CONTENT:
The following contents will be covered by the module:
It will introduce into the human factor; in risk and safety management as to this end, the module introduces sociological risk research (U. Beck, N.
Luhmann, O. Renn ...).
This module focuses on the societal dimensions of risks and safety, in particular the context of their emergence and application. It will address topics such as non-intended consequences and ignorance. How can trust be maintained in institutions (science, political consulting and politics and administration), which are responsible for the assessment and management of risks?
The module also introduces into approaches of interdisciplinary risk assessment (Technology Assessment, Responsible Research and Innovation, Anticipatory Governance, living labs).
Examples of possible fields of application include, but are not limited to: Extreme Events, AI, Critical Infrastructure, Consumer Protection, Chemicals, Pandemic, Climate Engineering, Carbon Removal Technologies ....

OBJECTIVES:
After successfully completing module, students are able to assess the societal risks and benefits, and to evaluate their management in terms of their safety requirements and social impacts. They have the competence to apply basic social science approaches to risk assessment in a targeted manner to the analysis of selected cases (e.g. critical infrastructures, health), to assess societal impacts and causes of respective risks, to include safety implications into their analysis and to develop responsible solutions. They have competences to reflect methodological choices and empirical findings in a critical, but constructive way.

Title: Risk Theory and Modeling - Lecture
Description:
CONTENT:
The objective of the course is to understand how economic decisions are made in the presence of risk. The module consists of 2 SWS lectures and 2 SWS exercises and is divided into four blocks that build on each other. Exercises mainly take place during the second and fourth block.
 
The first block includes the description of the relevance of risk in different fields with respect to management, policy, and research, followed by the introduction of the decision making process and the concepts of utility and prospect theory. 
In the second block, students are provided with the most important mathematical and statistical tools for risk evaluation such as probability distributions and simulation techniques. 
These concepts will be applied in exercises and then used in the third block to theoretically and empirically analyze price and production risk and the behavior of decision-makers. 
In the last block of the course, selected publications (both seminal papers and most recent ones) in risk research are presented and discussed.”

OBJECTIVES:
Upon completion of the module, students are able to
- understand the various sources of risk in a broad range of sectors and industries,
- discuss the role of individual risk preferences in the decision making process,
- apply mathematical tools to evaluate risk,
- and understand how decision-making under risk is analized in the literature

Title: Robotics Institute Germany Lecture Series
Description:
CONTENT:
The Robotics Institute Germany (RIG) Lecture Series is a nationwide coordinated seminar-style lecture series that brings together leading researchers in the field of robotics from across Germany. Each week, a distinguished expert from academia or industry presents recent advances in robotics and artificial intelligence, followed by an open discussion with students and participants.

The goal of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive overview of the diversity and cutting-edge developments in robotics research in Germany. The topics cover a broad spectrum—from robotic fundamentals and industrial automation to neurorobotics, soft robotics, cognitive systems, human-robot interaction, and the societal dimensions of robotics.

The lecture fosters academic exchange across institutions and allows students to engage directly with leading experts, gain insights into ongoing research, and build an understanding of current and future challenges in robotics.

Topics and Speakers (Winter 2025/26)
Oliver Brock (TU Berlin): Robotics and AI will never feel the same again
Werner Kraus (Fraunhofer IPA): AI-powered Industrial Robotics
Florian Röhrbein (TU Chemnitz): Introduction to Neurorobotics
Wolfram Burgard (TU Nürnberg): tba
Florian Hartmann (MPI-IS): Introduction to Soft Robotics
Nico Hochgeschwender (University of Bremen): Automated Validation and Evaluation of Cognitive Robots
Georgia Chalvatzaki (TU Darmstadt): Robot Learning of Mobile Manipulation / Intro to Structured Robot Learning
Jan Niehues (KIT): Natural Language Interactions with Robots
Tamim Asfour (KIT): Robot Learning from Human Demonstration for Manipulation
Uwe Aßmann & Sebastian Ebert (TU Dresden): Distributed Petri Nets for Cobotics
Svenja Breuer & Ruth Müller (TU München): Robotics and Society – Lessons Learned from the Responsible Robotics Project
Oskar von Stryk (TU Darmstadt): Commercializing Robotic Innovations: Insights and Lessons from Three Startup Frontlines

OBJECTIVES:
After completing this lecture, students will be able to:

- Identify and describe current research topics and methods in robotics within Germany,
- Understand interdisciplinary links between computer science, engineering, artificial intelligence, and societal aspects of robotics,
- Critically analyze recent research results and assess their impact on future developments in robotics,
- Build academic connections with researchers and institutions in the German robotics community.

Title: Robotik
Description:
CONTENT:

The lecture covers the description of the robot geometry and conversions between the workspace of the robot and the motions of the robot joints, the dynamic analysis of the robot motion. This analysis is used to derive the structure and parameters of the control to provide position- and force-control for manipulation tasks.


Any questions, please contat Andrei Costinescu, M.Sc. (andrei.costinescu@tum.de).

OBJECTIVES:
The lecture teaches how to implement a planned task in the robot's workspace on the hardware of a single chain manipulator. The lecture teaches the necessary transformation to convert between the  parameter space of the joints and the motion of the manipulator of the robot. The correct parametrization of the control values and the otpimization of the control is taught in this course.

Title: Robots, Androids, Clones and Transhumanism in Literature, Film and Culture
Description:
CONTENT:
Since antiquity, people have been fascinated by the idea of artificial life and have imagined its creation in various media. Thus, long before these fictions could become reality, literature and art already provided fictional spaces in which fundamental questions could be asked: Why do humans want to create artificial life? How do they treat the resulting creatures? How can we define “human”? Which gender dynamics are involved? How are society and human relationships changed by the existence of artificial life forms? And are there borders which should not be crossed? 
In this seminar we will discuss the current state of science and technology and analyze the depiction of artificial life forms in literature (e.g. in Ovid´s Metamorphoses, E. T. A. Hoffman´s “Der Sandmann”, Mary Shelley´s “Frankenstein”, short stories by Isaac Asimov and other writers, and in Kazuo Ishiguro´s “Klara and the Sun”), films, TV series and other media (computer games, comics and graphic novels). Students are very welcome to suggest texts and films.

OBJECTIVES:
The students research and discuss current discourses on the topics of the seminar. They read/watch literary texts, films, TV shows and other relevant media and learn how to analyze those using different criteria and methods.

Title: Robust Machine Learning
Description:
CONTENT:
* Foundations of adversarial robustness and Lp-norm threat models - Definition of adversarial examples, Lp-balls (L∞, L2, L0), white-box/black-box attacks, robustness vs. accuracy trade-offs
* Gradient-based attack and defense methods - FGSM, PGD, C&W attacks, adversarial training, gradient obfuscation, approximation of non-differentiable functions
* Discrete optimization for graphs and NLP - Adversarial attacks on Graph Neural Networks, textual adversarial examples, genetic algorithms for discrete optimization
* LLM robustness and jailbreaking - Prompt injection, discrete token-based attacks, red-teaming, alignment circumvention in language models
* Certified defenses and advanced attacks - Certified defense methods, interval bound propagation, randomized smoothing

OBJECTIVES:
After completing this course, students will understand the algorithmic foundations on which many modern methods of robust machine learning are based. These include modern (accelerated) gradient-based optimization methods and discrete optimization methods. Students will develop a deep understanding of the algorithmic aspects underlying known techniques, know their advantages and disadvantages, and can decide in application situations which methods are best suited to solve the problem.

Title: Rocket Propulsion I
Description:
CONTENT:
The purpose of this lecture is to give insight into liquid propulsion systems specifically and their components. 
The lecture however aims to be different to lectures otherwise given on the subject by presenting systems rather than individual components and by discussing these in the context of systems. In this sense this lecture is different as it presents the changes occurring in the system as we move from a pressure-fed propulsion system to a tap-off, to an expander-bleed, to a full-expander and so forth.
In addition, this lecture features an important section dedicated to liquid propulsion system ignition methods and system transients. A topic not found in books, and one which is difficult to gain insight into.
The lecture also discusses solid, hybrid and nuclear propulsion as well as touching briefly on the topics of electric propulsion and advanced propulsion systems.

OBJECTIVES:
Students will acquire an overview of liquid propulsion systems and their components, the functional principle of each and the equations necessary to determine their main performance parameters. In particular, the students will learn to recognise different chemical liquid propellant rocket engine cycles and to determine which cycle is most suited for a certain application. For each cycle the required components will be introduced, their functional principle and their design process will be explained. Finally, the students wil be equipped with the knowledge for the preliminary design and sizing of a complete liquid propulsion system and its main components.
On successful completion of this module, students should be able to:
1.	Distinguish and outline the main chemical propulsion engine cycles. 
2.	Select the most advantageous cycle depending on the specific application. 
3.	Name rocket engine components, describe their functioning principles and to determine their key parameters for design. 
4.	Discuss technical impacts of modern developments of space propulsion and transportation systems
