Title: Structural Reliability
Description:
CONTENT:
Course description:
Introduction to modern structural reliability methods for the evaluation of the performance of engineering systems subject to uncertainty and randomness. The course will introduce the theory and applications.     
Intention/aim of the course:
This course enables the student to perform reliability analysis for realistic engineered structures and systems, and to interpret the results of such analyses.

1. Introduction and brief review of basic probability theory
2. First Order Reliability Method
3. Risk acceptance and target reliabilities
4. System reliability
5. Monte Carlo Simulation
6. Importance sampling
7. Subset simulation
8. Responce surface methods (metamodels) and coupling with FEM codes
9. Random variable elimination
10. Time variant reliability analysis
11. Final project

OBJECTIVES:
- Formulate the reliability problem for realistic structures.
- Establish the probabilistic model for various loadings and materials.
- Compute estimates of the failure probability of engineered systems using various approximate methods.
- Construct response surfaces for the reliability analysis of systems that are analyzed with large FEM codes.
- Assess the relative importance of random variables.
- Assess the sensitivities of the results to model assumptions.
- Update the reliability estimates with observed data.
- Perform reliability-based optimization of engineered systems

The research areas encompass computational tools for structural design, geometry-based methods for structural design, innovative structurally-informed construction technologies, and historic structures and construction methods.

By the end of the course, students are required to submit a paper that provides a comprehensive overview of their chosen research topic. This paper should include an introduction, a state-of-the-art review, and a detailed account of the research development, highlighting the methods and processes used. In their conclusions, students must critically evaluate their findings and propose potential future developments. The research topics are categorized into the following areas:
•	Computational tools for structural design.
•	Geometry-based methods for structural design.
•	Innovative structurally informed construction technologies.
•	Historic structures and construction methods.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending the course, students will be able to:
•	Conducting independent research on a specific topic related to structural design.
•	Gathering references to assess the state-of-the-art of the assigned research topic.
•	Developing models and tools relevant to the research topic.
•	Producing, interpreting, and evaluating scientific data from tests and experiments.
•	Presenting research findings through presentations, scientific reports, physical models, and technical drawings.
•	Critically evaluating research findings and considering possibilities for further development.

Title: STS 0
Description:
CONTENT:
This course is designed as preliminary introduction to the field of Science and Technology Studies for RESET and STS Master's students. It is specifically oriented towards students who have limited background in the humanities and social sciences. 

In the course we will attend to some of the formative ideas, concepts, theories, methods, and debates underlying STS.  Both conceptually and chronologically, this course will be a sort of an intellectual pre-history/early-history of STS, rather than an up-to-date overview of the current state of the field. One key objective here is to understand how STS relates to and emerges from distinct intellectual lineages and theoretical frameworks. STS was - and is - in many ways a response to certain longstanding ways of thinking about science and technology. These include historical, sociological, anthropological, and philosophical traditions (among others).

In this regard, we will think about how STS stands in relation to other social science and humanities approaches, and in turn, students will also receive a broad introduction to these fields. Here we will examine some basic problems in social theory and historical analysis, as well as longstanding philosophical concerns in epistemology and even metaphysics (among others). What kinds of questions, assumptions, and explanations motivate or define different ways of knowing? And what happens when these are used to think about science and technology?

OBJECTIVES:
Upon the successful completion of the course, students will have acquired a basic understanding of the field of Science and Technology Studies. They will be familiar with a range of core terms, concepts, methods, theories, thinkers, and debates that have defined STS. This will enable students to start engaging with and making sense of current research and debates, placing it within different theoretical lineages, and identifying their own research interests. 

Ultimately, students will gain a set of conceptual tools for theorizing, describing, explaining, and evaluating science and technology, and crucially, commencing the practical task of studying these as social phenomena.

Title: STS 1
Description:
CONTENT:
This module provides a one-semester graduate-level introduction to the field of Science and Technology Studies (STS). Students are exposed to key STS concepts, questions, and empirical examples to explore how science and technology shape, and are being shaped by social and political processes, particularly with a view towards current debates (e.g. concerning the development and risks of new technologies) and societal transformations (e.g. the transformation from knowledge societies to techno-societies). 

On a theoretical level, this module is devoted to reading, analyzing, and critically engaging with foundational works in STS and related fields, addressing topics such as the construction of science and technology as contingent social practice, scientific and technical controversies, the politics and publics of science and technology (e.g. the governance of research and its communication), the nature of scientific authority, and the relation of science and technology to democracy and the state. Empirically, this module draws upon historical and contemporary examples and debates, with particular attention to important case studies that have become canonical in the STS literature. 

The module is structured as a sequence of short, intensive learning units that will introduce students to a range of topics and concepts in contemporary STS thinking. Topic units may include, but are not limited to, the following range of themes: Politics & Governance of Science and Technology, Biomedicine & Health, Gender & Diversity, Industries & Innovation, Infrastructures & Design, Knowledge Cultures & Institutions, Media & Digital Cultures, Nature Cultures & Sustainability, Co-construction of Technology & Users, Publics & Participation, Risk & Security.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module students

• have a thorough understanding of Science and Technology Studies (STS) as a field of research 

• have fundamental knowledge of classical STS concepts, analytical tools, case studies and historical developments 

• know how to systematically analyze complex problems using these concepts and tools, particularly with regard to current questions and debates at the interface of technology, society and politics.

Title: STS 2
Description:
CONTENT:
This course provides an introduction to philosophical inquiries into science and technology. The spectrum of posi-tions considered ranges from the classic ("positivist") philosophy of science to the historical and social turn (Fleck, Kuhn, the "Strong Programme") to classic philosophy of technology to the currently dominant focus on scientific practice and technoscience. Questions to be examined include the following: What are the key characteristics of scientific theory and practice? What are the conditions of their emergence and success? What techniques and technologies are involved in scientific discovery? Conversely, what influence do scientific discoveries have on technological innovation? What modes of knowledge are involved on either side?

OBJECTIVES:
Upon completion of this course, the participants will understand a wide range of philosophical issues related to science and technology. They will not only be informed of  the contemporary philosophical debates, but also acquire the conceptual and analytical skills to identify, defend, and criticise philosophical viewpoints.

Title: STS 3
Description:
CONTENT:
STS3 analyzes the historical development of academic research and technology, both as a material and cultural process. Its main educational focus is to exemplify how the production of knowledge, theoretical structures, technical systems, and artefacts transform the physical as well as the symbolic nature of our lifeworlds. This foundational analysis of the history of science and technology not only highlights the cultural impregnation and differentiation of various knowledge forms but also reveals their reification in technologized environments, and evaluates the social discourses surrounding their legitimation.

Key focal points are (among others):
- the secularization of scientific knowledge in the transition to modernity
- scientification of technology and mechanization of science
- organizations and institutions of science and technology
- patterns of techno-scientific competition on a global scale

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module students will understand essential historical evolutions of modern science and technology (e.g. the secularization of scientific knowledge in the transition to modernity, or the scientification of technology and the mechanization of science respectively). They will also be able to discuss, analyze, and evaluate central STS topics like risk and security, nature-cultures and sustainability, or co-construction of technology and users from a historical perspective, and can link former developments to current challenges. In particular, the students will have a basic understanding of the system characters of both science and technology.

Title: Study Techniques - Study Smart
Description:
CONTENT:
You know how to learn. That's part of what got you into TUM. However, studying at TUM is on a different quantum level from high school. So it’s smart to look at techniques and strategies to get the work done and not drown in stress.

The first step in any project is to assess what's on hand and what you need to acquire. To improve your learning you need to figure out where you stand, then we look at possibilities of improvement. In the course we will look at the following areas:
- Learning Style
- Time Management
- Studying Techniques
When it comes to learning and studying one size does not fit all: there is no single "right way to study". To find out what works and doesn't work for you, you will get to know a lot of tools and techniques you may not have experienced before. You may consider changes in the way you study.

- Know tools and techniques for making the best use of your time

Title: Supraleitende Quantenschaltkreise
Description:
CONTENT:
For approximately 10 years, superconducting quantum circuits printed on silicon chips are used to study the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics. Two prototypical examples for such circuits are transmission line resonators (boxes or memories for quantum light) and quantum two level systems (qubits). From a scientific point of view, superconducting quantum circuits allow for the investigation of fundamental quantum mechanical effects such as light-matter interaction. In addition, they are one of the most promising platforms for quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing. In these areas, superconducting quantum circuits are explored in industrial research and development worldwide.

OBJECTIVES:
In this seminar, every participant introduces one aspect of the current research on superconducting quantum circuits by means of a 45-minute presentation.

Title: Supraleitung und Tieftemperaturphysik 1
Description:

The content of the lecture includes the following topics:
- Basics properties of superconductors and superconducting materials (different types of superconducting materials, superconductors in a magnetic field, type-I and type-II superconductors, thermodynamic properties)
- Phenomenological description of superconductivity (London theory, superconductivity as a macroscopic quantum phenomenon, Ginzburg-Landau theory)
- Fluxoid quantization, Josephson effects
- Overview of microscopic BCS theory
- Critical currents
- Applications of superconductivity
- Unconventional superconductors (e.g. cuprates, iron-pnictides)

Title: Surface Acoustic Waves for Biomedical Applications
Description:
CONTENT:
Course content:
1.	[Lecture] Introduction to surface acoustics waves (SAW)-based microfluidics and SAW-based biosensors
a.	Overview of SAW? How to generate SAW using interdigitated transducer (IDT)?
b.	Type/mode of waves: Rayleigh waves (travelling SAW vs standing SAW); Shear-Horizontal waves, Love/Lamb waves, etc.
c.	Types of IDTs, e.g., straight, focused, chirped, slanted, etc.
2.	[Lecture] Piezoelectric materials
a.	Piezoelectricity and substrate properties specifically required for SAW
i.	acoustic velocity, coupling coefficient, piezo coefficients (elastic properties), temp. coefficient (for sensing applications)
b.	Fabrication and properties of wafers and thin film piezoelectric elements: 
i.	How to grow a single crystal ingot and cut it to prepare piezoelectric wafers
ii.	How to deposit a thin film e.g. using ZnO
iii.	LiNbO3 with different cuts e.g. 36 deg. vs. 128 deg. cut, ZnO thin film based piezo-elements, PZT, AlN, ScAlN, single vs. polycrystalline wafer).
3.	[Lecture] Mathematical modelling of straight IDTs (to design with minimum reflections)
4.	[Lecture] Design of a SAW-based acoustofluidic device for particle/cell separation (students can do this as a project)
a.	COMSOL simulations (Eigen/frequency modes, admittance/reflection: S parameters)
b.	PCB design-50 Ohm impedance transmission line
5.	 [Practical] Development of SAW chip, PCB and holder
a.	IDT Fabrication using photo-lithography, e-beam evaporation (only demonstration) and lift-off processes
b.	RF connector (SMA and spring pins) using soldering on PCB
c.	3D printing / micro-machining of a holder assembly for the device
6.	[Practical] Device characterization
a.	Calibration of network analyzer, measurement of SAW device-resonance frequency, reflection/transmission using network analyzer, Smith chart (for impedance measurement), etc.
b.	Manual estimation of the resonance frequency and actuation conditions
7.	[Practical] Applications of SAW-based acoustofluidics & sensors
a.	Sample preparation i.e. particles, buffers, etc.
b.	Acoustofluidic mixing, translocation, jetting, atomization/nebulization of sessile droplets
c.	Particle and cell separation using SSAW
d.	Acoustic tweezing with SSAW
e.	Sensing using SAW i.e. biomolecule conjugated on the surface

OBJECTIVES:
Objectives
In this module student will learn:  
1.	Basics of surface acoustic waves (SAW) transducer and sensor 
2.	Overview of piezoelectric materials and their properties
3.	Mathematical modelling of straight IDTs for SAW generation, 
4.	Designing and hands-on experience on fabrication of IDTs
5.	Hands-on experience on electrical characterization of IDTs
6.	Hands-on experience with different acoustofluidics and sensing applications 


Learning aims
Upon successful completion of this module, students are able to:
1.	Learn about the basics of surface acoustic wave (SAW), i.e., how to generate SAW using interdigitated transducer (IDTs) and get an overview of different types of wave modes and IDTs.
2.	Learn about the piezoelectric materials, substrates (wafers) and thin films e.g. ZnO, AlN etc.
3.	Discuss piezoelectric properties useful for acoustofluidics and sensing applications, and fabrication of piezoelectric material.
4.	Perform mathematical modelling of straight interdigitated transducer (IDTs), and understand the role of various parameters such as wavelength, acoustic velocity, coupling coefficient number of figure pairs in the designing of IDTs for SAW generation and performing COMSOL simulation of SAW devices.
5.	Design printed circuit board (PCB) in order to get 50 Ohm impedance for applying RF signal to the IDTs. 
6.	Understand the fabrication of IDTs, designing of device holder and 3D printing/micro-machining of holder assembly (holder will be needed for integrating complete assembly).
7.	Testing SAW devices using of vector network analyzer (VNA) and S-parameter measurement of IDTs (S-parameter measurement: return loss, smith chart analysis).
8.	Demonstrate of biomedical applications of SAW devices, i.e., prepare samples and conduct experiments such as particle separation, trapping, mixing, atomization, sensing of biomolecules etc and analyzing the data.

Title: Sustainability in Automotive Engineering

CONTENT:
The module examination takes the form of a presentation (100% of the module grade). Each student gives a presentation (20 min plus 10 min discussion) on a selected topic in the field of sustainability using suitable media (PowerPoint presentation, possibly other media of choice).  In doing so, students should demonstrate that they understand the concept of sustainability and its ambivalence and can transfer it to the complexity of social or industrial application. They should also demonstrate an understanding of the methods used to quantify sustainability. In addition, students should demonstrate that they know and can apply strategies and methods for designing and giving presentations, as well as researching, analyzing and discussing publications on a specific topic.

Ecological sustainability

Economic sustainability

Social sustainability

Title: Sustainability in Aviation
Description:
CONTENT:
'The module "Sustainability in Aviation - Destination Green?" focuses on aviation stakeholders’ efforts in supporting the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN-SDG) with emphasis on climate action based on life cycle thinking strategies. After discussing the UN-SDG and their implication for aviation, we will summarize and discuss scientific research on the current and expected future impact of aviation on climate change, e.g., contrail formation, radiative forcing, and local air quality until the year 2050 and beyond. An in-depth introduction to the relevant combustion physics and chemistry, with no prior knowledge assumed, will be given. Then, we will analyze promising options to reduce aircraft noise and CO2 emissions as well as to improve local air quality, i.e., technology, operational improvements, market-based measures, and sustainable alternative fuels. Besides, the students will use sustainability concepts and tools to assess products, services, and processes regarding their environmental impacts (Life cycle assessment: Goal and Scope, Inventory Analysis, Impact Assessment, Interpretation, Uncertainties, and Risks). Hence, they are able to gain the basics and competencies of understanding and determining environmental impacts to support decision processes and stakeholders' communication.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module, you are able to:

- explain the intention and content of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) published by the United Nations.
- describe the international aviation stakeholders’ efforts in supporting the SDGs.
- summarize scientific research on the current and expected impact of civil aviation on global GHG and local air quality until the year 2050.
- categorize options to reduce CO2 emissions and list options to reduce non-CO2 emissions, including noise from aviation.
- distinguish between EU ETS and the CORSIA CO2 trading schemes for aviation.
- develop an understanding of life cycle thinking principles.
- describe the steps for conducting LCA and sustainability assessment studies.
- discuss the achievements and shortcomings of common methodological toolsets and databases in the field of renewable resources.
- gather necessary information, choose suitable methods, and apply these for simple LCA studies.

Title: Sustainability of Buildings
Description:

By means of practical examples, certification processes are described and individual criteria of the various systems are discussed.

The students who have attended the course of lectures will be in a position to understand national and international evaluation methods and certification processes (DGNB, LEED and BREEAM) and to apply these tools for the comprehensive life-cycle assessment of buildings.

Lecture, exercise and homework:
The students who have attended the course of lectures will be in a position to understand national and international evaluation methods and certification processes (DGNB, LEED and BREEAM) and to apply these tools for the comprehensive life-cycle assessment of buildings.

Title: Sustainable Management - Bridging Economy and Ecology through Technology
Description:
CONTENT:
This course introduces the fundamentals of sustainability, covering ecological principles, the significance of ecosystems, and the science behind climate change, including its global impacts. It examines historical and modern responses to climate-related disasters, focusing on technological solutions like clean air regulations and sulfur dioxide controls, and highlights the importance of a circular economy.

OBJECTIVES:
After attending this course, students will have gained a comprehensive understanding of sustainability, including ecological principles, climate change, and its impacts. They will be able to explain, analyze, and critically reflect on historical and current climate-related challenges and solutions driven by technological advancements. Students will have built an understanding of political, legal, and economic frameworks related to sustainability, with practical insights into corporate sustainability practices, exemplified by Knauf. Moreover, they will acquire knowledge on energy efficiency, sustainable energy sources, and technological innovations. They will prepare a written assignment, hold a short presention and lead a discussion on a sustainability related topic, which enhances their ability to apply these concepts practically and improves their discussion skills. Furthermore, students will have the option to discuss actual activities at the multinational company Knauf, where they can observe and learn firsthand how a leading company integrates sustainability into its operations and practices.

Title: Sustainable Urbanism I
Description:
CONTENT:
In the context of accelerating climate change, cities have to develop new strategies to adapt and ensure a sustainable quality of life. Nature in cities is a key to ensure this quality of life as it provides cooling, recreation areas, habitat for animals as well as beautiful and enjoyable spaces. Over the recent years, urban planners, architects, and researchers have been working together to move beyond the city-nature dichotomy by placing nature as the core value for a future-oriented urban development. 

This course aims at exploring the core principles of integrating green and blue infrastructures as a baseline for urban planning concepts. The lecture series is carefully designed to address the technological, ecological and social dimensions of blue and green infrastructure, both in theory and practice. Guest speakers from diverse backgrounds will lay the foundation for an understanding of blue and green infrastructure, its dimensions and applications. These lectures will open a discussion on how to integrate natural solutions in early design phases to create lively and resilient urban forms for all living creatures.

The exam of the lecture series will consist of an academic essay where the student will be asked to choose a topic from in the lecture series intersecting social, ecological and technological dimensions, and will further discuss the subject thanks to a project example. In a second examination phase, each student will anonymously review the submission of one of his peers and submit a reflection upon this topic. This reflection paper will allow to evaluate the critical thinking capacity of the student and will not influence the mark of the reviewed paper.

MEETINGS: Mondays // 13:15 - 14:45 // Room 2770 Hörsaal
KICK-OFF: Monday 24.10.22

EVALUATION LECTURE SERIES: 
Format: Academic essay with reflection paper
Submission date: 23.01.23 // Academic essay
Submission date: 30.01.23 // Reflection paper

OBJECTIVES:
1. Understand the role of evidence-based approaches in planning social-ecological urban transformations
2. Evaluate an urban design project to identify knowledge gaps in terms of social-ecological aspects
3. Propose improvements to a project based on an evidence-based design approach

Title: Sustainable Urbanism Vertiefung
Description:
CONTENT:
Re- Generation
rethink, redensify and repair urban areas

Climate change and scarcity of resources and natural habitats push us as urban designers to rethink, redensify and repair our urban areas. The focus of this lecture series is to decode what urban regeneration stands for regarding climate adaptation, sustainable mobility, and shifts in uses. How can we achieve a healthy balance of economic, environmental and social aspects? We will unfold the topic by asking the questions of ‘why’ we need regeneration, ‘what’ is needed and ‘who’ drives this transformation. We will explore the processes and actors of these transformations using practical case studies.

The submission for the Seminar will be a 3-page report focused on a case study which illustrates urban regeneration and the topics discussed in the lecture series.

Please read further explanations under: https://www.arc.ed.tum.de/land/lehre/aktuelles-semester/sustainable-urbanism-vertiefung/

Title: System- und Funktionale Sicherheit
Description:
CONTENT:
The content of this module is the analysis of systems with regard to risks originating from interacting with systems and possible system failures, as well as the targeted definition of measures to ensure system and functional safety. For this purpose, it is shown how systems can be described in terms of architecture and functions, suitably abstracted and differentiated from their environment. Furthermore, important terms of system and functional safety and basic systemic relationships are discussed. In order to be able to predict possible paths of system failure already during system development, procedures for hazard analysis and risk assessment are taught. These include FMECA, DRBFM, HAZOP, FTA, STPA, DFA.
The Syllabus is:
Part 1: System – and Functional Safety 101
-- Product Liability
-- Definitions and Context
-- Introduction to Functional Safety
-- Hazard Theory and Accident Models
-- Fault propagation
-- Fault Tolerance Techniques
-- Systematic Faults
-- Systematic Development & Management of Functional Safety  
-- System Definition
Part 2: Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment Methods
-- Failure Mode and Criticality Analysis (FMECA)
-- Design Review Based on Failure Modes (DRBFM)
-- Hazard and Operability Analysis (HAZOP)
-- Fault Tree Analysis (FTA)
-- System theoretical process analysis (STPA)
-- Dependent Failures and Dependent Failure Analysis

OBJECTIVES:
After participating in the module courses, students will be able to:
(1) Remember the theoretical basics of System- and Functional Safety 
(2) Describe sociotechnical systems (processes and products) such that they can be analyzed efficiently and effectively
(3) Understand accident models and apply these to potential accident scenarios
(4) Apply methods for hazard analysis and risk assessment 
(5) Describe, assess, and prioritize risks of sociotechnical systems 
(6) Apply risk reduction measures

Title: Systematische Entwicklung eines Curriculums zur Förderung von Kriterien der Quellenbewertung in Finanzthemen
Description:
CONTENT:
Konsument:innen treffen zunehmend finanzielle Entscheidungen im Internet – von Investitionen über Neobroker (Colesnic et al., 2024) bis hin zu E-Commerce (Eurostat, 2025). Entsprechend haben sich auch wissenschaftliche Konzeptionen von Finanzkompetenz erweitert und schließen inzwischen digitale Finanzentscheidungen mit ein (Choung et al., 2023; Europäische Union & OECD, 2022; Council for Economic Education & JumpStart, 2021). Dennoch ist die Forschung zu Quellenbewertung bei onlinebasierten Finanzentscheidungen bisher limitiert.

Ziel des Seminars ist die Entwicklung eines Curriculums zur Förderung von Kriterien der Quellenbewertung, bezogen auf Finanzthemen. Dazu werden zunächst theoretische Grundlagen zur Curriculum-Entwicklung, zur Evaluierung von Online-Quellen bzw. Desinformation und zu Trainingsansätzen eingeführt. In der Entwicklung des Curriculums sollen diese Theorieansätze implementiert und überprüft werden.

Mögliche Fragestellungen können dabei lauten:
- Was sind vertrauenswürdige und nicht vertrauenswürdige Informationsquellen zu Finanzthemen im Internet? Wer entscheidet das?
- Wie erstellt man systematisch ein Curriculum, damit dessen Wirkung wissenschaftlich untersucht werden kann?
- Welche didaktischen Methoden eignen sich, um Kriterien der Quellenbewertung in Finanzthemen wirksam zu vermitteln?

OBJECTIVES:
Die Studierenden sind in der Lage systematisch Curricula zu erstellen. Sie können eigene Forschungsfragen auf Grundlage der aktuellen Literatur ableiten und empirisch untersuchen. Die Studierenden sind in der Lage die Wirkungen eines Trainingsansatzes bzw. eines Curriculums möglichst objektiv messbar zu machen. Die Studierenden sind sich der Bedeutung von Finanzkompetenz bewusst und entwickeln Ideen, wie Informationen im Internet die Bedeutung von Finanzkompetenz verbreiten können. Sie entwickeln zudem ein Problembewusstsein für die Limitationen der aktuellen Messverfahren zur Finanzkompetenz und stellen Überlegungen an, wie diese in zukünftigen Forschungsvorhaben verbessert werden können.

Title: SystemC Laboratory
Description:
CONTENT:
The SystemC Laboratory provides an introduction into the system level language SystemC, which is used to model and simulate digital systems consisting of hardware and software components.The following main aspects are covered: Motivation for SystemC, usage in the design flow, application on different abstraction levels, language elements of SystemC. Special focus is given to modeling on transaction level (TLM). An application form the area of data communications (IP packet processing) is explored on a HW/SW platform to demonstrate the features and the practical use of SystemC. The exercises are done independently by each participant on Linux workstations using publicly available tools.

OBJECTIVES:
After participation the student will know the basic concepts of the system level langauge SystemC. He/she will have the ability to create and simulate SystemC models, and to use SystemC for the exploration/evaluation of different architecture alternatives.

                    Standard Approximations: Butterworth, Tschebyscheff, Cauer, and Bessel filters 
                    *Time Discrete Circuits and Systems:

Title: System-on-Chip Technologies
Description:
CONTENT:
This course provides basics, current trends and challenges in the development of digital system-on-chip (SoC). We start with the main steps for building arbitrary CMOS-based combinatorial logic and sequential digital data processing and control circuitry (e.g. Finite State Machines) and explaining their role and significance in the scope of key system-on-chip components: microprocessors, memories and interconnects. The microarchitectural structure and building blocks of processor elements (RISC cores), on-/off-chip memory technology (SRAM, DRAM, Flash), bus and point-to-point interconnect standards (Processor Local Bus, Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture, FIFO) as well as the design of communications specific arithmetic blocks (adder, multipliers, shift and comparators) will be introduced and analyzed. Finally, we will introduce main implementation methods for SoCs, such as FPGA, standard cell and full custom design, and discuss methods for low power design, which is vital for the development of SoCs in embedded systems.

OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this course is to impart a general understanding of the structure and operation of systems-on-chip. Main building blocks of a system-on-chip, e.g. processor, on-/off-chip memories, interconnect are introduced. Implementation methods as well as techniques for low power consumption are addressed.

Title: Systems Theory and Modeling
Description:
CONTENT:
The content is divided into four parts on modeling and systems theoretic analysis of dynamical systems. A "classical" focus is on linear finite-dimensional state space models in continuous time. In addition, concepts of energy-based modeling, structure-preserving integration, and the state representation of infinite-dimensional systems are introduced. These are foundations for a "modern" computational and control-oriented treatment of multi-domain physical systems.

In the first part we summarize modeling principles that lead to state space models in finite and infinite dimension in terms of ordinary and partial differential equations. For lumped parameter systems, we focus on energy- and network-based modeling. For distributed parameter systems, we restrict our attention to the one-dimensional case, and we give examples from structural mechanics and fluid- or thermodynamics that result from the application of variational principles and conservation laws. We emphasize the role of boundary variables as system in- and outputs.

In the second part, we introduce linearization of finite-dimensional state space models at an equilibrium and revisit the necessary concepts from linear algebra and differential equations to discuss the solutions of the linear state space models. Based thereon, and with the help of canoncial state transformations, we analyze their fundamental properties like stability, controllability and observability, which are relevant for system design and control.

The third part of the lecture is devoted to numerical integration of state space models. We focus on structure-preserving integration schemes, which enforce conservation properties, and which can be derived from discrete variational principles. We highlight their importance in terms of the power-consistent simulation of interconnected systems.

Finally, we give a brief introduction to the most fundamental notions from functional analysis for infinite-dimensional state space models, such as functional spaces, boundary conditions and domains of differential operators. Based on the 1D modeling examples from the first part, we illustrate these concepts, which are instrumental for the analyis and numerical approximation of infinite-dimensional systems.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module the students
- know important modeling principles for finite- and infinite-dimensional systems,
- are able to establish state space models for lumped parameter systems based on their element equations and the network structure of their interconnections,
- understand the roles of power and energy for the modeling of multi-physical systems,
- can determine equilibria of finite-dimensional systems, linearize state space models, and compute their solutions,
- can analyze system theoretic properties of linear systems and assess their implications for state feedback control,
- can reproduce important structure-preserving integration methods with their properties and apply them to initial value problems,
- are familiar with the presented one-dimensional examples of distributed parameter systems and
- understand basic concepts from functional analysis for inifinite-dimensional state space models.

Title: Systemtheorie in der Mechatronik - Vorlesung -
Description:
CONTENT:
In various engineering domains (e.g. mechanics, process control or electrical engineering) dynamical systems are studied. The purpose of systems theory is to describe the dynamic behavior of these systems by means of mathematical models and thus to abstract from the physical function of the system components. The advantage of this approach is that powerful analysis tools can be applied to study the system dynamics independent from the physical domain of the system. Therefore, at the beginning of this course the mathematical modeling of the systems as well as general properties of systems (classification, states etc.) and signals are presented. These methods are then used in examples to model different physical/technical systems. Besides the presentation of different model representations (block diagrams, differential equations, transfer functions, state space representations) different analysis methods for the evaluation of the stability, controllability and observability of dynamical systems are given. Moreover, useful mathematical tools applied in systems theory are integral transformations, i.e. the Laplace-, Fourier- and z-transforms, which are presented in the lecture pointing out their applicability for the analysis and synthesis of technical systems.   
 
Content:
    1. Introduction
    2. Signals and Systems
    3. System Modelling
    4. Linear Time Invariant Systems in the Time Domain
    5. Continous Time LTI-Systems in the Frequency Domain
    6. The z-transform
    7. Discrete Time LTI-Systems in the Frequency Domain
    8. Sample-Data Systems
    9. The Fourier-Transform

OBJECTIVES:
The participants should be able to perform the following tasks after having attended the lecture. 

- To evaluate signal and system properties,
- To model dynamical systems from different domains by means of state-space models,
- To analyze linear time-invariant continuous systems in the time domain,
- To analyze linear time-invariant continuous systems in the frequency domain,
- To apply the z-transform,
- To analyze linear time-invariant discrete-time systems in the time domain,
- To analyze linear time-invariant discrete-time systems in the frequency domain,
- To understand sampled systems,
- To apply the Fourier-transform.

Title: Tanzkunst entdecken – wahrnehmen, explorieren und kreative Gestaltungsprozesse erfahren
Description:
CONTENT:
In diesem Modul geht es zum einen um das Erforschen von Begegnungsmöglichkeiten des Körpers, der Haltung, der Kreativität, der Freude, des Ausdrucks, der Präsenz, und der Verbundenheit. 
Zum anderen geht es um das Erfahren der Vielfalt im Tanz (in den Erscheinungsformen im Tanz).

Studierende lernen, durch somatische Achtsamkeit mit sich und ihrer inneren und äußeren Welt in Kontakt zu treten. Das Beobachten von inneren und äußeren Prozessen ist eine kraftvolle Strategie die mentale Gesundheit zu stärken.

Unsere Bewegungen haben Auswirkungen auf unser Nervensystem, unsere Gehirnfunktion und unsere physische und psychische Gesundheit. Im Kurs findet eine Vernetzung zwischen Theorie und Praxis (Körper- und Bewegungsbildung) statt. Es entstehen neue Möglichkeiten, sich und seinen Körper wahrzunehmen, zu entdecken, zu spüren, sich im Bezug zu sich selbst und zu anderen wahrzunehmen, auszuprobieren und Körper und Geist durch Bewegung und Tanz in Einklang zu bringen. Der Prozess der Entfaltung von Kreativität und persönlicher Gestaltungsprozesse haben Vorrang gegenüber dem normierten, technikorientierten Bewegungslernen und dem produktorientierten Arbeiten.

OBJECTIVES:
Nach dem Absolvieren des Moduls können die Studierenden die grundlegenden Begriffe somatische Achtsamkeit, Kreativität, Improvisation, prozess- und produktorientiertes Arbeiten, sowie Begriffe aus dem Bereich Tanz erinnern und verstehen. Sie können eine Vielfalt an tanzpraktischen sowie theoretischen Grundlagen bzgl. tanzspezifischer Bewegungsformen realisieren (auch bzgl. unterschiedlicher Erscheinungsformen des Tanzes Hip Hop, zeitgenössischer Tanz, kreativer Tanz, Volkstanz/kulturelle Bildung). Des Weiteren haben sie Techniken und Methoden künstlerischer kreativer Prozesse und Reflexionsprozesse erfahren.

Title: Technical Acoustics and Noise Abatement
Description:
CONTENT:
Introduction: acoustics and noise control, principles of noise reduction, sound fields, level calculation. 
Origin and propagation of sound: simple oscillators, resonators, types of sound waves. 
Point sources, geometrical acoustics, absorption, room acoustics: room modes, statistical room acoustics, reverberation time, simulation methods, psychoacoustics of rooms. 
Airborne sound insulation, body-borne sound insulation. 
Sound measurement technology and sound impact: Measurement microphones, weighted sound level (A, C, D), time constants (I, F, S), equivalent sound pressure level Leq, sound analysis with absolute and relative constant bandwidth, sound of rotating machinery, third-octave band analysis, insertion loss. Calculation procedures: loudness level, loudness, psychoacoustic annoyance, Speech Interference level (SIL), Temporary and Permanent Threshold Shifts (TTS & PTS). 
Noise control according to (European) law, codes and norms: noise at workplaces, noise from machines, industrial noise (“TA Lärm”), noise from road traffic, railroads and aircrafts. 
Practical introduction to acoustic measurements: applicable norms, use of measurement equipment, conduction of measurements in the anechoic chamber, analysis of measurements, creation of measurement reports.

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of the module students will be able to apply their understanding of fundamental aspects in acoustics to basic problems of noise control and noise reduction, to analyze them and to propose solutions. Therefore, students will be able to independently conduct simple acoustical measurements and to calculate and asses sound propagation and effects of sound insulation. Furthermore, students can assess and evaluate means of technical acoustics on the basis of important codes and norms, measurement instructions, as well as legal limits.

Title: Technical Acoustics II
Description:
CONTENT:
The mechanisms for sound absorptions are explained starting with the plane wave approach leading to the description of porous media by means of the theory of porous media. The importance of the impedances of absorbers is illustrated.
The basics of the in acoustics widely used Statistical Energy Analysis (SEA) are introduced and illustrated by examples. The advantages and disadvantages of the method are explained. Finally some special topics of Technical Acoustics are addressed, applying the basics learned in the previous part:
Room acoustics, Railway induced vibrations and reradiated noise, Flow induced noise and the prediction of the effect of diffraction at barriers. For each of the problems common solution strategies and engineering approaches are explained and supported by calculation examples.

Thematic outline:
Statistical Energy Analysis (SEA)
- Introduction in the averaging procedures in the SEA
- Introduction in the treatment of coupled systems
- Overview over the limitations of the method
- Applications to examples like transmission loss of walls, sound field in rooms
Room acoustics
- Physical background: Description of rooms acoustics and properties
- Impulse response
- Spatial distribution of sound
- Room acoustical parameters
- Design of halls
Railway induced vibrations and reradiated noise
- Mechanisms
- Measures for the abatement
- Examples
Flow induced noise
- Lighthill analogy
- Selected examples of practical relevance
Propagation of sound in the open space: diffraction at barriers
- Solutions at the basis of the partial differential equations
- General phenomena

OBJECTIVES:
In the lecture an insight in various fields of applications related with acoustics is provided. Doing the exercises and homework the students learn to evaluate the applicability of these fields for practical problems. Based on the knowledge in structural dynamics the students shall become prepared for the work as a consulting engineer in technical acoustics. They shall be able to identify appropriate models and adequate solution techniques. They shall understand the limitations about the applied models and be able to abstract complex acoustical issues. This is explained at the basis of various examples.

Title: Technikphilosophie - Texte zur Einführung
Description:
CONTENT:
Technik ist überall. Zweifellos bestimmen technische Verfahren, Apparaturen und Organisationen unsere Lebenswelt mehr denn je. Im beschleunigenden Fortschritt zeigt sich der Mensch nicht nur als raffinierter Erfinder und kunstfertiger Schöpfer von nie Dagewesenem. Er ist nicht nur das Lebewesen, das in vielfältiger und komplexer Weise die Welt mittels Technik gestaltet, sondern das auch von dieser Welt der Technik wesentlich bestimmt wird. Die Frage nach dem, was die Technik ausmacht, ist zugleich die Frage nach dem Menschen. 

Die Technikphilosophie bedenkt, was Technik ist, was Techniker tun und welche Folgen ihr Tun hat. Im Seminar werden anhand einer Textauswahl Grundprobleme des Nachdenkens über Technik erarbeitet. 

Voraussetzung für den Erwerb von ECTS-Credits ist die aktive Teilnahme (an Diskussionen, Feedbackrunden etc.) und die Übernahme eines Referats.

OBJECTIVES:
Die Teilnehmer sind in der Lage, philosophische Probleme der Technik zu verstehen und Konzepte insbesondere auf den implizierten Technikbegriff hin zu analysieren. Sie verfügen über Erfahrung, ihren Standpunkt in kontroversen Diskussionen argumentativ zu vertreten, andere Positionen kritisch zu hinterfragen und komplexe Argumentationen nachzuvollziehen und zu vermitteln.

Title: Technische Dynamik
Description:
CONTENT:
The energy and variational principles of analytical mechanics have gone a long way since the axioms of Newton. Today they are found in the extremely successful test- and simulation software used in industry (e.g. experimental modal analysis, multi-body simulations, finite element codes, etc.). The aim of the lecture is to equip the student with the most important basics and “thought concepts” for understanding the different methods and classifying them. The student will therefore be well prepared for a more thorough study of the different application fields of mechanical theories and specialization areas. An ambitious goal!
Starting with the principle of virtual work, we will derive the Lagrange and Newton Euler equations step by step. These methods will allow us to derive the equations of motion for complex mechanical systems (automatically). By linearizing of the (often highly non-linear) equations we will be able to examine the stability of systems around an equilibrium position and introduce the fundamentally important concepts of modal analysis and model reduction. To conclude the lecture, we will derive analytical methods to solve the differential equations of motion for one-dimensional continua (bars and beams). The more generally applicable approximation methods such as Rayleigh-Ritz and the FEM, will be derived in the context of the virtual work principle and their convergence will be studied with the comparison to the analytical solutions. 
The lecture is structured as follows:
1)	Analytical dynamics
2)	Dynamics of rigid bodies
3)	Linearized equations of motion around an equilibrium position
4)	Stability of systems around an equilibrium position
5)	Vibration-modes and mode-superposition
6)	Linear dynamics of continuous systems and discretization

OBJECTIVES:
After completing the course successfully, students are able to 
•	translate real mechanical systems into abstract mechanical models regarding their mechanical properties and analyse kinematic and kinetic relationships, 
•	apply classical formalisms to derive the equations of motion of rigid and linear-elastic multibody systems
•	summarize the basic concepts of engineering dynamics and apply classic approximation methods to continuous linear-elastic systems
•	evaluate discrete linear equations of motion concerning stability and modal analysis
•	describe classical mechanical phenomena (e.g in rotating systems or in the frequency response of systems) and can classify the stability of nonlinear systems with the ‘linearized stability’.

Title: Technische Mechanik für Elektroingenieure
Description:
CONTENT:
Die Mechanik als Teilgebiet der Physik ist eine grundlegende Disziplin in den Ingenieurwissenschaften. Sie beschäftigt sich mit der Beschreibung und Vorherbestimmung der Verformung und Bewegung von Körpern und mit den damit einhergehenden Kräften. Inhalt der Vorlesung ist in der Statik die Berechnung von ruhenden, ebenen Tragwerken und die Beschreibung von Starrkörperbewegungen in der Kinematik. Mit Impuls- und Drallsatz sowie weiterführenden Methoden ist die Dynamik starrer Körper und Mehrkörpersysteme wichtiger Bestandteil. Schließlich wird auch die Elastostatik in Form von einfachen, ebenen Problemen, z.B. dem Bernoulli-Biegebalken sowie die Elastodynamik zur Berechnung von Eigenfrequenzen einfacher ebener Systeme, behandelt.

Die Studierenden verstehen die elementaren Zusammenhänge zwischen Kräften und Verformung und können vereinfachte Modelle wie den Bernoulli-Biegebalken hinsichtlich Verformung und Eigenfrequenzen analysieren. Sie können die Bewegungsgleichungen von einfachen Mehrkörpersystemen unter Anwendung verschiedener Methoden aufstellen. Die erlernten grundlegenden Methoden tragen zur Entwicklung der Fähigkeit bei, mechanische Fragestellungen in Ingenieurproblemen zu formulieren und sie selbstständig zu lösen.

Title: Technische Mechanik 3
Description:
CONTENT:
Die Mechanik als Teilgebiet der Physik ist eine grundlegende Disziplin in den Ingenieurwissenschaften. Sie beschäftigt sich mit der Beschreibung und Vorherbestimmung der Bewegungen von Körpern und mit den damit einhergehenden Kräften. In den Modulen Technische Mechanik 1 und 2 wurden zeitunabhängige Kräfte und Verfomungen betrachtet (ruhende Körper), die Technische Mechanik 3 handelt nun von zeitlich bewegten Körpern. Die Schwerpunkte sind: Kinematik und Kinetik einer Punktmasse, Relativkinematik, Stoßphänomene, 2D und 3D Kinematik und Kinetik des starren Körpers, Kreisel, Einführung in die analytische Mechanik, Schwingungen.

Title: Technische Thermodynamik
Description:
CONTENT:
The module introduces the fundamentals of thermodynamics and their application to technical processes. The following topics are treated: 
•	Basic concepts, terms and definitions (system; intensive, extensive and specific/molar properties; state and process variables; thermodynamic equilibria)
•	First law of thermodynamics: energy and energy forms
•	Ideal gases and changes of state
•	Second Law of Thermodynamics: entropy and dissipation
•	Thermodynamic properties of pure fluids (equation of state; state diagrams and tables)
•	Technically important cycle processes (power cycles; work consuming cycles) 
•	Humid air and processes with humid air

OBJECTIVES:
After successful participation in the module, students are able to describe the fundamental quantities, relationships and laws of thermodynamics. They are able to distinguish between state and process properties and know the meaning of different state properties such as enthalpy and entropy. They understand the relationship between different types of energy and are aware of the limits of energy conversion. The students are able to describe states and state changes of ideal gases and pure fluids using equations of state and/or state diagrams. 
Students are familiar with basic cycle processes (e.g. Carnot, Joule, Clausius-Rankine). They know the difference between power cycles and work consuming cycles and are able to depict them in thermodynamics-related diagrams. The students are able to formulate and solve energy, entropy and exergy balances as well as analyze and evaluate simplified cycle processes energetically and exergetically. 
They can describe the state of ideal gas mixtures and gas-vapor mixtures (e.g. “humid air”). The students are familiar with the quantities used to describe the state of humid air (e.g. humidity ratio, relative and absolute humidity) and are confident in using the Mollier diagram. They are able to describe important processes with “humid air” (e.g. adiabatic cooling and heating, humidification, mixing of streams of humid air) both mathematically and graphically.

Title: Technologie und Anwendung aktueller und zukünftiger Kernreaktoren
Description:
CONTENT:
The module extensively presents the plans for the use of nuclear energy for the future, concentrating not only on the new under-development reactor designs and new nuclear fuel cycles but also on advanced areas of application, such as ship propulsion, space exploration, production of hydrogen and fuels, desalination and compact nuclear reactors.

Main topics:
• The perspectives and use of nuclear energy in the future. 
• Advanced nuclear energy systems, current and near-term use. 
• Future developments of nuclear energy: the new reactor designs for the XXI century. 
• Nuclear reactors based on new nuclear fuel, e.g. thorium fuel cycle. 
• Fusion Reactors. 
• Further purposes of nuclear reactors: Ship and Rocket Propulsion, Space applications, Hydrogen production and water desalination.

OBJECTIVES:
The aim of the module is that the students receive an in-depth overview of the future nuclear reactor designs and can understand the differences and the reasons for them in comparison with the currently used designs. Additionally the students are able to learn about other uses of nuclear reactors different from the production of electricity.

There are three main objectives:
• The understanding of the different types of nuclear reactor designs proposed for the future.
• The understanding of the technological reasons for these designs by comparing them to the designs currently used today.
• The understanding of the technical aspects of the use of nuclear energy for other applications such a propulsion, research, production of hydrogen and synthetic fuels and water desalination.

The students, who successfully complete this module, are capable of critically evaluate a wide variety of nuclear reactor designs. They will be able to develop a scientifically and technologically based opinion on the use of nuclear energy, in the near and long term future.

Title: Technology & Society
Description:
CONTENT:
Science and technology are arguably among the most powerful forces of change in contemporary societies. Yet, their creation and governance has traditionally been left to a small group of experts - scientists in the lab, engineers deciding on a product design, or regulators in remote government agencies - with little role for those who have to live with their consequences. In most cases, the broader public has remained at the receiving end of scientific of technological change.

Over the past two decades, new approaches have emerged to govern the science-technology-society nexus more responsibly. Many scientists, engineers and policy makers no longer conceive of the relationship between science, technology and society as a one-way street - where knowledge simply needs to be handed down from experts to irrational lay people, or where technology is being developed and assessed outside society - but increasingly as an open, deliberative process that benefits from mutual engagement, democratic accountability, and participatory processes. Practices of engagement have increasingly moved 'upstream' in the innovation 'pipeline' such as to include political, social, and ethical concerns into the processes of science and engineering themselves.

Over the course of the semester, students acquire a range of concepts and analytic lenses from the fields of Science and Technology Studies (STS), Public Policy, Innovation Studies, Economics, Law, Media Studies, and Ethics that help them identify and deal with challenges of responsible science and technology. Cases encountered in class draw, among other things, on topics such as genetically modified organisms (GMOs), climate change, geoengineering, nuclear power, environmental policy, nanotechnology and chemical hazards. Students are encouraged to take and defend a normative position on the questions and cases they encounter during the class. Among the range of topics covered are:

- What do we mean by 'responsibility' in the context of science and technology?
- Which challenges do new science and technology pose for societies?
- How can we collectively govern and shape them to further social goals?
- How should scientists, policy makers, and citizens interact? What is the 'right' relationship between experts and 'the public'?
- What is public engagement and why should we care?
- How can we democratize the governance of science and technology?
- Why do scientific and technological progress regularly face resistances?
- How can we anticipate the consequences of innovation?
- How can we regulate science and technology?

OBJECTIVES:
Upon successful completion of this module, students are able to:
•	identify different ethical concepts of reasoning, their opportunities and limitations, from a theoretical and practical point of view
•	identify specific ethical conflicts in different fields of ethical reasoning and their transforming in practice
•	Classifying the conflicts between e.g. technological innovation vs. ethical acceptance in society (e.g. genetic engineering)
•	evaluate these conflicts and apply them to concrete practical examples.

Title: Technology, Nature, and Society
Description:
CONTENT:
We live in a time when technology is no longer experienced as a separate subsystem, but rather as a superstructure of society and life, permeating all of its existence.  Recent prevailing ideas of a strict separation between technology and nature or between the technical and the living have become obsolete. A variety of life processes are technically mediated (growth, propagation, movement, death, nutrition, etc.) and developments such as those of genetic engineering testify that nature itself has been transferred to a state of technical reproducibility. In this lecture series, the social negotiation processes of the relationship between technology, nature and society are analysed in a historical context and the consequences of the cultural specific demarcations for the scope of human action are discussed.

OBJECTIVES:
The course provides a critical introduction to the issues, methods and approaches in the history of technology and environmental history.

Title: Teilchenoszillationen
Description:
CONTENT:
Oscillations of particles are fascinating quantum-mechanical phenomenons. In October 2015 the discovery of neutrino oscillations was honoured by the Nobel price for physics. It is th first direct and experimental hint for physics beyond the standard model. Also the discovery of oscillation of neutral kaons lead to new insights of very fundamental questions. In this case it was the inititive for the discovery of CP-violation in weak interaction, which is one of the three Sacharov-conditions for explaining the assymmetry between matter and antimatter in the universe.

In detail we will discuss the following topics:

- Particle- antiparticle oscillations of neutral mesons. Fundamental experiments and theoretical description. Link to CP-violation in the quark system.

- Neutrinooscillations. Fundamental experiments and theoretical description. Conditions for coherence. Matter effects of solar neutrinos. Open questions and new ideas.

- Search for sterile neutrinos. Theoretical models and experimental status. Link to the question of dark matter in the universe

OBJECTIVES:
After successful completion of the module the students are able to:

- understand the basical quantummechanical descriptions which lead to the phenomenon of particle oscillations

- understand common aspects but also differences betwenn oscillations of hadrons (consisting of quark-antiquark systems)

- differentiate (pros and cons) between several experimental approaches to neutrino oscillations.

The module should motivate students to think deeper about open problems in particle physics and finally act as a bridge towards a successful MSc-thesis in this field of physics.

Title: Tensor calculus and balance principles
Description:
CONTENT:
The module “Fluid mechanic” is made up by the two elements „Tensor calculus and balance principles“ and “Fluid mechanics basics”. Since the first element also provides some foundations for the parallel course “Engineering thermodynamics” it is taught as compact course of 2-3 weeks duration at the begin of the term.
This module element “Tensor calculus and balance equations” deals with the algebra and the analysis of vectors and tensors in Cartesian description. The structure of balance equations is presented. Different forms of conservation laws are derived using Reynolds transport theorem and the divergence (Gauss) theorem.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of this module element “Tensor calculus and balance equations” students are able to describe and analyse the behaviour of field quantities in terms of balance equations (conservation laws) in differential and integral form using vector/tensor notation in symbolic and indicial notation.

Title: Tensor Network Methods
Description:
CONTENT:
Tensors emerge from discretization of multivariate functions – one can simply view the grid values of a function of N variables as coefficients of a tensor with N indices. Tensor network methods are recent methods for the efficient approximation of high-dimensional functions, that is, large-N tensors. These methods have found tremendous applications in many fields (for instance: physical sciences; machine learning; high-dimensional partial differential equations). A main focus of the course is a key instance of these methods, the tensor train approximation. It can be viewed as a generalization to large-N tensors of singular value approximation for matrices, that is, singular value decomposition combined with thresholded discarding of small singular values. The course begins by explaining why traditional (canonical polyadic) low-rank approximation of tensors is numerically unstable and analytically ill-posed for N bigger than 2. We then discuss the TT method and cover its theoretical foundations, numerical algorithms, and carefully selected applications. Along the way, I will point out interesting and litle-known connections of the subject to other fields (for instance, you will learn that Strassen's theorem on the complexity of matrix multiplication is a beautiful application of tensor methods).

OBJECTIVES:
You will have understood cornerstone concepts and results such as CP rank and TT rank of a tensor,  the border rank problem for CP approximation, the structure of the manifold of TT states and its tangent space, and the DMRG algorithm. You have gained insight into some applications outside mathematics, and can analyse and simulate simple multivariate problems using tensor network methods.

Title: Testing Digital Circuits
Description:
CONTENT:
Principles of testing digital circuits; fault models and test quality; functional and structural test generation; fault simulation; complexity theory; design for test (passive, active test methods); memory test; test standards; miscellaneous topics (Iddq test, analog test, test pattern compression, yield management);

In detail:

The manufacturing process of integrated circuits introduces a large variety of physical defects. In order to prevent the delivery of failing silicon devices to the customer, the correct function of delivered integrated circuits has to be guaranteed by testing all devices after they have been fabricated.

Testing integrated circuits is one of the core competencies of a semiconductor company. It represents a significant factor in costs and quality. Therefore, testing is considered as an outstanding part of the entire design and manufacturing process of ICs.

Furthermore, testing is a domain-crossing topic: The test engineer within a semiconductor company requires a broad expertise covering circuit and system design, circuit simulation and design verification, and physical design.

One of the main challenges in testing is costs which have drastically increased over the past years. The access to circuit internal transistors and nodes has to be accomplished by a limited number of external pins. This is increasingly difficult due to the continuous shrinking of device structures.

This lecture conveys:
* The basic idea of testing.
* Relevant failure mechanisms of integrated circuits and the common fault models.
* The complexity problem of testing and its resulting limitations.
* Methods for test pattern generation (e.g. fault simulation and automatic test generation).
* Fundamental measures for designing integrated circuits in order to raise their testability (Design-for-Testability).
* Techniques for insertion of built-in self-test (BIST) in integrated circuits.
* Techniques for memory testing.

OBJECTIVES:
At the end of the module students know about the following topics and are able to employ this knowledge to define and evaluate test solutions for digital ICs and systems:
- Definition of testing and the difference to verification 
- Fundamentals of testing: fault models, fault detection, redundant faults, fault coverage
- Methods for test generation: Boolean differences, D-algorithm, fault simulation
- Analysis of test complexity with the help of complexity theory
- Principles of passive test methods: Ad-hoc measures, scan path / Principles of active test methods: BIST
- Overview over memory fault models and memory test algorithms.
- Outline of test standards (IEEE boundary scan test) and additional topics like IDDQ testing, analog testing, fault analysis.
Skills: ['Testing digital circuits', 'FPGA design', 'Hardware-software interfacing', 'Design for test', 'Verilog']
